sources.title: Simon Høiberg's 3-stage growth system for getting a bootstrapped SaaS to its first 1,000 users
sources.originalTitle: How to Get Your First 1.000 Customers & Early Users for your B2B SaaS in 2024, With Simon Høiberg
sources.summary: Simon walks through the user growth system he used across FeedHive, LinkDrip and Eightbase. Stage 1 is outbound plus referrals for the first ~100 users, stage 2 is a long content grind, and stage 3 adds ads and affiliates once unit economics are known. He also covers staying bootstrapped and delegating tasks, not areas.

principles.text: Build a minimum lovable product with a wow effect, then shape it with early users instead of trying to sell a finished product.
principles.quote: You go out, and then you try to acquire users for your product instead of trying to build a product for your users.

principles.text: For the first 5-25 users, reach out personally and give the product away free for life, even pay them if friction is high.
principles.quote: I would recommend simply giving away a lifetime for free on this product.

principles.text: Giving early users free access is not devaluing your product; it values how important they are.
principles.quote: I don't think you're devaluing your product. I think you are accurately valuing how important these first users are because they are fundamental to the success of your product.

principles.text: Put early adopters in a small community, take their feedback, and turn them into ambassadors with discount codes to bring in the next users.
principles.quote: You're going to try to get the very first initial users to become ambassadors, and you're going to try to have them help bring in new users.

principles.text: Stage 2 is a long, demotivating incoming content grind (blogs, YouTube, social) that compounds; budget a year or two to reach the first ~1,000 paying users.
principles.quote: If you allocate maybe a year, maybe even 2 years on just creating awareness organically through content, you should be able to get I would say somewhere between 200, 300, 500, maybe even the first 1,000 paying users in this way.

principles.text: Only scale with ads and affiliates once you know lifetime value; keep acquisition cost below it, and practice ads cheaply earlier.
principles.quote: You obviously want to make sure that the cost of acquisition for one user when running ads is less than the average lifetime value that you get for one user.

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg built FeedHive to ~$400K ARR: audience first, users shape the MVP, ads, delegation
sources.originalTitle: Interviewing Simon Høiberg about Lessons from His Journey to $400K ARR (episode 262)
sources.summary: Simon explains how his first SaaS failed with zero paying users, how giving away value on Twitter built the audience that launched FeedHive, and how 25 early users shaped its MVP. He also covers landing pages, paid ads creatives, when to hire, and documenting processes.

principles.text: Build the audience by sharing value for free, with no ask attached; it only worked once he stopped caring what he got back.
principles.quote: I'm gonna just Share value and not gonna care anything about what I will get out of it right right now I'm just gonna share value for free

principles.text: Let early users define the MVP: get a group in first, then listen to what they want to see first.
principles.quote: get the people in there first and then just listen closely to what what they would want to see first

principles.text: Tailor landing pages to market maturity: in a known category stress differentiating features; in an unfamiliar one lead with outcomes.
principles.quote: it's better to focus more on the things that make you stand out so that could for instance be a calendar view or the individual features that you have that other tools similar tools don't have

principles.text: Paid ads scale acquisition, but the creative is the part on you; platforms handle targeting. Expect to burn money learning.
principles.quote: it all comes down to the creatives and that is as an Advertiser that's the part that's on you you need to make killer ads ads that almost look like great content in itself

principles.text: Do a job yourself before hiring for it; the best thing to delegate is work you could already do but want the time back.
principles.quote: the best thing to delegate is things that you could already do but you just want to buy yourself time

principles.text: Turn every task into reusable building blocks and documented processes so each new output gets faster.
principles.quote: is there at least one or two things from this that I can make into more um general purpose components or building blocks that I can use for a later project

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg built a 30K Twitter audience before launching FeedHive and grew YouTube
sources.originalTitle: How to grow on social media the right way • @SimonHoiberg from FeedHive
sources.summary: Simon explains why he built an audience before his second SaaS by giving pure value for six months with no asks. He covers validating FeedHive with 25 free beta users, a multi-step Facebook ads funnel, YouTube title/thumbnail testing, paid Instagram shoutouts, and monetizing a niche YouTube channel.

principles.text: Build an audience before launching; launching to no audience means yelling into the void.
principles.quote: the worst feeling from that experience was this feeling of yelling out into the void and having everything completely drown

principles.text: Give pure value for months without asking for anything; it makes you taken seriously at launch.
principles.quote: pushing out content for a long long time i actually did this for six months without asking for anything in return this allowed me to be taken seriously once i launched FeedHive

principles.text: Validate with a small group of engaged users who co-build the product in a group chat.
principles.quote: i actually started building an mvp just for these 25 people and we i invited them to to start using the platform already after two weeks of building

principles.text: If charging upfront, only promise what you can realistically build; landing pages tend to over-promise.
principles.quote: people tend to completely over promise on what they're gonna build so they build a landing page and you will have all kinds of insane features

principles.text: Engage on bigger accounts by adding real value, never shameless plugs.
principles.quote: if you can truly add value to their post without kind of stealing their thunder or trying to steal their traffic not only will it be appreciated

principles.text: Test title and thumbnail before scripting a video; discard ideas that fail a one-second glance test.
principles.quote: i do with the thumbnail and title first before scripting and if i can't make that work either i just struggle with getting the the right thumbnail and the right title in place for this idea um i i don't go on from there

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg built a four-product SaaS portfolio and bundled it into a lifetime deal
sources.originalTitle: LaunchDay #2 – Simon Høiberg – FounderStack
sources.summary: Simon Høiberg recounts quitting freelancing for FeedHive, burning $50K on a premature team, surviving the X API shutdown, and expanding into LinkDrip, TinyKiwi and Abbase. He explains pre-selling lifetime deals to fund development and how he prices the FounderStack bundle so it stays profitable.

principles.text: Pre-sell a lifetime deal to validate a new product and fund its build before writing code.
principles.quote: And within a month or so, I think we had made around $75,000 just from pre-saling this.

principles.text: Build your second product from existing users' requests, using the audience you already have as distribution.
principles.quote: I started building LinkDrip simply out of people requesting it.

principles.text: Start with one product and let demand pull you into more; a portfolio is not the default path for newcomers.
principles.quote: I would I would advise everyone to start building one product first and then let the demand pull you from there.

principles.text: Don't overhire on confidence: building a full team before traction cost $50K and forced layoffs.
principles.quote: I was completely overconfident in what I could pull off. This this whole thing took way way way longer than I had thought.

principles.text: Make lifetime deals safe by bundling enough value to set a high price and checking that server costs take decades to exceed revenue.
principles.quote: It will it will take the average user decades before they ever become a losing investment for us.

principles.text: Cap variable AI costs in lifetime deals with monthly credits, then require users to bring their own API key.
principles.quote: We offer some AI credits for all users every month. That's part of the deal. But after that, they need to bring their own uh API key from OpenAI if they want to continue using it.

sources.title: SaaS lifetime deals: what AppSumo, pre-sales and LTDs really do for a bootstrapped SaaS
sources.originalTitle: SaaS Lifetime Deals - Is It Worth It?! (#2)
sources.summary: Simon Høiberg draws on his experience launching FeedHive on AppSumo ($300K in two months), pre-selling LinkDrip lifetime deals to his own audience ($100K+), and running TinyKiwi as an ongoing LTD. He covers the real upsides (distribution, feedback, word of mouth), the risks (operating cost, support friction) and when LTDs make sense.

principles.text: AppSumo's revenue split is fair because you are buying distribution you could not build yourself.
principles.quote: a distribution Channel this size and as powerful as the one of appsumo is so extremely valuable it is much more worth than your product

principles.text: Only run LTDs if your per-user operating cost is low; heavy AI or compute costs make one-time payments dangerous.
principles.quote: if you're running a product that's very heavy on AI using open AI apis or you're using any type of service that is really computationally expensive to run you should reconsider how the finances of this will work

principles.text: Lifetime users churn too, so you are not locked into supporting them forever.
principles.quote: lifetime users turn to for various reasons they either grow out of your tool they go on to something new they might they might love it so much that they want to upgrade

principles.text: LTD relationships create friction both ways: entitled buyers, and founders with less incentive to support them. Be fair and minimize that friction.
principles.quote: the moment the lifetime user has paid you there is Les less incentive for you to give them the same Sublime support experience than with a monthly payer because they can't churn

principles.text: The biggest LTD benefit is users and word of mouth, not the upfront cash.
principles.quote: the getting users on board getting Word of Mouth um and getting the promotion is the biggest upside that's bigger than the money that you get up front

principles.text: Pre-selling LTDs to your own audience can validate a product fast, but it requires an existing audience.
principles.quote: this was actually a part of my product validation I wanted to see if this was something of interest to people so at this point I had only spent I think around eight hours creating a landing page

sources.title: Paid ads for bootstrapped SaaS: how Simon Høiberg tests creatives and uses engagement to cut costs
sources.originalTitle: The Truth About Running Paid Ads for Your SaaS (#4)
sources.summary: Simon Høiberg explains why paid ads work for indie SaaS, using his best-performing Facebook ad for Aidbase as the example. Creative is the main lever, emotion and engagement make Facebook's auction cheaper, and the safe path is cheap multi-round testing before any scaling.

principles.text: Paid ads are a very effective channel for bootstrapped and indie products; don't be intimidated by big-brand ad budgets.
principles.quote: my answer to that would be 100% yes it is a very very effective marketing channel uh for promoting bootstrapped and Indie products at 100%

principles.text: On Facebook, Instagram and YouTube, targeting is automated, so your job is creating great creatives. Big companies' generic ads are easy to beat.
principles.quote: your only job to be successful with that is creating great creatives

principles.text: Emotional ads that earn engagement, even angry comments, are rewarded by the auction, so you reach more people for less money.
principles.quote: it's very desirable to have an ad that gets a lot of Engagement because Facebook will reward you for that

principles.text: Start with a small budget and test text and image combinations in rounds. Take the winning angle into the next round, and repeat for a few months.
principles.quote: you can run one ad for $10 a day you can do that for four five days maybe and then you're going to look at the numbers

principles.text: Don't scale on a handful of conversions. Premature scaling burns money, so build intuition cheaply first.
principles.quote: as soon as I saw like five conversions is like oh I have a winning creative this is going to be brilliant scale scale scale

principles.text: Make YouTube video ads native to the platform: a YouTube-style video with a short product pitch, not a TV-commercial-style ad.
principles.quote: really good performing YouTube ads are honestly videos that look like a YouTube video

sources.title: Simon Høiberg on why SEO blogging rarely moves the needle for a new SaaS, plus pricing and churn lessons
sources.originalTitle: Should You Be Doing SEO in 2024? (#3)
sources.summary: Simon debates co-host Kyle on whether SEO and blogging are worth it for a new SaaS in 2024. He argues it's rarely needle-moving, citing weak blog conversions and unstable rankings. He also shares lessons on pricing-plan psychology, churn-feature requests and leaning on unfair advantages.

principles.text: A new SaaS betting on Google blogging as its main channel is unlikely to see needle-moving results unless it's an outlier.
principles.quote: if you are going to launch a new SAS product in 2024 and you sit down and say my main acquisition channel is going to be me optimizing my ranking on Google to show up and people search I would say that unless you're in the outlier group you're probably not going to do anything needle moving

principles.text: Top blog rankings can bring little traffic and few conversions; measure conversions per article, not just rank.
principles.quote: when I count the number of clicks we're actually getting to that article and then tracking which conversions we got from that specific articles it's very very little

principles.text: Ranking on page one is fragile: competitors overtake you, so SEO isn't a set-and-forget asset.
principles.quote: once we get to get to page one on something it is incredibly difficult to staying there for a longer period of time

principles.text: Start from your unfair advantages and lean on the channel you already have expertise in.
principles.quote: if there's one thing that you should always consider when you go out and build something new and launch something new is where's my unfair advantages

principles.text: Use pricing psychology: an expensive anchor or a cheap, low-limit plan makes the middle plan look attractive.
principles.quote: you can have an anchor in terms of the most expensive price make the middle plan look less pricey you can also have a sort of a reverse anchor where you have something very cheap but also very low limits

principles.text: Churn feedback is unreliable: the most-requested feature may not reduce churn, while small nice-to-haves can.
principles.quote: we have had some features also on FeedHive that people kept asking for and it was the same thing this was the main reason people were churning and when we finally delivered it it changed nothing

sources.title: Simon Høiberg on taking a SaaS to $1M ARR: paywalls, free-plan widget distribution and bootstrapped growth
sources.originalTitle: Taking a SaaS to $1M ARR (#1)
sources.summary: First episode of Zero To Million SaaS. Simon explains why a $1M ARR SaaS is the right bootstrapper target, why SaaS is worth the risk, and how he is growing his new AI support tool 8base: a free plan with a branded chat widget as a distribution and backlink engine, funded at a loss, versus the hard-paywall trials that grew his other products faster.

principles.text: Aim for a $1M ARR SaaS, not a billion-dollar headline; it's achievable for normal bootstrappers.
principles.quote: forget all the big billion dollar headlines and just build a million dollar sass it's possible like we can do it many people can do it today

principles.text: A card-required, opt-out trial behind a paywall grew his products much faster than freemium.
principles.quote: as soon as we put everything behind a pay wall um our growth just increased much much much faster

principles.text: Use a free plan with a branded embedded widget as distribution; the priority is getting the widget on as many sites as possible.
principles.quote: my main goal is actually to get these chat widgets out on as many websites as possible

principles.text: Widgets built without iframes pass as normal backlinks, so every installed widget also helps SEO.
principles.quote: whenever people put this chat on their website it's a backlink

principles.text: A bootstrapper can deliberately run at a loss to fund a growth loop rather than chase early profitability.
principles.quote: happy to invest in getting these widget out on as many websites as absolutely possible

principles.text: A launch spike fades after churn; the real work is building a consistent, continuous growth engine.
principles.quote: growth has flattened a little bit so we're now working on how to get this growth engine running a little bit more consistently

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg runs four SaaS products with 3 people using an AI agent team
sources.originalTitle: AI Just Made Bootstrapping Totally Unfair
sources.summary: Simon explains how he cut his team from 11 to 3 by delegating video production, coding, DevOps, paid ads, outreach and support to AI agents. The key is a strong harness: scripts, QA gates, narrow permissions, spending limits and human approval for big decisions. He argues a small AI-native team is now an advantage over a large one.

principles.text: A small, highly efficient AI-native team is now a bigger opportunity than a large team, which is a disadvantage.
principles.quote: Not only do you not need a large team anymore, but I think it's straight up a disadvantage. Running a highly efficient small AI native team is the biggest business opportunity you get right now.

principles.text: Keep the ideas and opinions human. Let AI structure and produce, not invent, or you get generic slop.
principles.quote: if you let it invent the ideas, you get the same generic AI slop everyone is super tired of.

principles.text: Script first, then record against the script. The script becomes a map the editing agent can match to transcripts and build visuals against.
principles.quote: Once the recording matches the script, the script becomes a map for the whole production.

principles.text: AI coding only works with a harness: QA tests, guardrails and agent-friendly code structure. Spraying code with AI is not leverage.
principles.quote: don't fool yourself into thinking that just spraying code with AI is now some big leverage.

principles.text: Give ad agents full business context and real outcome events (trial, purchase, usage), not just creative generation, or platforms optimize for weak signals.
principles.quote: If you optimize for a weak signal, Meta will happily find thousands of people who produce more of that weak signal.

principles.text: Do outreach as slow, researched, one-at-a-time emails with hard send limits and approvals; the research becomes the message.
principles.quote: If you send out highquality personalized emails to carefully vetted, highquality leads, you don't have to blast and spam everyone.

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg builds an AI agent harness in five layers so model choice stops mattering
sources.originalTitle: The AI System Behind My 7-Figure Business (Full Agency OS Breakdown)
sources.summary: Simon explains that AI agent quality depends on the harness around the model, not the model itself. He walks through five layers he uses across his SaaS products and YouTube channel: eval classifiers, schema contracts, purpose-built tools, deterministic workflows, and failure replay.

principles.text: The harness around an agent matters more than the model; it owns your company's standard.
principles.quote: whenever you see companies doing really well with AI, it's almost never because of the model and always because of the quality of the harness.

principles.text: Split doing the work from judging it: use separate eval classifiers that return a narrow verdict with reasons.
principles.quote: The model understands the standard. It just has a hard time doing the job, following every instructions, and judging the result at the same time. So, we split that into separate jobs.

principles.text: Use deterministic code checks for objective rules and AI classifiers only where taste or judgment is needed.
principles.quote: The first check is a good example of a deterministic eval. It uses a blacklist for phrases like this is the part where and simple regular expressions to catch writing patterns like it's not X, it's Y. No AI is needed for that check.

principles.text: Define 'done' with a schema contract so agents can't invent their own definition of finished work.
principles.quote: The agent does not get to invent its own definition of done.

principles.text: Give each agent least-privilege, purpose-built tools; make dangerous actions impossible rather than prompting against them.
principles.quote: The system prompt isn't our security boundary. The capability simply isn't available.

principles.text: Save real failures as permanent regression tests and replay them before changing any model, rather than trusting public benchmarks.
principles.quote: Public benchmarks can tell me whether a model looks impressive on somebody else's test, but before I change a model, I care more about our own failure library.

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg uses AI agents to audit ICP, churn and new SaaS ideas
sources.originalTitle: I Gave AI My SaaS Data. It Found a Huge Positioning Mistake
sources.summary: Simon argues AI can now handle founder judgment if given real business data. He runs three audits: finding the real ICP from billing, database and domain data; reconstructing churn by joining cancellation feedback, support history and product usage; and mining reviews and communities for repeated buyer pain that fits his portfolio. Each audit ends in a prepared experiment.

principles.text: Derive your real ICP from payment, product usage and customer context data, not from a brainstormed persona.
principles.quote: for this to work, the agent needs access to the places where your real customer signals already exist. It starts with the payment signal.

principles.text: Founders review data in pieces; AI can connect payments, behavior and context at once and show which customers look alike.
principles.quote: AI is much better at looking at all of it at once. It can connect the payment signal, the product behavior, and the customer context

principles.text: Messy analytics don't block the audit; read-only access to the raw database is enough to find patterns.
principles.quote: If the agent has read-only access to the raw database, it can still dig through tables, run queries, and make sense of a lot of the messy product data.

principles.text: Turn every audit finding into an experiment: audit, hypothesis, experiment, validation, with landing page, ad angles and metrics.
principles.quote: Audit, hypothesis, experiment, validation. All done by my AI agents.

principles.text: Cancellation reasons are a thin version of the truth; rebuild the churn journey and split bad-fit customers from good-fit ones who failed.
principles.quote: separate the customers who were probably never a good fit from the customers who should have succeeded but didn't. Because those are completely different problems.

principles.text: Find new SaaS ideas from repeated buyer pain in reviews and communities, filtered by fit with the customers and products you already have.
principles.quote: the best idea is not always the biggest market. Sometimes the best idea is the one that you can test the fastest because you already have an unfair advantage around it.

sources.title: Why AI killed micro SaaS: own your stack and distribution (the drop shipping parallel)
sources.originalTitle: We’re Done. AI Killed Micro SaaS.
sources.summary: Simon argues micro SaaS is following the drop shipping path: founders renting 95% of their operation (hosting, database, AI, payments, traffic) get squeezed as AI makes software cheap to copy. Survivors own their infrastructure, data and audience. He shares his own response: a one-time-purchase bundle (FounderStack), self-hostable or open-source products, and eventually owned hardware.

principles.text: A business built almost entirely on rented services gets squeezed, because every layer gets paid before the founder does.
principles.quote: Meanwhile, every rented layer still gets paid before the founder does.

principles.text: Easy-to-start businesses attract everyone, and suppliers and platforms then slowly take the margin until nothing is left.
principles.quote: But easy businesses attract everyone. Then the suppliers, platforms, and advertisers slowly take the margin until there's nothing left.

principles.text: To survive, own your product stack: self-host, control data and configuration, and make every key dependency replaceable.
principles.quote: self-host the product, control the data and configuration, understand the infrastructure and make every important dependency replaceable.

principles.text: Own your distribution through social audiences and an email list you control; use ads to amplify it, not as your only channel.
principles.quote: Ads should amplify that distribution instead of being the only way you can reach a customer.

principles.text: Offer a one-time-purchase bundle next to subscriptions; efficient infrastructure makes it viable without monthly payments from every customer.
principles.quote: I've spent a lot of time making our infrastructure super efficient so that we can maintain these products without every customer paying us every month.

principles.text: Lifetime deals can work when the software is serious and keeps improving, so buyers genuinely own it rather than lease it forever.
principles.quote: My goal with FounderStack is serious software that we keep improving while the people who buy it get to own it instead of leasing it forever.

sources.title: Can you replace your team with AI? Three filters (human vs process-centric, leader vs operator, RIP)
sources.originalTitle: Can you ACTUALLY replace your team with AI? (Real talk)
sources.summary: Simon cut his team from 11 to 3 using AI while revenue and margins rose, but argues it only works for process-centric companies run by operator-type founders. He gives three checkpoints and the RIP model (Repetitive, Predictable, Isolated) to decide which tasks to hand to AI.

principles.text: AI replacement only works for process-centric businesses; human-centric, culture-driven ones can augment but not replace people.
principles.quote: if you are running a high culture human first organization you cannot replace your team. You can augment them but you cannot replace them.

principles.text: Founders who are operators (systems, data, logic) suit an AI workforce; natural leaders who run on empathy and motivation will struggle to manage AI.
principles.quote: If you are an operator, AI is your dream employee. Because AI doesn't need empathy. It needs logic. It doesn't need motivation. It needs instructions.

principles.text: Process-centric companies with SOPs, checklists, and clear task requirements transition to AI easily because agents thrive on clear instructions.
principles.quote: an AI agent loves a processcentric environment. It loves clear instructions. It loves SOPs. It loves checklists.

principles.text: Use the RIP model: replace a task only if it is Repetitive, Predictable, and Isolated; if it misses one, keep a human in the loop.
principles.quote: If a role handles tasks that are repetitive, predictable, and isolated, you can replace it today. If it misses even one of these, you have to at the very least loop in a human as a part of that workflow.

principles.text: The 'Isolated' criterion is where most AI implementations fail: tasks needing tribal knowledge or hidden dependencies will make AI break things.
principles.quote: Can the task be done in a vacuum or does it require tribal knowledge?

principles.text: Think in terms of replacing tasks, not people, and treat AI as a machine following strict instructions rather than a magic employee.
principles.quote: instead of thinking about replacing people, think about replacing tasks and apply the RIP model to figure out which ones.

sources.title: Best AI businesses to start in 2026: boring, paid-for problems, not SaaS
sources.originalTitle: The Best AI Businesses to Start in 2026 (SaaS Isn’t One)
sources.summary: Simon argues SaaS is no longer the main AI opportunity and lists five practical businesses built around problems companies already pay for: AI implementation, audience building, agent security auditing, AI-powered service companies, and AI workshops. The through-line: pick a market you understand, find one thing they already spend money on, and use AI to deliver it faster or cheaper.

principles.text: Build around problems companies already spend money on, not prestigious-looking AI ideas.
principles.quote: They're built around problems companies already spend money on.

principles.text: Become an AI implementation partner: pick an industry, find one expensive repeated workflow, make AI work inside the company.
principles.quote: Pick an industry, find one expensive workflow people repeat every day, and become the person who makes AI work inside the company.

principles.text: Charge for implementation, then keep a monthly retainer for testing and maintenance to create recurring revenue.
principles.quote: You charge for the implementation, then keep a monthly agreement for testing and maintenance.

principles.text: AI startups have money but need distribution, so an AI-focused audience monetizes through brand deals.
principles.quote: The companies building those tools need attention from exactly those people. So, they pay creators for brand deals.

principles.text: Creators can turn brand-deal relationships into early angel investments by offering to invest instead of taking a sponsor fee.
principles.quote: They wanted my rate for a 90-second slot in a video and I flipped it around. I said, why don't I give you my money instead?

principles.text: Sell AI-amplified services clients already buy; they care about the result, not the AI behind it.
principles.quote: Pick a valuable service you already understand, use AI to amplify your work and charge for the result.

sources.title: Why Simon Høiberg moved 80% of his SaaS off AWS to Hetzner bare metal
sources.originalTitle: I'm leaving the cloud! (...and why you probably should too)
sources.summary: Simon moved most of his five-product SaaS portfolio from AWS serverless to three Hetzner dedicated servers running Kubernetes, Postgres and Redis. He cut infra costs from about $7,800 to under $2,000 per month, avoided vendor lock-in, and made lifetime deals safer by keeping running costs fixed. He also explains what he kept on AWS and who should or shouldn't self-host.

principles.text: Usage-based cloud costs climb as users grow; fixed-cost dedicated servers cap them and the savings keep compounding.
principles.quote: At the beginning of 2025, I would pay AWS $7,800 per month on average to run my SaaS products. Because I pay per usage with AWS, this average is slowly climbing month after month as my user base grows.

principles.text: Self-hosting has a one-time learning cost, not a recurring one; judge the ROI on savings that keep growing.
principles.quote: unless you're already expert on this, there's obviously going to be an upfront cost in terms of time spent. But that upfront cost is fixed.

principles.text: Avoid vendor lock-in: if a provider raises prices or drops you, a rushed migration can sink the business.
principles.quote: If AWS were to raise their prices or decide they don't want you as a customer anymore, well, you're cooked. Your products just stop running, and migrating isn't something you can do quickly.

principles.text: Remove as many hard vendor dependencies as you can, and design so the product can run on any host.
principles.quote: I absolutely would recommend removing as many hard dependencies on specific vendors as you possibly can.

principles.text: Lifetime deals are safer to offer when ongoing costs are fixed rather than rising with user count.
principles.quote: if you can at least make those ongoing cost fixed instead of gradually rising as the number of users goes up, it's obviously going to be much easier and much less risky to do proper financial planning when offering a deal like this.

principles.text: Make products self-hostable so lifetime access is a credible guarantee for buyers.
principles.quote: I'm working on making all of my products fully self-hostable. So, everyone who bought lifetime access to my software can, in the unlikely event that my business won't be able to host it, simply install it on their own servers and host it themselves.

sources.title: Simon Høiberg's SaaS user growth roadmap: from first 5 users to 1,000+
sources.originalTitle: My SaaS User Growth System: Get Your First 100 - 1,000+ Users
sources.summary: Simon lays out a three-stage roadmap for acquiring SaaS users. Each stage uses a different acquisition model (method, channel, cost): manual outreach and referrals for the first 100, content and building in public up to 1,000, then ads and affiliates to scale or automate.

principles.text: Design every acquisition as a model: method, channel and cost, then match it to your SaaS stage.
principles.quote: every user acquisition has the following a method a channel and the cost and depending on the type of Acquisitions we're going for we need to plan these out

principles.text: Get your first 5 users by personally reaching out to your network with free accounts in exchange for feedback.
principles.quote: You will offer them a completely free account for live and all you will ask for in return is their feedback

principles.text: Serve the first users so well they become advocates, then use referral links to reach 100 users.
principles.quote: what we're trying to do here is to make these users more than just users we're turning them into Advocates

principles.text: Referrals usually don't need payouts; give new users a big early-bird discount so advocates have a strong offer.
principles.quote: I would Design This model with zero cost but instead offer the new users a big discount for joining early

principles.text: To reach 500 to 1,000 users, use incoming acquisition: content and building in public across social and search, and keep going.
principles.quote: the best way to create an acquisition model using the incoming method is by creating content and building in public

principles.text: After 1,000 users, turn proven content into paid ads and an affiliate program; a 3:1 return on ad spend leaves profit while funding growth.
principles.quote: you might aim for a 3:1 return on ad spend which means that for each $1 you spend on acquiring a new user that new user earns your SAS $3

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg built a SaaS factory to test and ship products 10x faster
sources.originalTitle: How to Build a SaaS Factory - Ship 10x Faster
sources.summary: Simon argues that SaaS is a high-failure game, so the best strategy is to test many products cheaply. He describes the parts of his "SaaS factory": a GitHub org of reusable packages and boilerplates, no-code automation templates, a creative asset library, a launch checklist, and a personal playbook. The factory only works if you build it yourself.

principles.text: Constantly testing new ideas is the best way to raise your odds of SaaS success, given how likely any one product is to fail.
principles.quote: constantly testing the market with new ideas is the best way to increase your chances of success but you need the right tooling to do this sustainably

principles.text: The most successful indie hackers win by pushing and failing more and faster than others.
principles.quote: the reason they're successful is that they've been pushing and failing more and faster than most other people

principles.text: Turn reusable code into private packages and boilerplates so new products start from a working base in under 30 minutes.
principles.quote: get into the habit of stopping regularly go through your code and pick out pieces that you know or at least feel very sure could be reused

principles.text: Use both code and no-code: automate non-core backend work like segmentation, retargeting lists and social updates, and reuse the automations across products.
principles.quote: people have this idea that it's either code or no code but in order to build a proper SAS Factory you should have both

principles.text: Keep a checklist for every new SaaS (payments, email, auth, privacy policy, terms) and document your processes, as quality control.
principles.quote: every time you set up a new SAS make sure you can cross everything on the list consider this quality control

principles.text: Build your own factory and playbook rather than buying someone else's; the learning from building it is the real advantage.
principles.quote: what truly gives you superpowers is the process of building the factory all the hard-earned lessons that make up the foundation you're building on

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg made $160K+ selling SaaS lifetime deals (and the 3 rules that make them safe)
sources.originalTitle: I Made +$160K Selling SaaS Lifetime Deals
sources.summary: Simon explains why common objections to lifetime deals (unsustainable, entitled users, cannibalized subscribers, no trust) mostly fail, using data from AppSumo, LinkDrip and his Founder's Stack bundle. He lays out three rules: price high, keep costs and support low, and build a public reputation.

principles.text: Lifetime users churn too, so a lifetime deal isn't a forever liability; pick a price high enough to be profitable before the average user leaves.
principles.quote: Lifetime users do churn. And they churn for just about the same reason subscribers churn.

principles.text: Set a relatively high price for a lifetime deal so the break-even horizon is far longer than any realistic customer lifespan.
principles.quote: Set a relatively high price point for your offer. We're selling Founder's Stack for $799 for all four tools.

principles.text: Sell simple, specialized, self-serve tools with minimal support so lifetime customers don't create ongoing cost; estimate costs conservatively.
principles.quote: Keep your products low touch and self-serve. Make a big deal out of the product onboarding experience and have a lot of guides, tutorials, and videos ready so the user can help themselves effectively.

principles.text: Underpricing a lifetime deal on a product with high running costs (e.g. AI usage) is the surest way to go bankrupt.
principles.quote: If you're pricing too low and your product costs too much to run, this is where you get into trouble.

principles.text: A big price gap between the lifetime deal and your monthly plan limits cannibalization; the deal can even bring new subscribers.
principles.quote: my clear impression is that if the price distance is big enough, you probably don't have to worry that your entire subscriber base is jumping the ship and grabbing your lifetime deal all at once.

principles.text: Trust is the key barrier to lifetime deals; the founder must be a visible, reachable public face who builds a reputation.
principles.quote: You, as the founder, should be the public face of your company. You should be on social media, on YouTube, in people's emails, building trust.

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg's SaaS A/B tests found a 52% revenue lift from forced onboarding
sources.originalTitle: This Switch Doubled Our SaaS Revenue (Crazy A/B Test Results)
sources.summary: Simon shares four A/B tests from his SaaS products (FeedHive, LinkDrip). Forcing users through onboarding with card and plan selection raised revenue 52% despite losing most signups. Hero social proof and G2 badges helped, monthly pricing as the default beat yearly, and most tests are inconclusive, so keep testing.

principles.text: Always run A/B tests; most are insignificant, but a few discoveries make a real difference.
principles.quote: we also ran hundreds of ab tests with totally insignificant results in fact most test results are like that which can make it seem a bit redundant to even bother but every once in a while you'll discover something that truly makes a difference

principles.text: Forcing users through onboarding (accounts, card, plan) loses signups but raises revenue through higher ARPU.
principles.quote: by forcing users through an onboarding flow we end up increasing our Revenue with 52%

principles.text: Compare tests on revenue per cohort, not just paying user counts; equal conversions can hide very different ARPU.
principles.quote: 11 paying users versus 13 paying users it seems more or less like a tie right but here's the kicker and it's the same every time

principles.text: Requiring upfront effort raises perceived value and filters out unserious users.
principles.quote: a product is valued higher if you force people to invest initial time and dedication into it I also think the onboarding serves as a good filtering mechanism for more unserious users

principles.text: Put social proof in the hero section; it lifted get-started clicks from 9% to 16%.
principles.quote: in group a 9% of visitors click on the get started button and in group b 16% of visitors click on the button

principles.text: Don't trust intuition on pricing defaults: monthly beat yearly even though people were split on the guess.
principles.quote: of the visitors in group a 133% click on the sign up button of the visitors in group b only 4% click the sign up button

sources.title: How to launch a SaaS from scratch with no audience: founder fit, one channel, build in public, reusable blocks
sources.originalTitle: How To Launch A SaaS From Scratch (4 Essential Steps)
sources.summary: Simon walks through how he would start a SaaS from zero (no audience, network or money) in four steps: pick a problem with founder fit, build one organic distribution channel, build in public with presales and no-code/AI, and turn everything into reusable building blocks. He draws on FeedHive, Linktrip and his failed Sigmetic.

principles.text: Pick a problem with founder fit first: you dogfood it, you're passionate about it, and you have unfair advantages.
principles.quote: the first thing I would look for is a problem that's a good fit for me as a Founder we call this problem founder fit and we need to address this way before we start thinking about whether the market needs our product

principles.text: Dogfooding makes you the ideal customer, so you speak users' language and stay motivated through the hard parts.
principles.quote: you should be so familiar with the problem you're trying to solve that you become a prime user of your own product

principles.text: Everyone has unfair advantages (expertise, experience, a connection); find yours and use them. They need not be special talents.
principles.quote: everyone has unfair advantages it's like playing Monopoly but you're allowed to cheat

principles.text: Build one organic distribution channel and double down on it. Find communities around the problem, answer their questions with content, then skip the channels that don't work.
principles.quote: I would focus on a single Channel and I would make sure I knew it very well

principles.text: Build in public with your community and don't fear idea theft; your authority, commitment and unfair advantages can't be copied.
principles.quote: just let them because they'll soon figure out that without your Authority your commitment and your unfair advantages in this particular area they don't have a chance to compete with you

principles.text: Presell to an engaged community before writing code. Linktrip's lifetime presale made almost $100k in about two months. Use no-code and AI to ship v1 fast.
principles.quote: we sold linktrip as a lifetime pre-sales offer before we wrote a single line of code and it generated almost a hundred thousand dollars in sales in just around two months

sources.title: Why I avoid five tempting AI SaaS ideas: copywriters, coding tools, therapists, detectors, summarizers
sources.originalTitle: 5 Tempting AI SaaS Ideas I’d NEVER Build (here’s why)
sources.summary: Simon explains the five AI SaaS categories his team rejects immediately: standalone AI copywriters, AI coding tools, AI therapists, AI detectors, and AI summarizers. The common thread is saturated markets, usage-based LLM costs that punish bootstrappers, liability risk, and ideas that are really features absorbed by big platforms.

principles.text: A thin wrapper over an LLM API is a race to the bottom on price and churn; it works as a feature inside a bigger product, not as a standalone product.
principles.quote: I think an AI copywriter is a great feature in a bigger product.

principles.text: LLM costs scale with usage, so a successful user base can become a cash-bleeding liability for a bootstrapper.
principles.quote: The cost is directly proportional to the consumption of the tool. Meaning the more users interact with your app, the higher your expenses climb.

principles.text: Don't compete head-on with VC-backed companies that can afford to bleed cash for market dominance.
principles.quote: It's not really about building the best product. It's about who can afford bleeding the most cash.

principles.text: Avoid high-stakes domains like physical or mental health; a small founder can't absorb the ethical and legal fallout.
principles.quote: Stick to products that are much more non-critical by nature. Anything that has to do with people's health, both physically and mentally, I would stay far away from.

principles.text: Don't build a tool that plays cat-and-mouse with a platform whose internal systems you can't see, or that patches the wrong problem.
principles.quote: you probably shouldn't build your business by attempting to play a game of cat-and- mouse with Google, where you have to constantly guess how their internal systems work.

principles.text: If big ecosystems ship a capability natively and for free, it is a feature, not a product, and you also face a heavy trust barrier.
principles.quote: An AI summarizer is no longer a product. It's become a feature.

sources.title: Eight SaaS positioning strategies to survive the AI "Temu effect" flood of products
sources.originalTitle: How To Survive The "Fast Fashion" Era of SaaS
sources.summary: AI coding tools will flood the market with cheap, mediocre SaaS, so positioning matters more than ever. Simon walks through eight positions (low-cost alternative, light version, enterprise, unique player, first mover, niche, privacy first, integrations) with pros, cons and real examples, and says niche is the best fit for a small indie SaaS.

principles.text: AI-built SaaS will flood every category, so unique positioning matters more than ever.
principles.quote: if you want to avoid joining this race to the bottom in the age of AI, it is now more important than ever that you find a way to uniquely position your product in this super crowded market.

principles.text: Openly call yourself a low-cost alternative: you skip educating the market and advertising works well. The risk is a cheap-knockoff vibe.
principles.quote: They don't have to educate the market. They don't have to convince anyone about the need for their tool.

principles.text: A light version of a complex tool captures overwhelmed, less technical users, but it is hard to stay light as you grow.
principles.quote: It's a perfect opportunity to capture users who are less techsavvy and find the alternatives way too complex and overwhelming.

principles.text: Hybrid software-plus-service enterprise businesses are most likely to survive the AI flood because they still depend on humans, and this is where real money flows.
principles.quote: I think these hybrid software service type businesses are the most likely to survive this Teemo effect in SAS simply because they still heavily depend on humans.

principles.text: Being unique or first is hard to defend: uniqueness gets copied, and first movers must educate the market and absorb the mistakes competitors learn from.
principles.quote: Very few business models and tech products are immune to being copied, so appearing unique might become very challenging over time.

principles.text: For a small indie SaaS, niche is the best position: build for a small specific group and ignore that big players solve the same problem. The cost is limited growth later.
principles.quote: Find a small group of users and build it for them. Don't worry that the other big players also solve the same problem

sources.title: 5 SaaS mistakes to avoid: lean pricing, real execution, and marketing from day one
sources.originalTitle: 5 Painful SaaS F*ckups You Should Avoid
sources.summary: Simon Høiberg walks through five common SaaS founder mistakes drawn from building FeedHive: underpricing, poor execution of the build-measure-learn loop, fearing existing markets, staying in your comfort zone, and neglecting marketing. He offers a concrete "lean pricing" method and argues distribution beats product quality.

principles.text: Don't price far below competitors; low price signals a bad product and can't fund support or marketing.
principles.quote: if you come across a product and they price themselves significantly lower than all your competitors what's your first thought that is a shitty product right

principles.text: Lean pricing: start a little below top competitors, then grow ARPU 5% monthly until you hit resistance.
principles.quote: you start at a reasonable pricing point a little below your biggest competitors but not too much now you should aim at increasing the average revenue per user by five percent each month until you meet resistance

principles.text: Raise ARPU via several levers (yearly discount, tier upsell, price anchor, price), not just raw price.
principles.quote: aiming at a revenue increase of five percent instead of only targeting the price Bond itself gives you way more room to experiment with your pricing model

principles.text: Good execution is the full build-measure-learn loop: don't get stuck researching, over-building, or endlessly restarting.
principles.quote: great execution is somewhere in between these two extremes you don't want a long and comprehensive business plan so to a certain extent you should definitely just throw yourself at it and get started

principles.text: Existing competitors in a market are a good sign: demand is validated and you can win with less friction.
principles.quote: if you don't want that if you're perfectly fine with building a small SAS that do a few Millions a year then you don't have to be discouraged when you go on search for your great idea just to discover that it already has huge competitors in fact that's a super good sign

principles.text: Products are easy to build now, so a clear go-to-market strategy and distribution channels are the real edge.
principles.quote: it has actually become really easy to create great products so everyone's got them now if you think your competitive advantages is a better more high quality product think again

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg hit $1,000 MRR in 30 days with FeedHive: audience, early adopters, building in public
sources.originalTitle: How To Reach $1,000 MRR in 30 Days (Most Startups Aren't Doing This)
sources.summary: Simon explains the three-part playbook behind FeedHive's first $1,000 MRR in about a month: build a social presence first, co-build the product with a closed group of early adopters, and build in public as a marketing strategy. He launched with a single tweet and no Product Hunt, Hacker News, or TechCrunch.

principles.text: Build a social media presence before you build the product; success comes from patience and consistency, not fancy gear.
principles.quote: it just takes a certain level of patience and consistency and it's really about just getting started.

principles.text: Post daily on one platform (Twitter or LinkedIn) about a topic you want to be known for, long term.
principles.quote: pick a platform of choice i suggest starting out with twitter or linkedin start posting daily one to two posts pick a topic something you want to be known for

principles.text: Don't monetize your audience early; share value with no strings, and use the time to build authority and connections with other creators.
principles.quote: you don't want to try to monetize your audience for a long time don't post affiliate links don't start selling an ebook or course have patience and just keep sharing valuable content without asking for anything in return

principles.text: Find early adopters and build the product with them, not for them; they shape it and multiply your reach at launch.
principles.quote: you need users to build your product with not for with this is an important difference

principles.text: Keep validating continuously instead of building far ahead on a single 'sounds great' response.
principles.quote: they think validation is having some users say sure that sounds great while presenting the idea once and that's it but that's not enough you need to keep validating your product

principles.text: Treat building in public as a social media marketing strategy: share honest, realistic journey content, no obligation to reveal revenue or secrets.
principles.quote: it's a social media marketing strategy that's all it is you want to create and share content that is interesting and valuable to your audience and which in turn drives awareness leads and subscribers to your sas

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg made $7,500 in a week selling a $19 e-book
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $7,500 in ONE WEEK Selling an E-Book
sources.summary: Simon breaks down his first e-book launch: 16 hours writing, 24 hours on website, email and marketing, $531 spent, 480 copies sold in week one. His thesis is that e-book success comes from distribution and pre-built audience, not writing, so pick a topic you know cold and spend your energy on acquisition channels.

principles.text: Info products sell because of marketing and distribution, not writing quality; most creators leave sales to chance.
principles.quote: they spend hours writing and then they almost leave it up to random chance whether someone is going to buy it or not

principles.text: Write about a topic you know cold so the book writes itself, and save your energy for marketing.
principles.quote: pick a topic that you're so familiar with that you would almost write an ebook about it in your sleep

principles.text: Spend more time on marketing and distribution than on creating the product.
principles.quote: i actually spent more time on marketing and distribution than i did creating the ebook

principles.text: Pre-launch at a discount to test demand and build hype for a month or two before the real launch.
principles.quote: you start charging people for the product before it's done on a discounted offer

principles.text: Give away a free ebook to build authority and collect emails, then sell to that list later.
principles.quote: imagine having a list of 10 000 qualified leads laying around the day you want to launch

principles.text: Pick just one or two acquisition channels; more channels make data messy and unmanageable.
principles.quote: creating multiple channels isn't necessarily going to increase your overall conversion rate and it probably ends up becoming unmanageable

sources.title: How Simon Høiberg builds SaaS products without burning out: reusable building blocks, ecosystem thinking, joy-driven work
sources.originalTitle: Simon Høiberg: Building a SaaS That Works for You (The Bootstrapped Founder 220 transcript)
sources.summary: Simon explains how he runs FeedHive, LinkDrip, a YouTube channel and a small team without burnout. He covers building reusable blocks, picking a pre-validated market and validating with 30 hand-picked users, using lifetime deals carefully, and replacing funnels with an ecosystem of products and content.

principles.text: Turn every output into a reusable building block or checklist so each next project is faster and effort compounds.
principles.quote: every time I finished a YouTube video, so strip that video apart and see is there anything in this video I can turn into a reusable building block that I can use to make the next video even faster?

principles.text: Pick a well-established, pre-validated market and win a small niche with a tiny difference, rather than trying to innovate.
principles.quote: I’m gonna try to be going into a market that is as well established and pre validated as I possibly can.

principles.text: Validate by building with ~30 people from your audience who voice a specific pain, asking them questions daily.
principles.quote: I built in secret with these 30 so users and it was literally fully community driven. I was in there talking to them daily asking them questions daily

principles.text: Sell lifetime deals only on a limited basis: model the costs first and communicate clearly that it is an early-access validation offer.
principles.quote: make that Excel sheet first of all to make sure that your finances can actually support this

principles.text: Think ecosystem, not funnel: people who drop off can land on another product or content, and each bet should feed the web.
principles.quote: whenever I put out something new, my first question that I asked myself is, does this fit into a web in any way?

principles.text: Run joy-driven with an empty calendar and async written work; burnout comes from forced work, so build processes to prevent repeats.
principles.quote: I think people don’t burn out from working a lot. I think people burning out from be feeling forced to work on something

sources.title: How FeedHive reached $65K revenue and $8.5K MRR in 9 months in a crowded market
sources.summary: A short milestone post from Simon Høiberg on FeedHive, an AI-driven social media marketing tool. Nine months in, it had $65K total revenue, $8,500 MRR growing about 20% per month, 3,000+ users and roughly 600 paying. Mostly a metrics snapshot with little tactical detail.

principles.text: A well-established market is still winnable with a differentiated, AI-driven product.
principles.quote: We entered a very well-established market with this product, so no doubt, I am _pumped_ that we managed to grow this to +$65K in revenue.

principles.text: Track compounding monthly growth and project forward from it to set targets.
principles.quote: We're currently at $8,500 MRR and growing with around 20% per month.

principles.text: Keep shipping features built on cutting-edge technology to give users outsized value.
principles.quote: We are working hard on adding new features and using cutting-edge technology to help our users get **superpowers** on social media!

sources.title: The Flight Manual: Simon Høiberg's lightweight, continuous agile framework from FeedHive
sources.originalTitle: The Flight Manual
sources.summary: Simon introduces "Flights," a ceremoniless agile framework for startups and SaaS teams working under extreme uncertainty. Instead of fixed-length sprints and meetings, work ships in continuous, overlapping flights with a pilot, an ETA, and an "Emergency Landing" escape hatch so nobody stays blocked.

principles.text: For startups and SaaS teams facing extreme uncertainty, ship continuously rather than in iterations.
principles.quote: For startups, SaaS development, and teams that generally work under the conditions of extreme uncertainty, a continuous approach will be far more beneficial.

principles.text: Keep process lightweight: adopt the core principles without forcing a rigid set of ground rules.
principles.quote: Flights does not claim that you need to follow the ground rules fully — you can adopt the core principles on top of other team practices and still benefit from using Flights.

principles.text: Give each piece of work an ETA instead of a fixed length, and accept early or late landings.
principles.quote: A flight does not have a fixed length (e.g. 2 weeks).It has an ETA, and it’s determined when the flight is created.

principles.text: Every flight needs one accountable pilot, and a person can pilot only one flight at a time.
principles.quote: The pilot can be anyone from the team, and is the person responsible for landing the flight smoothly in production, on time.

principles.text: Run multiple flights in parallel and keep the next one ready so freed-up people can start immediately.
principles.quote: It is a good idea to always have a flight booked and prepared for takeoff, in case another flight arrives early and frees up a pilot and staff.

principles.text: If work stalls badly, formally close it and return tasks to the backlog rather than blocking people.
principles.quote: Keeping the flight in the air would cause us to “block” a pilot, which we definitely want to avoid.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon walks through the user growth system he used across FeedHive, LinkDrip and Eightbase. Stage 1 is outbound plus referrals for the first ~100 users, stage 2 is a long content grind, and stage 3 adds ads and affiliates once unit economics are known. He also covers staying bootstrapped and delegating tasks, not areas.

chunks.heading: Starting from zero: build a minimum lovable product, not just an MVP
chunks.text:
- Simon says the most common mistake in SaaS is treating "build a product, then get users" as a sequence. Founders end up "trying to acquire users for your product instead of trying to build a product for your users."
- Because ad targeting is so good, founders assume someone out there will want exactly their version. Simon says this can work, but most founders get further by building as little as possible and using the first users to shape the product.
- He prefers "minimum lovable product" over "minimum viable product." The product should be early-stage but give a "wow effect" to the first users.
- His reasoning: SaaS products pop up everywhere and "everyone is chasing the users," so early users need a real reason to jump on an unfinished product.
- He says he mostly speaks about things he has done first hand: starting and running small, bootstrapped, self-serve SaaS. He runs FeedHive, LinkDrip and Eightbase, with a team of nine contractors and over $1M combined ARR.

chunks.heading: The four acquisition methods
chunks.text:
Simon says any online user acquisition has a channel, usually a cost, and a method. He sorts methods into four:

- **Outgoing (outbound):** the founder reaches out to users via cold DMs, cold email or cold calls.
- **Incoming:** content (blog posts, YouTube, social, speaking) that attracts people who then sign up self-serve.
- **Referrals:** current users bring in new ones, through affiliate programs or a viral loop (for example subtle branding inside the product).
- **Advertisement:** like incoming, but you pay for the placement, via Google or Facebook Ads or by sponsoring creators.

He uses a different method at each of three stages.

chunks.heading: Stage 1: first 5 to 100 users (outgoing plus ambassadors)
chunks.text:
- Use the outgoing method on your close network: early colleagues, people you have worked with. Tell them about the product and ask them to join.
- Give the first users a lifetime account for free. If the product has high friction or a high cost to get started, consider paying them to use it.
- Simon disagrees with "never give it away, you're devaluing your product." In his view, at this stage "you are accurately valuing how important these first users are because they are fundamental to the success of your product."
- Put the first users in a small community (Facebook group, WhatsApp, Discord). For FeedHive three years earlier, it was a Twitter chat group with about 20 people.
- Listen and let them shape the product. This gives real feedback instead of guessing, and makes users feel they are part of the project.
- To grow from roughly 10 users to 100, turn early adopters into ambassadors. Give them a voucher or discount to offer friends ("I'm a partner in this project, I can get you in for free or half off"). It is a referral method, not a formal affiliate program.

chunks.heading: Stage 2: up to roughly 1,000 users (incoming content)
chunks.text:
- Once the product has been shaped for two to three months and is ready for strangers, switch to the incoming method: blog posts, YouTube videos, social media, and speaking or booths.
- He calls this stage "very long and very hard" and demotivating, but the effort compounds. He estimates allocating a year or even two years of organic content can reach somewhere between 200, 300, 500, maybe the first 1,000 paying users.
- Outbound with a sales team can work, but it is no longer a self-serve SaaS. He says it suits VC-backed companies with money for a sales team, and he stays in the bootstrapped self-serve genre.
- Keep the stage 1 early adopters close, because they stay valuable in later stages.
- Advice for the 10K MRR phase: grind through outreach to the first 5 to 25 users, then show up on social media every day, write blog posts and make videos even through long stretches of low engagement. "Just keep going."

chunks.heading: Stage 3: scaling past roughly 1,000 paying users (ads and affiliates)
chunks.text:
- Keep doing stage 2 content. Add two scalable methods: advertisement and affiliate marketing.
- **Ads:** reuse content that performed well in stage 2 as ad creative, and create new ads too. He says this is his preferred method and he has used it for all his products. Ads are one of the highest-cost channels, so he waits until stage 3.
- **Ad math:** use the data from stages 1 and 2 to calculate average lifetime value (using churn). Cost of acquiring a user with ads must be below average lifetime value. If the math works and you are in growth mode, you can be willing to pay close to the full average lifetime value for one new user.
- **Affiliates:** turn current users into affiliate partners using existing affiliate tools. In growth mode, a generous program can work; he has seen tools pay up to 50% of recurring revenue. If you want more automation and less grind, offer less (in-app credits, gift cards, lower payouts), accepting that affiliates will promote less aggressively.
- Stage 3 "can keep going indefinitely" with no limit on new users.
- He cautions not to start affiliates too early, since you probably don't have people yet who want to recommend you for money.

chunks.heading: Learning ads cheaply before you need them
chunks.text:
- Ads were a big challenge. He says it is hard to get the creative format right and to understand how the platforms work, and they "burned quite a lot of money" on things that didn't work, especially with FeedHive, his first SaaS.
- His advice: start experimenting with ads during stage 2 without expecting conversions. Set aside a small budget (for example, "for the next 6 months, we're just going to blow this money on learning how to do ads") in a sandbox-style environment.
- Skill at content makes it easier to find ad creatives that perform. By the second SaaS, and now Aibase (the third), ad roll-out has become "significantly easier over time."

chunks.heading: How Simon runs his team and why he stays bootstrapped
chunks.text:
- **Delegate tasks, not areas:** he describes himself as "the single point of failure." Contractors (found via Upwork and Fiverr) do graphics, video editing, some writing and development. He sets up the ad campaigns, assembles final YouTube videos, and approves every code PR (he is a developer by background).
- His reasoning is partly financial: task-level contractors are affordable but weaker at planning and strategy for a whole area. He recommends small bootstrapped founders "get their hands dirty" and be in charge of everything, even if they delegate execution. He says other teams do well with independent owners and he doesn't claim his way is the only one.
- **No investors:** he became an entrepreneur "so that I wouldn't have a boss," and investors (who often reach out to successful bootstrappers) would become one. He dislikes giving a board seat for little money: "Now, not only do they have a boss again, they also have a boss they can't fire."
- He says he'd reach big numbers like 10M ARR slowly and steadily, and would likely never reach 100M ARR his way. Founders who want to go very big may need funding.

chunks.heading: Advice for founders at higher scale, and on persistence
chunks.text:
- **Keep showing up:** past roughly $100K per month, some founders think they can lean back into a pure strategy role. Simon says this doesn't work: keep appearing on YouTube, podcasts and stages, even if uncomfortable. It also shows the team the founder is still fully involved.
- **Content is underused:** he thinks many SaaS companies still "sleep on" content. Be on podcasts, YouTube and blogs, where people hang out.
- **What he'd tell his 20s self:** stop chasing shiny objects and "easy money overnight" ideas. Pick something you enjoy and can get good at, and keep grinding. Give it "at least two, three years before you start expecting to see actual tangible results," and choose something you like so you don't give up.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon explains how his first SaaS failed with zero paying users, how giving away value on Twitter built the audience that launched FeedHive, and how 25 early users shaped its MVP. He also covers landing pages, paid ads creatives, when to hire, and documenting processes.

chunks.heading: Starting without an audience: Simon's failed first SaaS, Sigmetic
chunks.text:
- Simon's first SaaS (about three years before this 2022 interview) was Sigmetic. It plugged into GitHub and crunched numbers on code pushed and pull request reviews to show managers who the high performers on an engineering team were. It also had a Leaderboard-style dashboard for a big TV screen.
- He got it fully built, with signup and paid plans, and ended with "exactly zero paying users."
- Root cause: he was thinking like a salesman (the 80/20 rule, where 20% of salespeople produce 80% of the sales) and applied sales culture to developers. Developers did not want to be on a leaderboard, and managers did not think it measured code quality or kept developers motivated.
- He had access to real users (the managers and engineers at the company he consulted for) and ignored their rejection. His mindset was "they just don't want to change... I know better," and he leaned on the Henry Ford "faster horses" story.
- His lesson: "Absolutely no one is going to be interested in this." Listen to the few people who comment on your idea, and don't wave the feedback away.
- He tried launching on Reddit, Product Hunt and Indie Hackers with no audience or online authority. It was "like yelling out on the board literally no one cared." This pushed him to spend a year building an audience before his next product.

chunks.heading: Audience building: give value with no ask, then wait for the audience before launching
chunks.text:
- The trigger was a chapter on audience building in the book Rework by Basecamp.
- His first six months of posting on Twitter and LinkedIn went nowhere. Every post said "follow me here, sign up for my newsletter, sign up for my SaaS." It was "extremely centered around what I wanted to get out of it," and that comes through when you are a small channel.
- He gave himself one last month: share value for free and ask for nothing. If he didn't reach 1,000 Twitter followers in that month, he would quit audience building.
- Result: he crossed 10,000 followers in roughly a month, over a summer.
- He then committed not to launch a new product until he had at least 30,000 Twitter followers. He spent another four or five months sharing content with no ebooks and no links to click.
- Topic choice: freelancing and how to get clients, because that was what he had accomplishments in. His rule is to have a bare minimum of authority before you teach a topic. That can be having built a SaaS, having worked at a startup, or having interviewed many startup founders.
- Short videos recorded in his living room in one take, with little editing, did well on Twitter. Followers kept saying he'd do well on YouTube. He put the videos on a YouTube channel, then tried one properly edited long-form video and "was completely sold." He edits his own videos in Adobe Premiere and learned from tutorials as a complete amateur.

chunks.heading: Building the FeedHive MVP with early users instead of choosing features himself
chunks.text:
- The idea came from his own need to schedule content. HypeFury (Twitter only) was doing well. Buffer and Hootsuite felt old and clunky ("imagine being an agency having to sit a full working day in that tool"). Typefully followed HypeFury. Simon saw demand for modern lightweight tools and decided to "take a bite of the big cake" and replace Hootsuite, Buffer and Agorapulse.
- His MVP method: don't pick the features yourself, "find users immediately to help you get there."
- He announced in a Twitter chat group of content creators that he'd build a multi-platform scheduler and needed help. He offered lifetime access for free to anyone who joined a small group to help build it. About 25 people joined.
- The first MVP was a website with a text box to write a tweet or thread and schedule it, nothing else.
- Their top request was a proper calendar view, since many tools only had a queue of tweets, while Hootsuite was one of the few with a calendar. So the MVP became a Twitter scheduler with automatic queueing and a real calendar view.
- Six weeks of building went on quietly with that group. Then he announced it on Twitter and shared screenshots and updates (building in public). A month later he started letting people in.
- Because the 20 to 25 helpers were big creators with large followings, they shared it widely at the public beta launch.
- His summary: "Get the people in there first and then just listen closely to what they would want to see first."

chunks.heading: FeedHive growth numbers and how users are acquired
chunks.text:
- The day of the public beta launch, FeedHive hit $300 MRR within the first 24 hours or so, and about $1,000 MRR by the end of that month.
- After that, he says it is "a very boring story." FeedHive added roughly $1,000 MRR every month, with no explosive growth and no down months.
- At the time of the interview it was about $30-32K MRR, and he was approaching $400K ARR.
- Acquisition mix: organic awareness campaigns (many run by Simon himself) plus paid ads. A lot of users come from paid ads, mainly Facebook and Google.
- Spend: more than $50,000 on ads in that year alone, and a lot of that was money wasted on experimenting.

chunks.heading: Paid ads: let the platform target, put the effort into creatives
chunks.text:
- Paid ads are not a silver bullet. Targeting is relatively trivial because the platforms' AI models handle it, so don't build ultra-narrow audiences or do heavy audience research. "You just let the platforms do the thing."
- What matters is the creative: "You need to make killer ads, ads that almost look like great content in itself." He says people who think ads are a magic tool usually have poor creatives and a weak offer presentation.
- It costs a lot to learn, but once you have a winning ad, "you just let it run and users just drop in." He calls it "user acquisition while I sleep." It is inherently scalable, unlike cold outreach, sales calls or constant influencer outreach.
- He has a Figma board full of ad creative assets and a team that helps produce ad creatives and videos.
- When to start: not as your first move. First be confident you have an onboarding flow and a way to convert paying users. Early on, while still finding product-market fit, ads can be used to validate ideas, but as an acquisition channel they are not the first thing he'd start with.

chunks.heading: Landing pages: sell the difference or the outcome, depending on how familiar the category is
chunks.text:
- If people already know the concept (e.g. a social media scheduler), focus on what makes you stand out: a calendar view or features competitors lack. The outcome ("you will grow on social") matters but people already get it.
- Picture the visitor with your site and five competitor tabs open, and help them pick yours instead of convincing them they need the category.
- If few people are familiar with the concept or the way you solve the problem, be much more outcome oriented and explain the problem first.

chunks.heading: Systems, templates and a reusable asset library as the way he produces so much
chunks.text:
- He says he works about 60 to 65 hours a week, more than a typical full-time job, and he pushes back on the idea that he works 120 hours. He says he does nothing magic to manage time. He works on whatever has priority or gives him energy, and he is good at context switching.
- The real driver is process focus. For anything repeated he asks: can I automate it, delegate it, or at least document it step by step?
- Every time he does something, he asks whether one or two parts can become a general-purpose building block for later projects.
- Examples of his asset library: pre-edited YouTube thumbnails, a stock b-roll library of himself filming with a computer and showing various emotions, code packages, landing page templates and boilerplate, and a large Figma board of ad creative assets.
- He keeps a huge internal wiki ("an internal Wikipedia page") with well-documented processes, so he can delegate or hire quickly without much onboarding.
- Example: after 100-plus YouTube videos, each one produced something reusable that makes editing the next one faster.
- Tools he names: FeedHive (to schedule his content, he was the first user) and ClickUp, which he prefers to Trello (a long-time favorite) and Notion, since it replaced several tools for him and his team as a calendar, notes and project management tool.

chunks.heading: Hiring, delegating and running contractors
chunks.text:
- He has no employees, only contractors.
- After launching FeedHive he brought on a few early adopters as part-time contractors and a friend from Denmark as a would-be co-founder, reaching a team of five fast. Growth did not materialize on its own, they were burning too much money too fast, and the co-founder arrangement (a Danish company with his Swiss company) had too much logistical friction.
