Within two to three months he removed the whole team and was alone for about four months. He then rebuilt the team slowly as revenue came in.
- His advice: before hiring for a role, try it yourself. For design, use Canva. For ads, build a full campaign and burn some money on your own bad creatives. Then you'll know how to specify and manage the work, since "they can't read your minds."
- Hire when you can write a clear specification and checklist (fonts, colors, border styles). Telling a designer "make it look good" leads to frustration on both sides.
- He goes further: the best time to hire is to buy yourself time, delegating work you could already do perfectly well yourself and can specify down to the smallest detail.
- Management without experience quickly leads to loose ends and stress.
- His remaining worry: if he pulled himself out completely, his company would not run well, because he is still working in the business more than on it. His fix is better-documented processes, "the whole manual to my company." His plan is to step back over five to ten years and eventually sell, since "it's a SaaS company, it's not going to be living forever."

chunks.heading: Going full-time, runway, salary and the LinkDrip pre-sale approach
chunks.text:
- Path: sales (starting around age 18-19, working on commission only, selling search ads for the Danish version of Google) to freelance web development (WordPress, Joomla), built up on the side until he could go full-time freelance. He rated freedom above the higher income he could have made in sales. He then did consulting at startups and bigger companies before his first SaaS.
- He moved from Denmark to Switzerland over two years before the interview. Swiss residency required a work contract, so he has paid himself a salary from day one of FeedHive. It is as low as he can get away with, and most profit is reinvested into the business, LinkDrip and the YouTube effort.
- He left consulting for FeedHive when it was around $500 MRR, with savings from consulting giving him roughly a year of runway. He said the plan was to "burn this money" and make it profitable within a year, and he would not necessarily recommend this because it is risky.
- On sales skills carrying over: the direct craft barely transfers because FeedHive is low-touch self-serve. The mentality does: he is not afraid of selling or marketing, which many developers are.
- LinkDrip (his new SaaS) differs from FeedHive by pre-selling first rather than launching to a free closed community. He sold many lifetime deals in the previous month, funding the build, and had over 650 early adopters on a waiting list. He kept the community-driven approach: a public Trello roadmap where people suggest and vote on features, reviewed every day to decide what to prepare for the private beta launching in a few months.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon explains why he built an audience before his second SaaS by giving pure value for six months with no asks. He covers validating FeedHive with 25 free beta users, a multi-step Facebook ads funnel, YouTube title/thumbnail testing, paid Instagram shoutouts, and monetizing a niche YouTube channel.

chunks.heading: Building an audience before building the SaaS
chunks.text:
- Simon's first SaaS failed. He built it in secret, nobody had the problem, and the launch on Reddit, Twitter and Indie Hackers "drowned" among other people's posts. He describes the worst part as "yelling out into the void".
- After reading *Rework* (Basecamp) and its emphasis on audience trust and attention, he decided the next SaaS might still fail, but "it's certainly not going to be from not being heard".
- His first audience attempt also failed. He was impatient and every post carried "follow me", "follow me on this other platform", "subscribe to my newsletter", and even kept promoting the failed SaaS. His agenda "shined through too clearly".
- He then ran an experiment: two months of sharing the best value he had with no asks (no follow requests, no sign-ups), ready to drop the whole approach if it failed. The goal was 1,000 Twitter followers in two months.
- Result: more than 10,000 followers after six weeks. He kept the no-ask approach for about six months and reached roughly 30,000 followers before ever mentioning FeedHive.
- Why it works, in his view: people are used to valuable content being "a secret sales funnel in disguise" and expect the conversion attempt around the corner. Six months of giving without asking meant that when he first asked for money, "I was taken so much more seriously".

chunks.heading: Growing on Twitter: content, engagement and time spent
chunks.text:
- Mix of two activities: writing original content and engaging with other people's posts, roughly a 50/50 split of effort at the time.
- Engagement tactic: add real value to posts by much bigger accounts, without stealing their thunder or traffic and with no shameless plugs. Big accounts notice and may retweet you. Valuable replies also get liked, which lifts them to the top of the comment section, and he calls this a far better way to direct traffic than asking for follows or stacking hashtags.
- Time: about 8-10 hours a week writing content. He batch-scheduled ahead, using a Sunday to write content, which left weekday time to engage (about 30-60 minutes a day).
- He engages less now that he has bigger audiences on multiple platforms.
- Current audience: about 100K on Twitter, 25K on Instagram, 30K on LinkedIn, about 12K on YouTube.
- Short, concise writing on Twitter helped him sharpen ideas, which carries over to writing YouTube titles. He notes good short titles are harder than they look.

chunks.heading: Validating FeedHive with 25 users and a lifetime offer
chunks.text:
- The idea came from his own pain. He tried Hootsuite and Buffer ("I absolutely hated it"), found them monolithic, clunky and slow, and found smaller startup tools too Twitter-specific. He wanted one fast tool with first-class LinkedIn and Instagram support plus newer features like Twitter threads and conditional posting.
- Despite a crowded market, he paid attention to discussions on Twitter and LinkedIn and found others with the same problem.
- He collected 25 people from Twitter (also active on LinkedIn and Instagram) and built an MVP just for them, inviting them in after two weeks of building.
- Offer: lifetime free unlimited usage in exchange for being the early group. Feedback ran in a Twitter group chat ("could have been a WhatsApp group or a Slack server").
- The core product was shaped in daily discussions with this group over about two months, then he launched a public beta.
- The beta got good traction on Twitter and LinkedIn, and within a few weeks FeedHive had its first ~$1K MRR, which told him "there's actually something here".
- He posted screenshots and progress updates ("building in public") to his 30K followers to check for outside interest, and some people wrote saying they would pay to get in early.
- He admits the lifetime-free offer is a leap of faith: free users saying "yes I would have paid" is biased validation.
- On pre-selling: he likes charging before the product exists as "the ultimate validation", but warns people over-promise with landing pages full of features they will never build. If you charge upfront, make sure what you promise is realistic. The fact that 25 people stayed engaged for two months was his secondary validation that he could deliver.

chunks.heading: FeedHive's growth and ad funnel
chunks.text:
- FeedHive was founded in late 2020. At the time of the interview (July 2022) it was around $200K ARR, with a team of five contractors and no employees. Hiring permanent staff in Switzerland is expensive, so he uses contractors.
- Most FeedHive users come from Facebook ads, run as a multi-step funnel with retargeting:
  1. Promote relevant content to a cold audience (blog posts such as "best alternatives to Later", or "is it worth using Canva as a social media scheduler" after Canva announced a scheduler).
  2. Retarget people who visited the blog post with ads about social media and its benefits, moving them from unaware to problem/solution aware.
  3. A further sequence for people who engage with the retargeted audience: discounted offers, trials, sign-up prompts, feature highlights.
- Principle: in a super competitive space like social media schedulers, "you can't just promote an ad saying sign up for my product". Warm people up so they recognize your brand patterns in text and graphics.
- Consistent branding matters: an in-house graphic designer produces recognizable creatives, and an agency produces content written to work both for SEO and for ads.
- Calculating acquisition cost per user gets more complicated with multi-step funnels, which he accepts.

chunks.heading: Selling ebooks with Instagram and Facebook ads
chunks.text:
- His ebooks are software development titles, priced at $19 (on sale at $29 at the time he mentions "290 on a sale" in the transcript, which is ambiguous, so treat the price as roughly $19). About 98% of ebook revenue comes from Facebook ads, mostly shown on Instagram.
- Instagram audience as social proof: when someone sees an ad, they click the profile to see who is selling it. Many followers, engagement and helpful comments make the ads convert better.
- Engagement also earns a small reward from Facebook: slightly cheaper ads, and an edge in the ad auction if the content is engaging.
- Ebook funnel is simple: one ad, a tiny funnel and some retargeting. Cheap price allows impulse purchases from cold audiences, with retargeting for those who only visit the site.
- He never "boosts" organic content. He keeps ads separate so he can track return on ad spend (ROAS).
- Selling directly from posts does not work well for him on Twitter, though he plugs products on viral tweets.

chunks.heading: Paying Instagram pages for shoutouts
chunks.text:
- Early on he did not run ads, because ads with no social proof are ineffective and expensive. Instead he paid big profiles open to promotion to share his content and mention him.
- Includes curated accounts that mostly repost the best content in a niche (for example, a JavaScript account), which credit the creator properly.
- Example price: about $150 for a post plus a 24-hour story plus his name in the page's bio for 24 hours, on an account with about 800,000 followers.
- He calculated roughly 10 cents per follower from some of these promotions, which can beat most ad platforms if followers are the objective.
- Caveat: he found this works better on Instagram than anywhere else. When he asked bigger YouTubers about paid channel shoutouts, nobody was interested.

chunks.heading: Building a YouTube channel alongside the SaaS
chunks.text:
- He initially did not want YouTube (too time consuming, too much to learn). He had built a brand on Twitter with 2-minute explainer videos (JavaScript, getting freelance clients) before Shorts and Reels took off. People kept asking for a channel, so he posted those short videos on YouTube and had about 1,000 subscribers almost overnight, then went into it more seriously.
- Channel topic: online business (SaaS, selling ebooks and info products, dropshipping experiments, ways programmers can start businesses). About 60 videos, around 12.6K subscribers at the interview.
- Revenue: about $4K per month, split roughly 70% sponsors, 15% ad revenue (about $500/month), 15% attributed ebook sales. He cautions that 13K subscribers earning $4K a month is not typical.
- Topic matters: advertisers bid more for online business, e-commerce and personal investing than for programming or gaming, so ad revenue per view is higher.
- Sponsorship pitch: he charges more than a typical YouTuber his size, with the promise that he is determined to reach 100K subscribers that year. Sponsoring now is a good investment because videos are evergreen and the price will rise once he hits that mark. His other social audiences act as extra proof.
- Schedule: one big video every other week, plus two Shorts in the off week. He does scripting, filming and editing himself. He plans to hire editors and is working on onboarding systems.
- Strategy: he aims at the YouTube home page (browse features), where most of his traffic comes from, rather than search. Thumbnails and titles are key.
- Sourcing ideas: look at similar channels to see what themes work, and listen to repeated questions from his own audience. He adds storytelling, which raised retention "tremendously". A topic must pass a checklist, including whether he can tell a good story about it.

chunks.heading: Thumbnail-first video process and scripting
chunks.text:
- Order of work: idea, then title and thumbnail, then script, then film and edit. If he cannot produce an exciting title and a thumbnail that gives the right association, he discards the idea before putting in the effort.
- Test: paste the title and thumbnail into a screenshot of the YouTube home grid, glance at it, then look away. You have about one second to create the right association. He sends the screenshot to a few brutally honest people and asks "would you click?" and drops the idea if they say no.
- Scripting: he writes full scripts and reads them from a teleprompter, about 95% word by word, because as a non-native English speaker he rambles when freestyling. He adds annotations (pause here, emphasize this word) so the delivery does not sound read.
- Hours: a few hours a day on planning, scripting and writing for YouTube.

chunks.heading: Avoiding burnout and delegating
chunks.text:
- Working on two things (FeedHive and YouTube) keeps him from burning out. Switching to the other project is his rest, because doing one thing constantly is "flexing the same muscle". YouTube is the creative outlet; the SaaS is management, systems and programming.
- Main upcoming challenge: both FeedHive and YouTube are taking off and he must recruit and onboard help without onboarding structures yet. With contractors, turnover is high, so he needs a repeatable process for people coming and going.
- On delegation: delegating is about buying time, not about hiring people more specialized than himself. Mentally it is hard because he knows he could do many tasks better himself in the moment.
- Recommendations he gives: *Build to Sell Radio* podcast (John Warrillow), the book *Storyworthy* (Matthew Dicks, on storytelling for videos and ads), and Arvid Kahl as a bootstrapper he follows.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon Høiberg recounts quitting freelancing for FeedHive, burning $50K on a premature team, surviving the X API shutdown, and expanding into LinkDrip, TinyKiwi and Abbase. He explains pre-selling lifetime deals to fund development and how he prices the FounderStack bundle so it stays profitable.

chunks.heading: Leaving freelancing for FeedHive and the $50K team mistake
chunks.text:
- Simon is a self-taught software engineer. He freelanced for roughly 10 years, starting with simple WordPress and Shopify work and moving on to React and AWS cloud builds.
- He launched his first SaaS product, FeedHive (a social media management tool), in 2021, when "being an engineer that could build stuff was a massive advantage" because AI could not yet code for you.
- He cancelled all his client contracts as soon as FeedHive had about $300 MRR.
- He then went too big too fast. He was so confident in the product that he hired a full team, including Twitter influencers from his network.
- Over 3 months he spent around $50,000 on that team, while FeedHive barely moved and reached about $2,000 MRR. He had to fire everyone.
- He kept building solo for about another year and a half before he broke even on that initial loss.
- He says those 18 months were agonizing, and he kept thinking he would go back to consulting. He credits his savings for getting through; without them it "would have just been a really really big waste of money."
- The lesson he draws from his own story is that he was "completely overconfident" about how long things would take.

chunks.heading: Surviving the Twitter/X API price shock
chunks.text:
- When Elon Musk bought Twitter (renamed X), a $42,000/month enterprise-grade API tier was introduced. Simon heard about it only about two days before it took effect.
- Rumors had floated for a month, first around $100/month and then $42,000. Simon dismissed the $42,000 rumor.
- The tools hit were the Twitter-centric ones: Hypefury, Typefully, Tony Dinh's Black Magic and others. Some bigger ones could afford the API because Twitter was their whole product. Black Magic was making about $14-15K/month, far too little to pay for it.
- FeedHive was at about $50K MRR at the time. It could technically have paid, but it would have swallowed nearly all revenue, and it also had a team and ad spend to fund.
- Simon decided not to pay for the API. For a while FeedHive let users enter their own API key to keep access, but this was a poor experience. The $100/month entry tier was not worth it for most users when competitors still offered Twitter.
- Result: FeedHive lost about 30% of its users within days of announcing it. It took about a year and a half to recover.
- He says he is glad he made that call, because FeedHive had already added LinkedIn and Instagram and become a multi-platform tool. Without that diversification, "we would have been in a pickle."
- Today only the occasional user asks for Twitter/X support.
- The same episode also led to Abbase (see below): support was swamped with the same three questions, about Twitter, 95% of the time.

chunks.heading: Building a product portfolio by letting demand pull you
chunks.text:
Simon now runs four SaaS products aimed at founders and small businesses: FeedHive, LinkDrip, TinyKiwi and Abbase.

- **LinkDrip** (link shortener plus automation) came from user requests. FeedHive users wanted Bitly or Switchy integrations.
- **TinyKiwi** (a mini Canva-style graphics tool) came from Canva closing its integration option just before FeedHive could add it. Simon messaged Yosef, TinyKiwi's builder, on Twitter to propose integrating it. Yosef did not reply for about 3 months, then said he wanted to sell it, and Simon bought it immediately. TinyKiwi now opens inside FeedHive's composer.
- **Abbase** (AI support tool with live chat, ticketing and AI-assisted replies for human agents) was built to scratch his own itch. It is a separate product, not integrated into the others. Competitors include SiteGPT and Chatbase, which showed him there was clear demand. His one human support person uses it to answer faster.
- Integration example: in FeedHive's composer you can shorten a link with LinkDrip, add UTM tags, and use a custom branded short domain, all without leaving the editor.

His advice on portfolios:
- Start with one product, "then let the demand pull you from there." Expand only if users or audience ask for it.
- Some builders (Pieter Levels, John Rush, Tibo) run portfolios, and he thinks newcomers see this and wrongly assume it is the way to start. He does not agree.
- What he likes about his own path is that each new product extends from his existing users and audience, so he did not start from zero on distribution.

chunks.heading: Pre-selling a lifetime deal to validate and fund a product
chunks.text:
How Simon launched LinkDrip:
1. He spent a weekend building a landing page.
2. He posted about it on social and showed a popup inside FeedHive announcing the new product.
3. He sold it as a lifetime deal in pre-sales: back the product early and own it forever.
4. Within about a month he made around $75,000 from pre-sales.
5. He used that money to hire developers on Upwork to build the actual product.

- He calls this "a classical validation by pre-sales": the money arrived before the product existed.
- The existing FeedHive user base was the distribution, so there was no cold start.
- He had also sold FeedHive itself as a lifetime deal on AppSumo years earlier, shortly after launch, so this was not his first lifetime deal.

chunks.heading: FounderStack: bundling four tools into one lifetime deal
chunks.text:
- He bundled all four products into one offer, FounderStack (founderstack.pro). It is a lifetime deal for the whole bundle only, and you cannot pick individual tools.
- Pricing: $1,299 is the normal price, and it was discounted to $799 at the time. Subscriptions to each tool are still available separately.
- Two more SaaS products are planned for this year. Anyone who buys the bundle now automatically gets them when they launch, so buyers effectively pre-buy access.
- He acknowledges the objection to lifetime deals: it is dangerous to sell something with ongoing costs for a one-time payment.
- His cost logic: he calculated server cost per user, and at $799 or even more at $1,299 it would take the average user "decades" to become a losing investment.
- He advises against his earlier AppSumo pricing: the cheapest plan sold at $49, and he would not recommend doing that.
- His rule is to package the products so the bundle carries enough value to justify a high price.
- Most buyers do not use all four tools equally; they mostly use one, so cloud cost is not multiplied by four per customer.

chunks.heading: Handling AI costs in a lifetime deal
chunks.text:
- AI is the expensive part of a lifetime deal and the one to be careful about.
- His solution: every user gets a monthly allowance of AI credits as part of the deal.
- After the allowance runs out, users bring their own OpenAI API key to keep using AI features.
- This caps his exposure on AI cost while keeping the deal attractive.

chunks.heading: Product quality as a competitive edge in a crowded category
chunks.text:
- Simon's positioning against incumbents like Hootsuite, Sprout Social and Buffer: they are "old and dusty tools."
- Agencies, which have employees sitting in the tool for 8 hours a day, especially value FeedHive being fast, snappy and quick to navigate.
- He notes that small page-load delays add up when someone clicks around all day.
- He also says that FeedHive supports many platforms and content types (memes, short video, text) without feeling overwhelming.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon Høiberg draws on his experience launching FeedHive on AppSumo ($300K in two months), pre-selling LinkDrip lifetime deals to his own audience ($100K+), and running TinyKiwi as an ongoing LTD. He covers the real upsides (distribution, feedback, word of mouth), the risks (operating cost, support friction) and when LTDs make sense.

chunks.heading: Simon on lifetime deals (LTDs) as a pricing and distribution tactic
chunks.text:
- Simon defines a lifetime deal as "pay once instead of paying monthly or yearly and then own it forever."
- He sold LTDs on AppSumo for his SaaS FeedHive and says he has "never had any concern" or felt cheated by the platform.
- His main advice is to plan the finances first. He warns founders not to make a "killer deal" just to be sellable, and to be fair to their own future finances.
- Lifetime users are not a permanent burden. He says LTD users churn for several reasons:
  - They outgrow the tool.
  - They move to something new.
  - They love it and upgrade to a higher monthly or yearly tier. Some FeedHive users did this.
- On FeedHive, he says the churn rate for the average LTD user is higher than for the average subscriber.

chunks.heading: How AppSumo works and why Simon thinks the cut is fair
chunks.text:
- Simon's description of the split: AppSumo takes about 50% of all revenue and puts it into advertising (ads, newsletters, events). Of the remaining 50%, the founder gets 30% and AppSumo keeps 20% as profit.
- He rejects the objection that AppSumo is greedy and only leaves founders 30%. His argument:
  - A distribution channel this size is worth far more than the product itself.
  - Product-centric founders think they are doing AppSumo a favor by listing; he says it's "the other way around."
  - If you can reach that audience yourself, "go sell it yourself."
- He cites AppSumo's reach: a newsletter of about 800,000 people, large-scale ads on YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn, and more than 10 years of experience selling these deals.
- He describes the operations as professional: deadlines kept, payments on time, help with legal forms and integration, and someone always available to answer questions.

chunks.heading: FeedHive's AppSumo results
chunks.text:
- Simon says his startup made about $400k in its first year, and about $300k of that came in the first two months from lifetime deals.
- FeedHive ranked in AppSumo's top five best-selling products during the roughly two months it ran there. He notes AppSumo products have done over $1M in total, so it was top five for that period, not of all time.
- Of the roughly $300k in sales he took home about $100k (his roughly 30% share).
- He says he was very satisfied with that result and that it beat what he expected.

chunks.heading: Selling an LTD yourself: the LinkDrip pre-sale
chunks.text:
- A year after FeedHive, Simon launched LinkDrip, a link shortener that integrates with FeedHive, and sold LTDs himself as a pre-sale instead of using AppSumo.
- The pre-sale doubled as product validation. He spent about eight hours on a landing page, set up a Stripe account, posted on social media and made a promo video.
- Results: $75,000 in the first month and more than $100,000 over two months.
- Many buyers were existing FeedHive LTD owners who wanted the integration.
- This only worked because he had an audience. At the time he reached hundreds of thousands of people on Twitter, 50,000+ on YouTube, and 200,000+ people in total.
- He warns that self-listing without an audience gets "close to nothing." Founders need to build their own distribution channel first.
- He says LinkDrip later reached about $100,000 ARR (last time he checked).
- He would not do it again. Reasons:
  - Holding $100k of pre-sale cash with no finished product felt stressful.
  - He had to ship against a promised date, which went against how his team normally works (no scrum, no sprints, no deadlines, because he finds deadlines stressful for founders and developers and says quality is "infinitely much better" at a comfortable pace).
  - He says he probably spent significantly more than he otherwise would have because of the rush.

chunks.heading: The risks and friction of LTDs
chunks.text:
- Operating cost is the biggest con. He says a tool with heavy ongoing costs, for example one that leans on OpenAI APIs or other computationally expensive services, should reconsider whether an LTD works financially.
- Lifetime value math he suggests:
  - Divide the average monthly subscription by the expected time before a user churns to get average lifetime value.
  - FeedHive's monthly churn is around 8%.
  - In theory you could charge that lifetime value up front and the economics would match a subscription, assuming equal churn. He notes LTD churn is actually higher.
- Relationship friction runs in both directions:
  - Some LTD users show entitlement, expecting premium support for a one-time payment. He compares it to the freelancing meme where the $200 client demands endless revisions and the $10,000 client is easy.
  - Founders also have less incentive to give the same support to someone who cannot churn: "no matter how we want to say this or not the moment the lifetime user has paid you there is less incentive for you to give them the same sublime support experience."
  - Many LTD users have had bad experiences with founders who treated them poorly, so he says the blame is not one-sided.
- He advises founders to minimize friction in this financial and support dependency.

chunks.heading: TinyKiwi: an LTD-only business that works
chunks.text:
- Simon bought TinyKiwi, a lightweight browser-based Canva alternative, from a founder he found on Twitter, a bit over a year before this recording. He originally wanted to integrate it into FeedHive and compete with Canva.
- The vision fizzled and the developer lost motivation, so he moved the developer to another product and decided to sell it as a lifetime deal.
- He runs Facebook ads for a $67 lifetime deal. They are still running and generate $5,000 to $10,000 in sales per month.
- It suits an LTD because costs are near zero:
  - The tool runs almost entirely in the browser, with no heavy API or backend.
  - Backend usage makes only a few database calls plus authentication.
  - He calculated only a slight server cost increase for every additional 10,000 users.
- The main running cost is a designer he hired to keep building new templates.
- The lesson he draws: an LTD fits best when new users add almost no marginal cost.

chunks.heading: Other benefits Simon sees in LTD launches
chunks.text:
- Word of mouth and getting users on board matter more to him than the up-front cash.
- A launch brings hundreds of users into the product at once, which surfaces bugs and feature suggestions fast.
- He is considering an LTD (own audience and/or AppSumo) for his other product, 8base, and says he is "considering both options."
- Practical downside he flags: after an AppSumo deal ends, the AppSumo page can outrank the product's own site in Google for the brand name for about 60 days. New users see what they missed, which makes the subscription look less attractive. He notes that a founder can ask AppSumo for favors on this.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon Høiberg explains why paid ads work for indie SaaS, using his best-performing Facebook ad for Aidbase as the example. Creative is the main lever, emotion and engagement make Facebook's auction cheaper, and the safe path is cheap multi-round testing before any scaling.

chunks.heading: Simon's case for paid ads as a bootstrapped SaaS channel
chunks.text:
- Simon says paid ads are a "very very effective marketing channel" for bootstrapped and indie products, and answers "100% yes" to whether indie founders should run them.
- Set aside organic social media, paid ads is the channel he personally masters best, and he has been heavy on them since starting his SaaS products.
- Big-brand ads (he names monday.com and Zapier) often look like TV commercials, with huge production budgets. He argues they perform poorly on YouTube, and some big companies run ads at a loss just to stay top of mind.
- He says these companies are not hard to compete with. He cites an Intercom ad with 200,000 views and six likes: "everyone just scrolls by".
- A founder who already makes good social or YouTube content will likely do ads well, because most big companies do not use creators from this generation.
- Targeting and setup are now easy on Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and Google. The platforms' machine learning finds the right people, so the founder's job is "creating great creatives".

chunks.heading: Facebook and Instagram ads: creative is the whole game
chunks.text:
- Simon separates direct-response search ads from creative-led platforms (Facebook, Instagram, YouTube).
- On creative-led platforms, setup is streamlined. Success comes down to creative.
- He warns against ads with no emotion. His examples are competitors' (Hootsuite, Buffer) "try it for 30 days, sign up today" ads with a logo. "No one's going to stop scrolling for that."
- Creative that stops the scroll, spikes a reaction and gets engagement beats generic creative.
- He says to wait on video ads unless you already know how to make video. If not, start with image ads on Facebook.

chunks.heading: Google search ads: expensive and landing-page-dependent
chunks.text:
- Google search ads are a direct-response format shown to people actively searching, so they are intent-based.
- There is little creative lever (a headline and a description). You mostly pay Google to appear in search.
- Simon does not recommend them to beginners. For someone inexperienced they are likely where you waste the most money.
- They are quite expensive and rely heavily on the landing page doing the work.
- He does run search ads and says they convert very well.
- The other speaker (not Simon) mentioned a Google new-account coupon. That point is left out.

chunks.heading: The rage-bait Aidbase ad and why engagement makes ads cheaper
chunks.text:
- Simon's best-performing Aidbase ad on Facebook says "Let's face it, it's time to replace your chat support team with AI". It shows a stressed support agent with a 19-minute average response time next to a happy robot with a 3-second average response time. It has about 800 reactions, roughly 150 comments and 18 shares.
- Almost all the comments are hostile, for example "I would rather talk to literally nothing than a chatbot". Simon says only about two are positive.
- None of the comments criticise Aidbase as a product. They bash AI and the idea that it takes human jobs. He calls it rage bait, deliberately designed to tap emotion and provoke this reaction.
- Simon says the tracking shows that for every one negative commenter, 5 to 10 people sign up.
- Why it still converts:
  - The likely buyer may be pro-AI and wants AI to take over support. The negative comments do not put them off.
  - Visible likes, comments and shares signal that something is happening around the tool.
- How the Facebook ad auction works, per Simon:
  - Each ad opportunity triggers a small auction among advertisers targeting that person.
  - Normally you let Facebook set your bid from your ad budget and the cost of a conversion.
  - Ads are not equal in the auction. Facebook values ads that perform well as content (people stop, read comments, reply, debate).
  - Facebook rewards good content with a small discount, so you show to more people at lower cost and use the budget more effectively.
- He is not saying to design ads to anger everyone. His point is that engagement is rewarded mechanically, and an emotional ad stops the scroll.

chunks.heading: How the winning ad was found: testing, then building on one sentence
chunks.text:
- An earlier Aidbase ad pitched the freedom a founder gets from AI support. In a testing round, one caption line stood out: "it's time to replace your live chat support team with AI".
- That sentence spiked angry emojis and "replace" comments, even though the image did not match it.
- Simon took that sentence and built an image to emphasise the emotion:
  - Generated a tired man with headphones looking down in Midjourney.
  - Generated a happy robot with headphones in Midjourney.
  - Combined them in Figma in a split view with text.
  - Ran two to three more rounds of tests and tweaks.
- The tired-man image is Midjourney-generated, not a stock photo.
- Takeaway: let the data show which line resonates, then design the creative around that emotion.

chunks.heading: A testing process for founders on a small budget
chunks.text:
- Simon says you can start with $100 to $200 a month. Do not expect many signups at first. Use the ads to test creative.
- Platforms let you combine different images and different text and show the combinations. Collect data on which image, caption and description resonate best.
- Process:
  1. Put new creatives in a dedicated test campaign (he does this for every new creative).
  2. Run a test at about $10 a day for four to five days.
  3. Look at which combination of caption, description and image resonates.
  4. Build the next test round on the winners.
  5. Repeat for roughly two to three months until you have a few winning combinations and a good intuitive feel.
  6. Then slowly scale the budget and see whether the ads give results.
- His goal in the first months is to learn, treated as "a game that you're paying a little bit of money for".
- Simon does not claim any one ad is the winner up front. He lets the data decide.

chunks.heading: Scaling too early and the cost of learning
chunks.text:
- Simon says he spent more than $20,000 on ads for FeedHive before they started converting.
- He was aggressive and inexperienced. After about five conversions he decided he had a winning creative and scaled, which "is a great way to waste a lot of money really fast".
- Advertising has no free credits, so some money will be wasted while learning.
- He says you can learn this with a small budget, slowly, testing and iterating a lot.

chunks.heading: How to get started this week, plus YouTube video ads
chunks.text:
- Simon's steps for a beginner:
  1. Create a Facebook ad account (about 5 minutes).
  2. Make a Canva or Figma account. Canva is a great choice for images and short videos.
  3. Use ChatGPT for ad copy. Do not use its output directly. Describe your product and target users, ask for three angles of ad creative and a suggested image, then tweak it.
  4. Put a few hundred dollars into Facebook and see what happens.
- He expects no results at first. His bet is that you will get hooked once you see comments, clicks and visits.
- If it does not click, ads may not be your channel, but he urges trying.
- YouTube video ads are the best-performing medium across his products, and he is heavy on them.
- Good YouTube ads look like a YouTube video. Make it in your normal YouTube style, spend one to two minutes promoting the product, and run it as an ad.
- He says that with some tuning and practice (the hook, the format) this would likely beat big TV-style commercials on return on ad spend.
- He suggests a YouTuber retarget their existing subscribers with a one-minute product ad.

chunks.heading: Side notes from the episode: Aidbase embeds and building with contractors
chunks.text:
- Aidbase is Simon's AI chatbot and ticket-form product. Embeddable widgets previously used iframes, which he calls heavy and slow, with a bad user experience.
- He moved to Web components with Lit elements, which he now calls a "horrible decision" for developer experience. The team rebuilt it and now offers web components and an npm React version.
- On the free plan the widget carries small Aidbase branding. Because it is not in an iframe, Google crawls those links, so they act as backlinks.
- On managing developers, Simon says he sometimes jumps into code when he shouldn't. A task he expects to be quick can take five hours, so delegating is usually better. He sees being forced to manage as helping build clear communication and processes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon debates co-host Kyle on whether SEO and blogging are worth it for a new SaaS in 2024. He argues it's rarely needle-moving, citing weak blog conversions and unstable rankings. He also shares lessons on pricing-plan psychology, churn-feature requests and leaning on unfair advantages.

chunks.heading: Simon's view on SEO and blogging as a SaaS acquisition channel in 2024
chunks.text:
- Simon posted that "SEO content blogging is very unlikely to be a needle moving channel in 2024". He says most commenters on LinkedIn, Threads and YouTube disagreed, though people mostly agreed with his other six points.
- He later clarified that this is a "bold statement" and a "bit of a stretch". He does not think blogging hurts, and he still does it for all his products.
- He employs an SEO specialist who works on blog content all day.
- His core claim: if you launch a new SaaS in 2024 and make Google ranking your main acquisition channel, then "unless you're in the outlier group you're probably not going to do anything needle moving".
- Blogging works as a supporting channel. It is not what he would build a business on.

chunks.heading: Evidence from FeedHive: rankings that bring little traffic
chunks.text:
- FeedHive has several articles on page one of Google. For example, the "TikTok bios" article ranks in the top five.
- When Simon counts clicks to that article and tracks conversions, the numbers are "very very little". Some come through, but not much.
- He says: "if we were only doing this we wouldn't be in business".
- He has published hundreds of blog posts across FeedHive and LinkDrip, and is now doing the same for Aidbase. He calls this "standard blogging".
- He admits they have not tried building larger topic structures such as hubs, and says that could be worth testing.

chunks.heading: Rankings are not permanent
chunks.text:
- A common pro-SEO argument is "once you rank, you're set". Simon's experience is different: "there isn't really a once you rank".
- On his Saas products, once an article reaches page one it is very hard to stay there. Someone else comes in and outranks you.
- Ranking is something you keep working on.
- Simon notes that Google keeps rolling out core updates. A March 2024 update was meant to remove "unhelpful content", with a stated goal of cutting low-quality, unoriginal results by 40%.
- Seen from that angle, SEO is a year-long investment that Google can undermine overnight with an algorithm change.

chunks.heading: Why AI content could weaken search itself
chunks.text:
Simon describes a hypothetical, not a prediction:

- With a model like GPT-5, one person could generate 10,000 articles pushing a false claim (his example: that vaccines cause cancer), complete with fake citations and AI-generated video, and publish them to rank on Google.
- If that happens at scale, the open web becomes a "wasteland" where nothing can be trusted, and people stop searching it.
- Trusted information could end up in a few protected databases owned by big players, and a new blog could not simply publish its way in.
- When Kyle answered that the practical response is to build authority now, Simon called it a good comeback. He agreed that becoming a trusted source early matters if that future arrives. He stressed it is conjecture.

chunks.heading: Pricing experiment on Aidbase
chunks.text:
- Aidbase's cheapest paid plan was $99/month, with a top plan at $399/month.
- Simon added a $29/month plan and set its limits somewhere between the free plan and the $99 plan.
- Result: "substantially more signups", but almost all on the $29 plan. Barely anyone takes the $99 plan, and almost nobody the $399 plan.
- The few $399 customers are mostly ones Simon talked to personally. He closed them with a sales conversation and added something extra to make the plan worthwhile.
- He explains the pressure as a symptom of the SaaS market: "so many offers… so many competitors" that prices keep getting driven down.
- Next steps he is considering:
  - lower the limits on the $29 plan so it is less attractive, or
  - widen the gap in limits between the $29 and $99 plans so the jump in price looks worth it.
- Pricing psychology he uses:
  - An **anchor**: a high top price makes the middle plan look cheaper.
  - A **reverse anchor**: a very cheap plan with very low limits pushes people toward the middle plan, because "I might as well jump to the middle one".
- He checks whether the extra subscriptions raise total revenue, and he sets limits so the new plan does not cost more to deliver.

chunks.heading: Fixing churn from feature requests
chunks.text:
- Simon warns that building the feature churned users ask for is "a little bit like playing Russian roulette".
- On FeedHive, users kept saying one missing feature was why they cancelled. When the team shipped it, nothing changed, because users found a new reason to churn.
- Smaller things users had phrased as "it would also be nice" were different. When FeedHive added those, churn dropped significantly.
- Interviewing users one-to-one about why they leave is hard to do, but it is the way to collect these data points.

chunks.heading: Simon's rule on using your unfair advantage
chunks.text:
- He agrees with Kyle that you should lean on your existing expertise when choosing a channel.
- His own: "video ads for me and we all have these things that will just get us ahead of the game faster".
- When launching something new, he asks where his unfair advantages are and capitalizes on them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: First episode of Zero To Million SaaS. Simon explains why a $1M ARR SaaS is the right bootstrapper target, why SaaS is worth the risk, and how he is growing his new AI support tool 8base: a free plan with a branded chat widget as a distribution and backlink engine, funded at a loss, versus the hard-paywall trials that grew his other products faster.

chunks.heading: Why Simon builds bootstrapped SaaS and why $1M ARR is the target
chunks.text:
- He frames $1M ARR as a huge milestone for "normal people" building bootstrapped businesses, even if VC-backed startups would shrug at it.
- His mantra: "forget all the big billion dollar headlines and just build a million dollar SaaS." He thinks many people can do it today.
- He has run three SaaS products, was about to launch a fourth, and runs a YouTube channel about SaaS and online business. He was a software developer and freelance consultant before going full-time into entrepreneurship about three years before this episode.
- He has tried other models and compares them to SaaS: dropshipping (a business reaching almost $1M a year, since gone), affiliate marketing, courses.
- Why SaaS wins for him: recurring income, the enjoyment of building, and the scalability of "sit and type some stuff on my keyboard and put it on the internet and then random people will just come by and give me their money."
- He notes most users of his tools have never spoken to him, and many don't know who he is. He likens that to the SaaS tools most people use daily without knowing the founders.

chunks.heading: The scale of his portfolio and the state of the market
chunks.text:
- FeedHive: social media management tool. LinkDrip: link shortener. Both are his main revenue drivers.
- TinyQ: a small editing tool he acquired.
- 8base (eightbase): an AI support ecosystem covering chatbots, ticket forms and email, with AI as the primary helper and automation layer.
- He acknowledges SaaS growth rates were declining at the time (a ProfitWell chart of annual growth since 2021 was discussed), but he stays in the game anyway.
- He flags that SaaS is arguably the riskiest business model, because you can lose a lot of money.
- He says the downside is real, and that his co-host's six-figure-in-the-red experience shows how it can go.

chunks.heading: 8base launch trajectory and the post-launch plateau
chunks.text:
- He launched 8base about two months before recording and made a YouTube video that drove the launch.
- MRR went up to about $7,000 relatively fast, then "the initial round of churn kicked in" and settled at roughly $4,000-5,000 MRR.
- The pattern: a launch spike from hype ("Simon's launching a new SaaS, let's try it out"), then growth flattened.
- His current job is turning spiky, launch-driven growth into a consistent, continuous growth engine.
- On reaching $1M ARR within a year: "I don't know man, it's a stretch." He says he is not in a big hurry.

chunks.heading: Free plan vs. opt-out trial: a deliberate departure from his other products
chunks.text:
- FeedHive and LinkDrip use a 7-day opt-out trial. The credit card is required up front, access is blocked until trial signup, and the user is auto-upgraded after 7 days unless they cancel.
- Early on, FeedHive tried a freemium model. It "just didn't work." Putting everything behind a paywall made growth increase "much much much faster."
- With 8base he is deliberately trying the opposite, partly because of his open-source background:
  - A premium plan plus a fairly generous, fully free plan.
  - No trial, and no aggressive upgrade prompting.
  - Signup drops people straight into the tool. There is only a small modal in the corner, and upgrade prompts appear when limits are hit.
  - Features aren't locked out. Users can start using the tool immediately.

chunks.heading: The free-plan growth strategy: chat widgets as backlinks and branding
chunks.text:
- The core of 8base is a chatbot. On the free plan the widget shows "Powered by 8base" branding.
- His main goal for now is getting the widget onto as many websites as possible rather than driving revenue.
- Reasons it works:
  - Backlinks: he does not use iframes. Google reportedly doesn't count widget links as backlinks if its crawler can identify them as widgets, and without an iframe it can't tell. So each embed is effectively a backlink.
  - Traffic and exposure: other visitors see the branding when they open the chatbot.
- Other levers: influencer marketing (the first round of influencers started posting the day of recording) and advertising a bit later. The influencer goal is again to get people onto the free plan and the widget onto their sites.
- AI cost is real. Free users get included AI, though they can bring their own OpenAI key to bypass limits. The result is that 8base is running at a loss.
- His stance: he expects to run in the red for most of the year and does not aim for profitability this year. He is happy to invest in widget distribution.
- He hopes to reach profitability before $1M ARR, and admits burning toward a million with no profit would be uncomfortable for a bootstrapper.

chunks.heading: Distribution experiments and "sneaky" growth ideas
chunks.text:
- His general belief: bootstrappers competing with VC-backed tools in SEO and ads "need to be sneaky" and creative, because they lack budgets and staff.
- Idea he floated, which he says he doesn't plan to do: manual chatbot outreach. Crawl websites that have chat widgets, open the chat, strike up a conversation about their site, then pitch 8base. A small team of five could be hired on Upwork.
  - Best targets would be small ecommerce and dropshipping stores and small SaaS, where the founder is staffing the chat personally and is stressed.
  - Poor targets would be larger companies with live support agents, who may not want to promote a tool that replaces them.
  - He notes he has never heard of anyone doing this.
- On cold email, he points out that buying email lists and spamming is now clearly illegal (especially in the EU) without consent. He had not tried automated outbound at scale and called it a future experiment.
- Suggestion he received and says he'll check out: use a tech-detection tool like BuiltWith to build a list of sites using competitors' live chat, then run a multi-channel outreach tool (lemlist) combining LinkedIn interaction and email sequences.
- His sources of SEO and ads advice for others are limited here: he says SEO is not his strong suit, and that he leans on influencer marketing and advertising.

chunks.heading: Experimenting as an operating principle
chunks.text:
- He wants the podcast itself to run "the lean way," like his SaaS: drop a bunch of experiments, try different formats, and use audience feedback to decide what works.
- He and his co-host agreed to hold each other accountable for outlandish growth experiments and report results in later episodes (a viral-style post test on one side, chatbot outreach or lemlist outreach on his).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon explains how he cut his team from 11 to 3 by delegating video production, coding, DevOps, paid ads, outreach and support to AI agents. The key is a strong harness: scripts, QA gates, narrow permissions, spending limits and human approval for big decisions. He argues a small AI-native team is now an advantage over a large one.

chunks.heading: Running an AI-native company: the video production pipeline
chunks.text:
Simon's rule: the ideas and opinions stay human, and AI does the production. He says nothing has moved his business more consistently over five years than video (YouTube plus social, putting his face behind the products). He used to spend "hundreds, maybe even thousands of hours editing" and had people on research, strategy, editing and thumbnails.

- **Script first.** He talks to his agents by voice, spills the argument and nuance, and an AI script writer structures it. If AI invents the ideas you get "generic AI slop." Every line has to sound like something he would say.
- **Record to the script.** He follows it almost word for word on a teleprompter, which takes practice.
- **Script as map.** A transcription model returns every word with a timestamp. The editing agent matches the recording to the script and finds fail takes, restarts and the right take.
- **Editing stack.** DaVinci Resolve is scripted and controlled by agents (computer use only when needed). Remotion handles most motion graphics, Blender is used for 3D, and AI-generated visuals are used when they fit. A library of reusable components and Fusion templates is built against exact script lines.
- **QA loop.** The AI team reviews exports for broken renders, bad graphics and pacing, and sends problems back to the agent that made them. He then spends about 30 minutes on a final polish in Resolve.
- **Distribution.** Done through FeedHive (one of his products), which connects to Claude Code and OpenClaw via REST API and MCP. Agents prepare posts and media, schedule, and he reviews the plan before anything goes out.
- **Weekly output:** one long-form YouTube video, three clips for Twitter/LinkedIn, and three Shorts/TikToks/Reels.

chunks.heading: AI coding: discipline, harnesses and self-hosting
chunks.text:
Simon runs a portfolio of four SaaS products (tens of thousands of users, seven figures in yearly revenue). He warns AI coding is a double-edged sword: "complete utter garbage software and slop websites" are everywhere, and it "requires discipline."

- **Infrastructure.** He moved from AWS (DynamoDB, Lambda, Fargate; expensive and locked in) to self-hosted Docker, Kubernetes and Postgres, with AI help.
- **AI as 24/7 DevOps.** Agents watch the cluster, detect anomalies and often fix them before users notice. Setup: a privileged Ubuntu user with a Kubernetes role, and agents SSH in with it to run commands.
- **Team change.** The dev team went from four (including him) to him plus one human dev. Neither writes code, and "we barely even read code anymore." They act as product managers: plan features, talk to users, set the roadmap, make architecture decisions and review.
- **QA gates.** Agents use browser automation like Puppeteer. Work needs automated tests plus screen recordings from agents proving the feature works before it reaches production.
- **Making the codebase agent-friendly.** Moving fragmented code into monorepos (which he "used to hate"), plus linting, eval rules and change locks the agents can access.
- **Takeaway:** spraying code with AI is not leverage. The advantage comes from the harness, QA and guardrails, which large engineering teams can't easily copy.

chunks.heading: Paid ads run by agents
chunks.text:
Early FeedHive marketing was Simon sharing builds on Twitter, but that keeps you in the "founder bubble." Paid ads reach cold audiences and quickly show whether people care, but they are a lot of work (offer, creatives, setup, tracking, new versions).

- **Weak-signal risk.** "If you optimize for a weak signal, Meta will happily find thousands of people who produce more of that weak signal." Asking an agent for 50 headlines from a landing page is "almost completely useless"; creatives are the easiest part.
- **Setup.** Agents connect via the Google Ads API (developer token) and Meta API (access token), with exposed actions, budget limits and campaign rules. Bigger changes need his approval.
- **Context given to the agent:** the offer, audience, landing page, previous creatives, and the post-click events that matter.
- **Creative production.** Remotion and HeyGen templates let the agent swap hooks, footage, text, screenshots and CTA, then render for each placement. When a human is needed, he records on his phone.
- **Example: the Founders Stack campaign.** Two phone-recorded videos: one for cold audiences, one for skeptical visitors doubting a lifetime deal across four SaaS products. Agents built the Meta ads with separate audiences, exclusions, tracking and copy.
- **Analysis.** Agents pull Meta and Google data and compare it with his own backend: click, trial, purchase, real usage. With FeedHive they compared Meta against Google Search and Performance Max, found wasteful search terms, added negative keywords, and separated curiosity signups from people with a real problem.
- **Loop:** pause a variation, make three more hooks, remove terms, scale a test. He approves large changes, and the agent applies them. This replaces handoffs between copywriter, editor, media buyer and analyst.

chunks.heading: Personalized outreach through Gmail
chunks.text:
Simon likes direct outreach for testing an offer early: no audience needed, just find the right people and see the reply. Manual work is heavy, and big Apollo/Clay/Instantly/Zapier stacks often end up as "spam with more software involved."

- **Setup.** Connect Gmail via API, give the agent the offer, target company type and campaign rules, set hard sending limits, and put sensitive actions behind approval.
- **Research first.** The agent uses Puppeteer and web search to find companies, their customers and products, and why the offer is relevant. If it can't explain the fit in plain English, "the email just doesn't go out."
- **Slow and case by case.** No big lists or blasts. The research becomes the message, and the agent sends from Gmail within the limits.
- **Replies.** The agent reopens the original thread with the offer, research, sent email and reply in front of it, so follow-ups reflect the real conversation. He takes over when a reply crosses an approval rule.
- **Safeguards:** narrow permissions, a hard sending ceiling, and a separate approval step for anything sensitive.
- **Tradeoff:** it won't scale as far as outbound stacks, "but it also doesn't have to." Quality emails to vetted leads beat spam.

chunks.heading: Support as an agent workflow
chunks.text:
Simon says the support inbox tells you what is actually wrong with the business, and it catches bugs, confusing decisions and annoyances. But support gets expensive: a hard ticket moves from frontline to technical support to a developer and back, with the account re-explained at each handoff, and "a strange ticket can eat up half a day."

- **Agent capability.** Six months ago such jobs often failed halfway (lost context, bad calls). Now an agent can use tools, inspect logs and traces, investigate, and keep working until the ticket is resolved.
- **Tooling.** He uses AbBase (his own product), which connects to OpenClaw, Hermes, Claw Code or other agent setups through a full API for the support workflow.
- **In-app forms.** Each product has an in-app support form that can ask for product-specific details and attach existing customer and account data. The agent gets the message, form data, customer history and account.
- **Resolution path.** The agent pulls logs and traces, reproduces the problem, follows the evidence into the codebase, prepares the fix, runs tests, and in many cases ships it and replies, "without any human involvement." The conversation stays in one ticket, and the agent asks the customer for missing info there.
- **Pattern detection.** One agent handles all conversations, so it spots the same bug in different wording, confusing workflows and small frustrations, and shows what to fix or redesign.
- **Results:** customers report "higher satisfaction than ever before," and the agent does work that used to occupy several full-time employees.

chunks.heading: Small AI-native team as a bootstrapping advantage
chunks.text:
Simon went from 11 people to three (himself included). Under tight human supervision, his agents plan, execute and run most of the business. He says a large team is "straight up a disadvantage," and that running "a highly efficient small AI native team is the biggest business opportunity you get right now."

- **Human roles that remain:** deciding what to say, recording the video, approving results, product management, architecture decisions, and approving sensitive actions.
- **Pattern across every function:** give agents API/tool access, business context, hard limits and approval gates, then review evidence-backed recommendations.
- **Caveat:** "It's not for everyone and it's not always as easy as some people make it seem."
- **Lifetime-license model.** His tools (FeedHive for social, AbBase for support) are sold as one-time lifetime licenses with no monthly subscription, bundled at foundersstack.pro.
- **Advice:** give your AI the video link plus his full list of tools, models, versions and harnesses, and ask how to apply the ideas to your business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon explains that AI agent quality depends on the harness around the model, not the model itself. He walks through five layers he uses across his SaaS products and YouTube channel: eval classifiers, schema contracts, purpose-built tools, deterministic workflows, and failure replay.

chunks.heading: The core claim: the harness decides quality, not the model
chunks.text:
- Simon runs several SaaS products and a YouTube channel with a team of AI agents handling support, product development and marketing, including video production.
- He has moved those agents between GPT, Kimi, GLM, Fable and weaker models. Each produces different work, but "none of them gets to decide what our company accepts."
- His thesis: "whenever you see companies doing really well with AI, it's almost never because of the model and always because of the quality of the harness." A better model can improve output, but "it still doesn't own the company standard. Your company does."
- He built five layers of custom harness around the agent team. With them, older Opus models or small models like Qwen or DeepSeek still produce very good work. Without them, even GPT-5.6 and Fable produce sloppy work and drag you into tedious review.
- His advice for beginners: give this video's transcript to an existing agentic system (OpenClaw, Hermes), ask where each layer would help company operations, and have it set them up.

chunks.heading: Layer 1: eval classifiers (separate doing the work from judging it)
chunks.text:
- Problem: an agent can repeat your rules back, still break them, and then spot the exact mistakes when asked to review afterwards. Following instructions and judging the result in one pass is hard, so he splits them into separate jobs.
- An eval checks one piece of work against one standard and returns a simple verdict, like a unit test for AI work.
- Deterministic evals are plain code (missing field, failed test). Judgment evals use another model with a system prompt that has one job: inspect this input against these rules and classify it. Input is the work, the rule, and a few pass/fail examples. Output is one class (usually approved or rejected, or a score) plus the reason and evidence.
- YouTube script example: each chapter runs three independent checks:
  - **Slop gate** (deterministic): a phrase blacklist ("this is the part where") plus regexes for patterns like "it's not X, it's Y". No AI needed.
  - **Voice check** (AI): compares the chapter with a large collection of his past scripts for style and tone.
  - **Job check** (AI): does the chapter do its job (intro creates tension and makes a clear promise; a middle chapter advances the argument and sets up the next part), using past scripts and official YouTube writing guidance.
- A rejection returns the exact reason. These evals send the writing agent back to redo its work "more than a hundred times on average" before a script reaches him, so he spends his time on argument and taste instead of nitpicking.
- The same principle is applied to scripts, code, support replies and research.

chunks.heading: Layer 2: schema contracts (define "done" in a machine-checkable format)
chunks.text:
- Problem: an agent can finish a task without returning what the next step needs. The work looks complete, but the evidence was never saved and the handoff falls apart. A vague definition of finished work lets the agent fill in the blanks.
- His analogy: you wouldn't hire a contractor to "renovate the office and make it look kind of nice." You agree on deliverables, evidence and format.
- Implementation: give the model a JSON schema listing fields, what belongs in each, and which are required (OpenAI's structured outputs is one implementation). Required only means the field exists, so add tighter rules: ID formats must match, reproduction steps can't be empty, at least one log or trace must be attached. Normal software validates this and rejects bad handoffs immediately.
- Example, a support-to-technical handoff for a login bug needs: customer ID, account ID, exact reproduction steps, expected vs actual behavior, and logs or traces from the failed request.
- Predictable placement lets a separate eval judge whether the logs actually support the claimed cause without digging through a long conversation.
- Used for research, code delivery, sponsor qualification and production handoffs.
- A valid schema can still contain garbage (wrong request's logs, misread logs), so evals still run after contract validation.

chunks.heading: Layer 3: purpose-built tools (least privilege)
chunks.text:
- Problem: people give an agent a general database tool or broad API credentials and write "only use it when necessary" in the prompt. He calls this insane, since you wouldn't give a human employee that access. His analogy: sending someone to collect a box from one storage room with the master key to the office.
- Principle of least privilege (NIST: you get only the access you need for the job).
- A purpose-built tool exposes one narrow company action. Normal software handles permissions, validation, filtering and formatting. The model only requests a tool call; software checks the inputs, the agent's permissions, and whether a human must approve before anything runs.
- Sponsor-inquiry agent example: it can list active sponsor conversations, fetch one specific conversation, read the content schedule and allowed price ranges, and prepare a reply for approval. It cannot browse unrelated records, pull other customers' conversations, or send the reply itself. No tool exists for those actions.
- Product development: no agent can push broad changes to production or write directly to the production database.
- "The system prompt isn't our security boundary. The capability simply isn't available."
- This matters most for frontier models like GPT-5.6 and Fable, which are very smart and "very, very eager to go out of their way."
- Narrow toolsets exist for support, publishing, development, analytics and finance.
- Side note: software your agents use needs proper APIs, or you end up with workarounds that break these boundaries. His SaaS products (FeedHive, Aidbase) are built for humans and agents with APIs, MCPs and connectors for OpenClaw and Claude Code. FeedHive lets agents and humans create, review and publish together; Aidbase has a public API, customizable ticket forms and inboxes for support. (Founder's Deck is a one-time purchase bundling four tools.)

chunks.heading: Layer 4: deterministic workflows (software controls the sequence)
chunks.text:
- Problem: models are probabilistic, so the same job can yield different decisions. That's fine for interpreting research, but terrible when the agent decides an approval "feels optional that day," skips a failed check or publishes early. An apology afterwards is worthless.
- His analogy: pilots use checklists after thousands of hours. The AI makes judgments inside a job; normal software controls the order of jobs.
- Bug-fix example (FeedHive post composer), as workflow states:
  1. **Reproduction:** agent must reproduce the bug and return exact steps plus failure evidence.
  2. **Regression test:** it writes a test and shows that it fails; an eval or human reviewer checks that the test actually captures the original bug.
  3. **Implementation:** only after approval, the agent changes code in an isolated workspace.
  4. **Verification:** the regression test and the broader suite must pass, and the original reproduction steps are rerun with the result attached. Any failure or missing evidence sends the task back.
  5. **Review:** a human inspects the diff, the failing-before test and the passing evidence. Only his approval lets the workflow merge.
- Allowed moves between states are transition rules. The agent decides how to fix the code, but cannot decide reproduction was unnecessary, swap in an easier test, or declare victory because the patch looks sensible.
- Also used for support, escalation, sponsor replies, social publishing and YouTube videos. "It never gets to improvise our company process."

chunks.heading: Layer 5: failure replay (regression tests for agent mistakes)
chunks.text:
- Problem: the same mistakes returned after being fixed. Adding a prompt instruction felt like a fix, but weeks later a model or tool change brought the issue back, so you pay for the same lesson twice.
- Example: a research agent returned a claim with every schema field filled, but the cited source didn't support the claim. Fixing that one result is easy; three weeks later a new model made the same mistake in another document and nobody remembered the case. Aviation turns lessons into checklists, training or aircraft design, and he wanted the same.
- What he saves per failure: the original task, the bad claim, the source that failed to support it, and the exact reason the eval should have rejected it.
- Two replays:
  - **Eval replay:** feed the old bad claim and source into the current eval; it must still reject it. Rerun old cases before any eval change goes live.
  - **Producer replay:** before moving research to a smaller or cheaper model, give it the original research task again. It must produce fresh research with claim, URL and supporting excerpt, and the eval checks that the excerpt proves the claim. Fabricated sources, wrong passages or confident claims with no evidence fail the switch. Adjust the prompt or harness and rerun until "the old failure stays dead."
- The failure library covers missing delivery evidence, wrong tool selection, actions outside permissions and sloppy writing patterns.
- Model-switching test: public benchmarks show how a model does on someone else's test; he cares whether a model survives the mistakes that already cost his company time. "This is the test I care about before I let any new model anywhere near my business."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon argues AI can now handle founder judgment if given real business data. He runs three audits: finding the real ICP from billing, database and domain data; reconstructing churn by joining cancellation feedback, support history and product usage; and mining reviews and communities for repeated buyer pain that fits his portfolio. Each audit ends in a prepared experiment.

chunks.heading: Giving an AI agent real business data to find the true ICP
chunks.text:
Simon argues the standard advice ("use AI for execution, keep judgment for the founder") no longer holds. He now runs three continuous AI audits where the agent decides what to focus on, fix and test next.

- **The ICP audit starts from real signals, not persona brainstorming.** Asking ChatGPT for a persona gives "generic founder BS".
- **The agent needs three inputs:**
  - The payment signal (Stripe or the billing platform), which shows who stays long enough to matter.
  - Product behavior from the database, even if analytics tracking is imperfect.
  - Customer context, such as what the company does, usually visible from the website behind the user's email domain.
- **Why AI beats the founder here:** founders look at Stripe, dashboards and support in separate pieces. The agent connects payment, behavior and context at once and shows which customers look alike.
- **The simple version:** give the agent Stripe and read-only database access, let it enrich users from their domains, websites and support history, then ask which customers get the most value and how to find more of them.
- **Read-only database access is enough.** The agent can query raw tables even when tracking was never finished.

chunks.heading: FeedHive: the ICP was more technical than assumed
chunks.text:
Simon ran the ICP audit on FeedHive using mostly raw database data rather than the formal tracking setup.

- **His assumed ICP:** social media managers, agencies and small businesses wanting a clean UI to schedule content. These users exist, so it wasn't wrong.
- **What the audit found:** many of the strongest users are more technical. These are startup teams, founders and technical marketers who want social media plugged into a larger automation workflow. They are comfortable with APIs, MCPs and agents, and care about connecting FeedHive to the rest of their operating system.
- **Implications he drew:** the landing page, the ad angle and the first features shown to new users might all need to change for this segment.
- **The loop he runs with agents:** audit, hypothesis, experiment, validation. The research agent turns its findings into a landing page version for the segment, a few ad angles, a campaign structure and the metrics to judge it by.
- **Agent setup:** agents that code, agents with direct access to his Google and Meta ad accounts, and an ICP research agent that feeds them.

chunks.heading: Churn audit: reconstruct the journey, don't summarize the cancellation reason
chunks.text:
- **Cancellation reasons are a thin version of the truth.** They show how the customer explained the decision at the end, not what caused it. Causes can include slow time to value, signing up for the wrong thing, a landing page attracting the wrong customer, or getting stuck in onboarding.
- **The problem is fragmentation.** The cancellation form, support conversations, product usage and the pre-signup promise (ad or landing page) each tell part of the story.
- **His goal for the agent:** reconstruct the customer journey around churn rather than summarize churn reasons.
- **His 8base setup** (an AI-powered support tool he and his team run):
  - Support emails go into 8base.
  - Each app has an in-app support page that creates tickets.
  - An 8base form replaces Stripe's generic cancellation question and collects the churn reason before the customer cancels.
  - The embedded form sends context with each ticket: who the user is, which account, what they last did in the app.
- **Without a full agent setup:** export the support data from 8base as a CSV and let ChatGPT or Claude analyze it.

chunks.heading: Separating wrong-fit churn from product-failure churn
chunks.text:
Simon wants the churn agent to do one simple thing: split customers who were probably never a good fit from customers who should have succeeded but didn't. These are different problems.

- **Wrong customers leaving** points back to positioning, ads or the promise made before sign-up.
- **Right customers leaving** points to where the product failed them: confusing onboarding, never reaching the first useful result, or support seeing the same issue repeatedly without it becoming product work.
- **The simple version:**
  1. Get cancellation feedback and support history into one place.
  2. Add product context around each customer.
  3. Have the agent compare that with what they did in the product before leaving.
  4. Have it prepare the next fix: an onboarding step, a support article, a product fix or a positioning change.

chunks.heading: Opportunity audit: find new SaaS ideas from repeated buyer pain
chunks.text:
- **Ideas come from repeated market signals, not brainstorming.** Examples: a customer asks for an integration, a community says existing tools are too complicated, a review says one workflow is still painful. Simon did this manually for years by looking at products people already pay for and finding where users are clearly unhappy.
- **Don't ask ChatGPT for 20 SaaS ideas.** He calls the result generic "micro SaaS garbage ideas that everyone else gets".
- **Agent inputs:** categories to watch, competitors and adjacent tools near his portfolio (for example near FeedHive, 8base and the business systems he has built), and the products he already runs.
- **Where it collects signals:** review sites (G2, Capterra, Trustpilot), Reddit threads, comparison pages, comments and competitor communities.
- **What it looks for:** repeated complaints, missing workflows, integration requests, pricing complaints, and awkward workarounds where people stitch several tools together.

chunks.heading: Filtering ideas by portfolio fit and preparing validation
chunks.text:
- **Fit filter:** the agent checks whether an idea serves a customer he already understands, sits close to an existing product, connects naturally into the portfolio, and can be validated with his existing audience.
- **Principle:** "the best idea is not always the biggest market." Sometimes it is the one you can test fastest because you have an unfair advantage around it.
- **Validation step the agent prepares:** a simple landing page, a waitlist form, a few ad angles around the pain point, and a clear metric for whether people care.
- **The simple version:** give the agent categories, nearby competitors and your products. Ask it to find repeated buyer pain, rank opportunities by pain and portfolio fit, and prepare one small validation test for the best idea.

chunks.heading: AI as an advisor inside the business
chunks.text:
- Simon used to see agents as useful only when he already knew what he wanted done. With enough real business context, they can now look at the situation, say what is going on, and point toward the next decision.
- **Why:** the agent can hold more messy context than he can.
- **His guardrails:** start read-only, and decide where approval is required before anything goes live.
- His conclusion: founder judgment is no longer completely off-limits to AI. With the right context, an agent can help run the business at a higher level.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon argues micro SaaS is following the drop shipping path: founders renting 95% of their operation (hosting, database, AI, payments, traffic) get squeezed as AI makes software cheap to copy. Survivors own their infrastructure, data and audience. He shares his own response: a one-time-purchase bundle (FounderStack), self-hostable or open-source products, and eventually owned hardware.

chunks.heading: Why micro SaaS is getting squeezed (the drop shipping parallel)
chunks.text:
- Simon compares micro SaaS today to drop shipping around 2017: cheap to start, easy to copy, good margins at first.
- The drop shipping playbook: find a cheap product on AliExpress, list it on a Shopify store, run Facebook ads, and the supplier ships directly to the customer. In his words, "95% of the e-commerce operation belonged to someone else."
- The squeeze: more sellers of the same products, pricier Facebook ads, suppliers and Shopify taking their share, and customers learning to spot generic stores. Margins went paper thin because drop shippers stood "at the end of a long line of companies that all got paid first."
- E-commerce did not die. Winners started owning more of the operation: real brands, their own products (often via manufacturers or controlled inventory), and their own distribution through social channels and email lists.
- He argues SaaS is following the same path right now.

chunks.heading: The rented-stack micro SaaS model and why it is dying
chunks.text:
- Micro SaaS boomed because one founder could build almost everything by wiring together rented services.
- Typical stack he describes: Vercel for hosting, Supabase for data, OpenAI for every AI request, Stripe for payments, and customers from Google, Meta, X, Product Hunt or "whoever controls the traffic this month." Again about 95% of the operation belongs to someone else.
- This worked while software was hard to build and customers had few options.
