- AI now makes software "ridiculously cheap and fast to produce." Every small SaaS faces new competitors, free alternatives, open source projects, and bigger platforms adding the same feature into existing products.
- Meanwhile every rented layer (hosting, database, AI provider, payment processor, ad platform) gets paid before the founder, who keeps whatever is left.
- His conclusion: SaaS stays enormous, but the micro SaaS playbook of wrapping a few APIs, adding a monthly subscription and renting the whole operation is dying.

chunks.heading: What survivors need to do: reclaim infrastructure
chunks.text:
- Self-host the product.
- Control the data and configuration.
- Understand the infrastructure.
- Make every important dependency replaceable.
- He admits this is harder than "connecting five services and launching another wrapper over the weekend," but argues easy businesses attract everyone, and then suppliers, platforms and advertisers slowly take the margin until nothing is left.

chunks.heading: What survivors need to do: own distribution
chunks.text:
- Build an audience on social channels people actually follow, plus an email list you control.
- Ads should amplify that distribution instead of being the only way to reach a customer.
- Same lesson as the e-commerce brands that stopped paying Facebook for every customer.

chunks.heading: FounderStack: one-time purchase instead of subscriptions
chunks.text:
- Most of Simon's SaaS products were sold as subscriptions. A little over a year before this video he introduced FounderStack, a bundle of all of them as a one-time purchase.
- It was meant to be a short campaign lasting a few months, but people kept buying consistently, so he kept it available alongside the subscriptions.
- He says the unit economics "actually work really well" because he has spent a lot of time making infrastructure very efficient, so products can be maintained without every customer paying monthly.
- He thinks "the old idea of buying software and actually owning it deserves a comeback."
- He acknowledges lifetime deals have a bad reputation, associated with cheap marketplace deals (he names AppSumo and Dealify) where you buy a random tool and hope the company exists next year. His goal is serious software that keeps improving while buyers own it instead of "leasing it forever."
- The bundle currently has four tools, with numbers five and six about to launch. He wants to keep expanding the portfolio with useful products sold through FounderStack.

chunks.heading: Simon's plan: self-hostable, open source, and owned hardware
chunks.text:
- Stated as plans, not done: "We're not there yet."
- Make the entire SaaS portfolio self-hostable, and possibly open source.
- Move hosting from Hetzner to a Swiss company called Private Layer.
- Eventually rent real colocation space in a data center in Lucerne, running products on hardware he physically owns.
- That hardware would also run open-weight models such as Kimi, GLM and MiniMax, instead of depending on a rented AI provider.
- His reasoning: AI makes good software easier to build and maintain, and his infrastructure keeps getting more efficient.
- Stated direction: customers actually own the software they buy, with at least the option to fully self-host every product.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon cut his team from 11 to 3 using AI while revenue and margins rose, but argues it only works for process-centric companies run by operator-type founders. He gives three checkpoints and the RIP model (Repetitive, Predictable, Isolated) to decide which tasks to hand to AI.

chunks.heading: Checkpoint 1: Human-centric vs process-centric company DNA
chunks.text:
- Simon cut his team from 11 people to 3 over the last year by replacing their work with AI. Revenue went up, output increased and margins improved. He runs a portfolio of 5 SaaS products.
- He cites an MIT study saying 95% of AI initiatives fail to deliver measurable value, so only 5% of companies actually succeed in replacing human work with AI. He says AI is not the problem; the failure is treating AI like a magic employee instead of a machine that follows strict instructions.
- He argues that replacing a team with AI only works for a specific type of company run by a specific type of owner. For others it "might be a terrible idea."
- **Human-centric business:** run by people for people, with the focus on culture, collaboration and goal alignment.
  - Flat structure, everyone involved in key decisions, a lot of effort on motivation and personal alignment with the mission.
  - Examples: creative agencies, high-touch consultancies, typical startups where culture fit matters as much as skills.
  - The value comes from the friction and chaos of human collaboration. Replacing the team with AI "will rip the soul out of your company." AI doesn't care about your mission, doesn't need to feel heard and is bad at nuanced cultural decisions.
  - In this kind of company you can augment your team with AI but not replace it.
- **Process-centric business:** runs like a machine on SOPs, guidelines and checklists.
  - Each person gets a specific task with clear requirements, a deadline and dependencies. Decisions are made at the top by the owner and the team executes.
  - Simon's business has always been heavily process-centric. His biggest hiring selling point was "no meetings, no ceremonies, work whenever you want as long as stuff gets done."
  - The flip side was little culture. He rarely involved the team in big strategic decisions and didn't require passion for the company vision. The team cared only as far as they needed context for their work.
  - He says this is why his AI transition worked: an AI agent loves clear instructions, SOPs and checklists, and needs no pep talk or Zoom meeting to feel included.

chunks.heading: Checkpoint 2: Are you a leader or an operator?
chunks.text:
- Simon says the common advice that a successful CEO must be a great leader (rallying the team, empathy, resolving conflict, motivating people) is not true.
- **Leader:** superpowers are empathy, communication and culture building. He names Steven Bartlett, Dan Martell and Gary Vaynerchuk as examples.
- **Operator:** gets things done, is obsessed with systems, data and logic, strong at systems thinking, often lower on soft skills. His example is Elon Musk, who cares about "the physics of the problem, the efficiency of the line, and the output of the system."
- A great operator is usually not a great leader and vice versa. Natural leaders hire COOs or project managers to handle systems; natural operators hire team leads to handle people.
- Simon calls himself an operator, not a natural-born leader. He loves building systems and optimizing workflows but has never enjoyed motivation, conflict resolution or emotional alignment.
- Operators tend to end up running process-centric businesses, and leaders human-centric ones.
- For an operator, "AI is your dream employee": it needs logic and instructions, not empathy or motivation.
- A natural leader who thrives on personal connection will struggle to manage an AI workforce, because you can't motivate an AI, inspire it with a vision or take it to a one-on-one to resolve conflict.
- His conclusion: a leader running a human-centric business should not try to replace the workforce with AI and should invest in becoming a better leader instead, because that is where their ROI is. An operator running a process-centric business is in the perfect position to replace the team with AI.

chunks.heading: The RIP model: which tasks to hand to AI
chunks.text:
- Even with the right business and the right personality, Simon says you can't fire everyone at random. He uses a framework he calls the RIP model (Repetitive, Predictable, Isolated) to pick which roles or tasks to replace.
- **R, Repetitive:** the task is identical every time. Examples: copying data from an email into a spreadsheet, formatting a monthly report, categorizing support tickets. "If a human is doing this effectively like a robot, an actual robot will do it better, faster, and cheaper."
- **P, Predictable:** there is a clear right or wrong answer.
  - Good fit: writing an SQL query that pulls active users from the database.
  - Bad fit: replying to the biggest enterprise client who is threatening to churn after a server outage. AI can write a polite apology but "can't read the room," doesn't know the client and doesn't know he needs an honest phone call to be saved.
  - "AI thrives on formulas. It fails on nuance."
- **I, Isolated:** the task can be done in a vacuum without tribal knowledge. Simon says most founders get R and P right but ignore I, and that this is where "90% of AI implementations fail."
- **Rule:** if a role's tasks are repetitive, predictable and isolated, you can replace it today. If it misses even one, at least keep a human in the loop in that workflow.
- Think about replacing tasks, not people.

chunks.heading: Why isolation matters: the tribal knowledge trap
chunks.text:
- Simon uses AI to write code every day and says it is excellent at clean, high-quality code, but it assumes your code base makes sense, which most don't.
- Example failure modes: AI randomly refactors code, removes old functions or deletes an unused database table. It doesn't know about a Zapier automation set up 2 years ago that reads that exact table to run payroll.
- AI doesn't know the history of the company, the invisible dependencies or why a weird decision was made years ago.
- If a task needs deep integration with other moving parts of the business or deep historical context, it is not isolated. Replacing that role with AI means it "won't just fail," it will probably break things and "make a big mess."
- You can only give AI tasks that need no prior knowledge, or where the needed knowledge can be included briefly with the task itself.

chunks.heading: How the 5% succeed
chunks.text:
- The failing 95% try to replace leadership, tribal knowledge and strategy with a chatbot.
- The successful 5% act as operators: they strip out the repetitive, predictable, isolated tasks and hand them to agents so humans can focus on "the things that actually require a pulse."
- Simon admits he has helped fuel the hype, with videos on building AI agents, social media content writers, SEO blog writers and AI support systems, and says this video is a caveat to that.
- As a worked example of a task that passes the RIP test, he points to a news research agent he built that creates an isolated workflow doing the work of a human researcher.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon argues SaaS is no longer the main AI opportunity and lists five practical businesses built around problems companies already pay for: AI implementation, audience building, agent security auditing, AI-powered service companies, and AI workshops. The through-line: pick a market you understand, find one thing they already spend money on, and use AI to deliver it faster or cheaper.

chunks.heading: AI implementation partner (the "AI automation agency")
chunks.text:
Simon says SaaS is no longer the opportunity it once was. Among the founders he knows who use AI to build, he is "one of the few who's still doing SaaS". The ones doing well with AI are doing something less glamorous: solving problems companies already spend money on.

- **The gap:** Almost every company is under pressure to "do something with AI". Employees have tried ChatGPT and management has seen Claude Code and agent tools, but nobody knows how to connect it to the business. Simon cites a study that only about 5% of businesses have gotten real financial value from AI.
- **The business:** Be the person who makes AI work inside a company. He thinks "AI automation agency" sounds more sophisticated than the work is.
- **Example, 50-person e-commerce company:** The support team answers the same questions all day (where is my order, check the store back end, read the history, write a reply). You map that process with the team, then build an internal agent that reads the conversation, checks the order in Shopify, looks up company policies and drafts the reply.
- **Human in the loop:** Simple questions are handled automatically. Refunds and unusual cases go to an employee for approval.
- **Scope:** The job covers everything around the agent: tools and permissions, testing against real support cases, training the team, and monitoring after launch.
- **Pricing model:** Charge for the implementation, then keep a monthly agreement for testing and maintenance.
- **How to start:** Pick an industry, find one expensive workflow people repeat every day, and build the agent for it.

chunks.heading: Build an audience around AI (brand deals and angel investing)
chunks.text:
AI startups are raising enormous amounts of money, and once the product is built they all need people to know it exists. With thousands of AI tools competing for attention, much of that investment money ends up spent on distribution.

- **The business:** Make videos, posts or a newsletter about what is happening in AI. Test new tools, show what they can actually do, and build an audience that wants to keep up with the space. Tool companies pay creators for brand deals to reach those people.
- **His own case:** This is already a meaningful part of his business. He partners with some of the bigger AI tools and occasionally does brand deals with them. Simon admits it is "probably the least surprising idea" on the list, but it belongs because it is one of the most direct ways to make money from the AI boom.
- **The less-discussed angle:** Many creators he knows are becoming angel investors. He has five promising AI startups in his angel portfolio, one of them Lovable. These are early-stage private companies most people can't buy into.
- **How he got access:** Some companies came to him for a brand deal and asked his rate for a 90-second slot in a video. He flipped it: "why don't I give you my money instead?" He invests and has a reason to keep supporting the product as it grows.
- **Why it works for both sides:** The company gets an angel investor who can help with distribution. He gets in before the company reaches the wider market.
- **Takeaway:** The obvious business is brand deals. The more interesting opportunity can come from the relationships with the founders behind those deals.

chunks.heading: AI agent security auditing
chunks.text:
Companies are giving AI agents access to customer data, emails, payments and internal tools. Once an agent can take action, one bad instruction or permission mistake can cause real damage. Simon says most companies are moving much faster on giving agents access than on testing them safely.

- **Example, a finance agent** that reads invoices, looks up vendors and prepares payments. Before production, the company hires you to attack it.
- **Step 1:** Map every tool and every piece of data the agent can access.
- **Step 2:** Check whether it can see more than it needs, or act without the right approval.
- **Step 3:** Try to manipulate it:
  - Hide instructions inside an invoice telling the agent to ignore its rules.
  - Change a vendor's bank details.
  - Ask it to reveal employee payroll information.
  - Ask it to prepare a payment above its approval limit.
- **Turn failures into tests:** Every failure becomes a test the company can re-run before the agent is updated.
- **Ongoing work:** Model changes, prompt edits and newly connected tools can bring old problems back, so testing continues after launch.
- **Revenue structure:** The company pays you to audit before launch, build the evaluation suite, and keep testing as the system changes.
- **Barrier to entry:** It needs real security expertise and a lot of trust, which gives it a much higher barrier than a normal AI agency. It is a natural fit if you already work in cybersecurity, penetration testing or software QA.

chunks.heading: AI-powered service company
chunks.text:
Companies already pay for research, recruitment, bookkeeping, design and legal support. They know what they are buying and a budget exists.

- **Example, an interior design studio:** A client renovating an office gives the use, style and budget. Normally you spend days finding furniture, checking measurements, comparing materials and building a mood board and floor plan, then rebuild when the client wants a different table, warmer floor or new layout.
- **With AI:** Feed it the client brief, room dimensions and supplier catalogs. It finds options that fit the room and budget, builds a first mood board and prepares the shopping list. You still decide what looks good.
- **3D rendering:** AI can now work inside 3D rendering software, so you can ask it to swap the table, change the floor or move the lighting instead of rebuilding by hand.
- **Client view:** The client doesn't need to know about AI. They hired an interior design studio and that is what they get. Behind the scenes, work that used to take several people is done by a much smaller team or solo.
- **Key insight:** "Some of the smartest people I know and some of the people making the most money with AI right now aren't selling AI. They're using it to amplify work their clients still expect humans to do."
- **Recipe:** Pick a valuable service you already understand, use AI to amplify your work, and charge for the result.

chunks.heading: Practical AI workshops for companies
chunks.text:
Many companies have already bought ChatGPT or a copilot for employees, but usage is all over the place: one person uses it daily, another pastes sensitive customer data into a random tool, and half the team barely uses AI because nobody showed them how.

- **The business:** Sell a day that turns employees into AI superusers.
- **Prompting:** Teach the whole team to write prompts with proper context, examples and constraints, then turn prompts that work into a reusable company library.
- **Technical staff:** Help set up Claude Code properly and give it rules and context for their codebases.
- **Workflow builders:** Teach people who build repeated workflows to take real examples from the business, define what a good result looks like, and test whether the AI gets it right before the rest of the company uses it.
- **AI hygiene:** Cover which tools are approved, what data must stay private, and where a person still needs to check results.
- **Packaging:** The exact workshop changes per company, but you can package a few modules, tailor the examples to their work, and sell it as a half-day or full-day session.
- **Recurring revenue:** Come back for recurring training as tools change and employees become ready for more advanced workflows.

chunks.heading: Don't feel late: start boring and useful
chunks.text:
Simon acknowledges that Twitter and YouTube are full of people building autonomous companies and raising millions, which can make the AI opportunity feel like it has already passed.

- **His view:** Some of the best current opportunities are "much more boring and straightforward": helping companies answer support tickets, test agents, train employees, and do the same expensive service work they paid for before AI.
- **Customer mindset:** "Your customer doesn't care whether the business looks impressive on Twitter. They care that you solve a problem they already have."
- **What to do:** Pick a market you understand, talk to the people in it, and find one thing they already spend money on. Then use AI to deliver it faster, cheaper or with a much smaller team.
- **Sequencing:** "You can always build something more sophisticated later. First, build something useful."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon moved most of his five-product SaaS portfolio from AWS serverless to three Hetzner dedicated servers running Kubernetes, Postgres and Redis. He cut infra costs from about $7,800 to under $2,000 per month, avoided vendor lock-in, and made lifetime deals safer by keeping running costs fixed. He also explains what he kept on AWS and who should or shouldn't self-host.

chunks.heading: Why Simon moved most of his SaaS stack off AWS
chunks.text:
- Until early 2025 all of Simon's SaaS products ran on AWS. He then began migrating to dedicated bare metal servers at Hetzner.
- About 80% now runs on dedicated servers with open source software; about 20% remains on AWS.
- He says the move cut costs, sped up his products, sped up feature deploys, and "opened new business opportunities."
- Context: he runs a portfolio of five SaaS tools with 50,000+ users, heading toward $2 million ARR in 2025, generating over $100,000 per month.
- He frames the real downside honestly: he now manages the infrastructure himself.

chunks.heading: Old stack vs. new stack
chunks.text:
**Before (managed, serverless, pay-per-use):**
- ECS, Fargate and Lambda for code
- AWS Amplify for hosting apps
- DynamoDB for data
- SQS for message queues
- CloudWatch for monitoring and logs
- AWS bills exact usage: milliseconds of execution, database reads/writes, log storage time.

**After:**
- Three dedicated Hetzner servers
- Docker containers managed by Kubernetes
- Postgres for data, Redis for caching, BullMQ for queues
- Grafana (free community edition) plus Prometheus for monitoring and logs
- Everything except the servers is open source or free, so the only bill is a low, fixed monthly server cost.
- He notes "leaving the cloud" is used loosely: he still rents servers in a data center. The shift is from managed serverless infrastructure to managing his own dedicated servers.

chunks.heading: Reason 1: Cost, and why the time investment still pays off
chunks.text:
- Early 2025 AWS bill: about $7,800/month on average, and climbing as usage grew (pay-per-use means cost rises with users).
- After moving 80%+ of infrastructure: below $2,000/month, likely heading below $1,000/month once the last migrations finish.
- Hetzner itself costs about $200/month; the rest of the bill is the remaining AWS share.
- Counterpoint he raises himself: with $100k+/month revenue, is $7,800 a big deal, and what about the time spent learning Kubernetes, Docker and basic sysadmin?
- His answer: infrastructure time spiked at the start of 2025, but as he learned and as AI got better at helping, it returned to normal levels, "if not even less than it was before." Managing AWS is not zero effort either; it gets complex and has its own learning curve.
- Key argument: the time cost is a one-off, fixed upfront cost, while the savings are uncapped and grow every month. He thinks people fear the effort stays "in the red" forever, and in his experience it doesn't.

chunks.heading: Reason 2: Avoiding vendor lock-in
chunks.text:
- DynamoDB, Lambda, Fargate and similar are robust and fairly priced, but they run only on AWS.
- If AWS raises prices or drops you as a customer, "you're cooked." Migrating needs careful planning, and a forced rushed migration could sink the business because users won't wait.
- He sees this as the biggest reason to consider leaving: it's not in the interest of AWS, Azure or GCP to make leaving easy.
- His new setup runs on any host offering a VPS or dedicated server.
- He proved it by running one smaller product for two days on three Raspberry Pis in his office. Internet speed and memory were issues, but he doesn't think users noticed. He doesn't recommend it, only the principle: remove as many hard vendor dependencies as possible.
- Remaining dependencies: Stripe and OpenAI. He is exploring Coinbase as an alternative payment method and dedicated GPU instances from independent vendors for AI, and says neither is simple.

chunks.heading: Reason 3: Making lifetime deals credible
chunks.text:
- Besides subscriptions, he sells lifetime access to all five tools for a one-time payment.
- A one-time price with ongoing, rising costs is risky. Fixed infrastructure costs make financial planning for lifetime deals much easier and less risky.
- Users ask what happens to lifetime deals if his business fails, and he admits he has no satisfying answer beyond "my business is doing well."
- His fix: make all products fully self-hostable, so lifetime buyers can install the software on their own servers if he can't host it. This is "the best way I can guarantee that lifetime access really does mean lifetime access."

chunks.heading: What still runs on AWS (and what he tried)
chunks.text:
- **Storage (S3):** Hetzner storage buckets and Cloudflare R2 are S3-compatible and cheaper, but still lock him in. S3 cost isn't the issue; lock-in is. He tried self-hosted MinIO on a 15 TB Hetzner drive attached to the main server. It worked "kind of," but backups were complex, MinIO is designed for distributed setups with multiple drives per node, and it wasn't stable. He went back to S3, calling it "probably a skill issue."
- **Authentication (Cognito):** similar to Auth0. Security-critical, so he's cautious. The only open source alternative he found, Keycloak, had poor user and developer experience in his view. He stayed on Cognito rather than risk a critical component.
- **Edge (CloudFront):** the public entry point proxying all requests to the Hetzner servers, so all inbound traffic is protected by default. He values its firewalls and DDoS prevention that he wouldn't know how to set up himself.
- **AI:** still relies on OpenAI, Replicate and Vesta AI. He hopes standalone servers will soon have the GPU power for reliable self-hosted inference.

chunks.heading: Who should leave the cloud
chunks.text:
- **Small hobby project, not expected to grow:** stay on the cloud with Vercel, Netlify, Lovable or other one-click deploy tools.
- **Very large business needing serious scaling, or mission-critical to users:** use a managed hyperscaler like AWS.
- **Anywhere in the middle:** consider dedicated servers. Managing infrastructure yourself is "absolutely doable" and the savings are serious.
- Bonus: running on your own infrastructure lets you use open source tools internally too. He says he saved another $10,000 per year by replacing expensive tools with self-hostable alternatives.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon lays out a three-stage roadmap for acquiring SaaS users. Each stage uses a different acquisition model (method, channel, cost): manual outreach and referrals for the first 100, content and building in public up to 1,000, then ads and affiliates to scale or automate.

chunks.heading: The three-stage user acquisition framework
chunks.text:
Simon frames every user acquisition as three parts: a method, a channel and a cost. Combining them yields many possible ways to get a user, from free and manual to paid and automatic. He argues you need a road map matched to your SaaS stage, because some methods work only early and others suit growth or automation mode.

He sorts all online marketing into four methods:
- **Incoming:** the user finds you and signs up or requests contact.
- **Outgoing:** you reach out first and convert them.
- **Referrals:** current users bring in new users, who bring in more.
- **Advertising:** like incoming, but you pay to get in front of them.

His road map, which he says he used to build and scale three products and would use again:
- **Stage 1:** first 5 users, then up to 100.
- **Stage 2:** 500 to 1,000 users.
- **Stage 3:** 1,000+ users, continuous growth.

chunks.heading: Stage 1a: Get your first 5 users with manual outreach
chunks.text:
- **Method:** outgoing. **Channel:** email or DMs on whatever message app you use. **Cost:** $0, done manually one by one.
- Reach out to your close network: family, friends, colleagues, partners, anyone you think would benefit.
- Say you're launching, that you have an MVP ready, and that you want the first few users.
- Offer a completely free account for life. The only ask is their feedback.
- Not everyone will fit, but if the product solves a real problem, five is achievable.
- Put these users into a small community (Discord, Facebook group, WhatsApp, whatever works).
- Spend time with them: listen to feedback, fix bugs, ship the features they ask for, smooth rough edges.
- Let them have a big say in direction. He calls these "the most important" users because the goal is to turn them into advocates, not just users.

chunks.heading: Stage 1b: Go from 5 to 100 users through referrals
chunks.text:
- **Method:** referrals. **Channel:** referral links your early users share. **Cost:** usually zero.
- He could offer them a revenue cut per referral, but in most cases thinks it's unnecessary. If you served the first five really well and made them feel part of the project, they'll happily refer people unpaid.
- Instead, give new users a big early-joiner discount. It makes advocates and newcomers feel part of something up and coming, and it gives advocates a strong offer to pitch.

chunks.heading: Stage 2: Reach 500 to 1,000 users with content and building in public
chunks.text:
- Manual emails/DMs and referral incentives won't scale to this level. He designs a new model.
- **Method:** incoming. Users find you and sign up themselves, so you need awareness at scale.
- **Channels:** social media and search engines. He admits he sounds like a broken record: "the best way to create an acquisition model using the incoming method is by creating content and building in public."
- Tactics:
  - Long-form video for YouTube search.
  - Blog posts to show up on Google.
  - TikToks, Reels and YouTube Shorts to catch attention.
  - LinkedIn updates on highs, lows, discoveries and milestones.
  - Lessons shared on Hacker News and Indie Hackers.
- Most important: keep doing it. This stage is "long and hard" and results are slow.
- **Cost:** you should expect to invest in good content. What you can pay per acquisition depends on your ARPU (average revenue per user).
- There will be long stretches with little engagement and no conversions, so monitor and optimize closely.
- He guarantees the model works but takes time. Let revenue from existing users fund acquiring new ones until you hit at least 500 users.

chunks.heading: Stage 3a: Scale with paid advertising
chunks.text:
- At 1,000+ users, keep the content engine running (stage 2 doesn't end). Add two models.
- **Method:** advertising. Take the content that proved itself in stage 2 and turn it into paid ads. Also craft, test and scale new creatives and strategies.
- Recommended channels:
  - Google Ads for search ads and YouTube video ads.
  - Meta for image and video ads on Facebook and Instagram.
  - TikTok for video ads.
- Cost depends on ARPU and the return on ad spend (ROAS) you want:
  - **Growth mode:** you may not care about return at all and just reinvest all revenue into new acquisitions.
  - **Profit mode:** aim for roughly 3:1 ROAS. Each $1 spent on a new user returns $3; reinvest $1 into the next user and keep $1 as profit.

chunks.heading: Stage 3b: Scale with an affiliate program
chunks.text:
- **Method:** referrals again, but now as an open affiliate program where anyone can sign up, create referral links and promote.
- At this scale you need proper compensation. He has seen programs pay 10%, 20% or even 50% of recurring revenue from referred customers.
- Payout depends on your direction:
  - **Growth mode:** share a big chunk of revenue to keep affiliates highly motivated.
  - **Automation mode:** go lower, down to gift cards, unlocking features or raising usage limits for affiliates.
- In stage 3 you choose between maximizing growth (reinvesting every dime) or taking profit and automating acquisition so new users arrive on autopilot.

chunks.heading: Why this matters: what high-growth SaaS have in common
chunks.text:
- He points to bootstrapped SaaS products making nearly $1M a year, and one making nearly $1M a month at only two years old.
- His claim: they are great products, but what makes them exceptional is that they figured out how to blow up their user base and sustain growth month after month.
- "This is not just luck, this is science." He says you can break down what they do and reproduce it.
- The framework is not the only valid road map. You can run ads from the very early stages or scale cold outreach later. It is simply the one he has used.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon argues that SaaS is a high-failure game, so the best strategy is to test many products cheaply. He describes the parts of his "SaaS factory": a GitHub org of reusable packages and boilerplates, no-code automation templates, a creative asset library, a launch checklist, and a personal playbook. The factory only works if you build it yourself.

chunks.heading: Why most SaaS products fail, and why Simon builds a factory
chunks.text:
- Simon says SaaS has become very competitive, and going all in on a single SaaS is risky.
- For a beginner on a first product, he says failure is "statistically overwhelmingly likely... almost a guarantee."
- Amazon, Google, Apple and Microsoft each have a "massive graveyard of failed products", much bigger than their portfolio of successes.
- The most successful indie hackers are successful because they have "been pushing and failing more and faster than most other people."
- His answer is to test the market constantly with new ideas, which needs tooling that makes it sustainable.
- A SaaS Factory makes it easier and faster to test and launch new products and take them to market.
- He built 8base, FeedHive, LinkDrip and other products in his factory.

chunks.heading: Room 1: a code library of packages, templates and boilerplates
chunks.text:
- Simon keeps a GitHub organization full of reusable packages, such as custom utilities, list manipulation, themes, common Stripe operations, login, user permissions, subscriptions, workspaces and team management.
- Every new project goes out on the same tech stack: React, Chakra UI, AWS and Pulumi.
- A full-stack SaaS boilerplate (backend, front end, authentication, payments and a basic UI) lets him spin up a working SaaS in under 30 minutes.
- His team also built a small CLI that asks a few questions and choices at project start, then generates the new SaaS.
- How to build it:
  - Stop regularly, go through your code and pick out pieces you are fairly sure can be reused.
  - Refactor them into general-purpose solutions.
  - Push each to a GitHub repository and publish it as an npm package.
  - Write a good README with documentation and getting-started instructions ("be nice to future you").
  - Turn boilerplate repositories into GitHub templates so a new repo is one click.
- Simon says indie hackers tend to under-prioritize staying organized in the heat of building.
- Maintenance is real: you must keep packages updated and compatible with each other (he jokes about a SaaS breaking because the Chakra version was out of date).
- His argument: once this room is running, it saves "hundreds if not thousands of hours" on engineering, probably the most expensive part of a SaaS business.

chunks.heading: Room 2: a no-code automation library
chunks.text:
- Simon says it isn't code versus no-code; a proper factory needs both.
- He uses Zapier and Make for backend operations that involve third-party tools:
  - adding new users to retargeting lists for Facebook and Google
  - segmenting users into lists for email drips
  - writing product updates in Notion and pushing them to FeedHive to share on social media
  - adding each new sign-up/sale to a spreadsheet for financial planning
- These are things not directly tied to the app's backend.
- Tactic: Zapier's integration platform lets you build private custom integrations.
  - Private integrations don't need approval from the Zapier team, and are free.
  - Hook them to your own APIs and use them in your own Zapier account.
  - Build a custom integration once and reuse it for every new SaaS, instead of spending hours on complex automation each time.
- Combined with the GitHub packages and boilerplates, a new SaaS means installing an npm package and using a custom Zap.
- It takes time to learn and set up initially, "that's the whole point of a factory: it's time-consuming once and fast in the future."

chunks.heading: Room 3: a creative library of reusable graphics and video templates
chunks.text:
- Simon stores reusable images, graphics and video templates for thumbnails, ad creatives, social media graphics, video demos and video ads.
- His reasoning: "Getting stuck creatively is horrible," so whenever he needs something new he picks up a template.
- Tools:
  - Figma for images: use components to build template graphics with variants so new graphics can be composed easily. Also build a library of reusable parts such as fonts, scribbles, characters and icons.
  - Adobe After Effects for video: turn animations and clips into Essential Graphics with customizable layers, then adjust them in Adobe Premiere when editing.
- These serve as building blocks to speed up editing.
- He stresses keeping it nice and organized, because the factory is about making future life easier.
- If you don't want to set this up yourself, he notes you can buy a ready-made version, but see the next section for why that is risky.

chunks.heading: The lesson from buying a ready-made SaaS factory
chunks.text:
- Simon once bought a ready-made SaaS factory in a hurry to get his first SaaS started. The seller said it had everything and he could start printing SaaS products right away.
- He had no idea how to operate it, and the manual was extremely poorly written. He spent a lot of money on it, got frustrated, pressed a button, something went wrong and it all "burned to the ground."
- At his most demoralized, he decided to build a new factory from scratch, planning how it would work in detail.
- Because he built it himself, he knew it "inside and out", and it did not fail on him.
- His argument: using someone else's factory and expecting the same results "is most likely going to end in disaster."
- What gives you superpowers is the process of building the factory: "all the hard-earned lessons that make up the foundation you're building on... it's not something you can buy."

chunks.heading: Protocol: checklists, setup requirements and documentation
chunks.text:
- Every new SaaS needs a checklist of setup requirements: payment system, email system, user authentication, privacy policy, terms and conditions, and so on.
- Simon suggests using Notion for this:
  - save all legal documents as templates
  - keep checklists for all parts of SaaS development
  - cross off everything on the list every time you set up a new SaaS
- He treats this as quality control.
- Document all parts of the factory and describe all processes so you don't end up confused and forgetting what to do.

chunks.heading: The playbook: play the same game again and again
chunks.text:
- A playbook goes beyond the factory: a framework of practices and strategies, a rule set you follow to plan and execute each SaaS.
- Simon says most successful serial entrepreneurs and indie creators "tend to play the same game again and again."
- He follows the same playbook himself in how he launches and markets his products.
- He deliberately refuses to sell his playbook or factory, saying he's "not some snake oil salesman." Even though it works for him, it is highly unlikely to work the same for you.
- Takeaway: build your own factory, playbook and protocol, because the lessons from building them are the asset.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon explains why common objections to lifetime deals (unsustainable, entitled users, cannibalized subscribers, no trust) mostly fail, using data from AppSumo, LinkDrip and his Founder's Stack bundle. He lays out three rules: price high, keep costs and support low, and build a public reputation.

chunks.heading: Why most lifetime-deal objections are wrong: Simon's case from $160K in sales
chunks.text:
- Simon's SaaS products had been stuck for almost two years, with no revenue growth. New users kept getting offset by high acquisition cost, expensive ad placements and churn.
- A few months before this video he ran a lifetime deal (LTD), the move other founders told him not to make. It lifted his revenue by more than 56% so far.
- Common founder objections he lists: it's unsustainable (one payment against infinite server and support cost), the audience is demanding and entitled, and it will cannibalize current subscribers.
- The user-side objection is trust: how does a buyer know the founder won't take the money and shut down?
- His claim: three things make these concerns go away: a high price, tight cost control, and a strong public reputation.

chunks.heading: Evidence base: Founder's Stack, FeedHive on AppSumo and LinkDrip pre-sales
chunks.text:
- Founder's Stack launched about two months before the video. It is a bundled lifetime offer for four tools (social media, AI support, link tracking, graphics design), built by his team over four years. It also includes two new SaaS products not yet launched, due later that year.
- FeedHive ran a two-month campaign on AppSumo in 2022 and ranked among the top five best-selling products in that period. It generated more than $300,000 and onboarded more than 5,000 lifetime users.
- Later in 2022 he pre-sold lifetime deals to early adopters of LinkDrip before launch. Many of those users are still active three years later.
- This gave him real data on how lifetime users behave and what the economics look like.

chunks.heading: Lifetime users do churn
chunks.text:
- Myth: lifetime users never churn because there is no subscription to cancel.
- Reality: they churn for the same reasons subscribers do:
  - They go out of business.
  - They outgrow the tool and need something bigger.
  - They outsource the work to an agency with its own tool chain.
  - They move to a shiny new tool that solves the problem differently.
- Instant churners: some buyers (his "Jonathan" example) buy as an investment for a future business, never redeem and never become users. In the data they buy and leave immediately.
- Once these users are counted, the average lifetime user churns before the average subscriber. In his cohort comparison, lifetime users who do activate stick around slightly longer, but the instant churners flip the average.
- Takeaway: you are not stuck with all your lifetime users forever, so the job is to pick a price high enough that the average one never becomes a losing investment before churning.

chunks.heading: Rule 1: Set a high price point (Founder's Stack at $799)
chunks.text:
- Founder's Stack costs $799 for all four tools. He calls it the sweet spot: still a great deal for buyers, and safe given current cost per user.
- Results: about 230 buyers and more than $160,000 in revenue.
- Break-even horizon: given his cost per user, it would take roughly 37 years before this group of buyers starts costing him money.
- His point: on paper, a one-time charge against ongoing costs eventually goes negative, but most founders wildly exaggerate how near that horizon is. In 37 years, buyers won't be using the tool and "it's at least not going to be my problem by that time."
- The long runway comes from two things: the high price and low cost.
- Warning example: a $39 lifetime deal on a product that uses AI heavily has a high cost per user and is a quick route to bankruptcy. This has happened many times.

chunks.heading: Rule 2: Keep costs tight with simple, self-serve, low-touch products
chunks.text:
- Sell simple but specialized tools that are fully self-serve with very low support needs.
- Avoid demo calls, presentations, sales meetings, manual onboarding, designated customer success agents and account managers. "It's way too expensive."
- Invest heavily in the onboarding experience and have many guides, tutorials and videos so users can help themselves.
- Trouble starts when you price too low and the product costs too much to run. When planning, use safe, conservative cost estimates.

chunks.heading: Cannibalization: the lifetime deal barely hurt subscribers
chunks.text:
- Subscribers who left: 10 cancelled their subscription and replaced it with Founder's Stack. That is only about 4.5% of Founder's Stack buyers.
- Subscribers gained: at least 15 new subscribers found him through the Founder's Stack website, so the net is +5 subscribers.
- His theory, which he says he can't prove conclusively: the high price creates distance from the monthly plan. Many users on the $29/month FeedHive plan only need that one tool, so $799 for four tools isn't compelling, even though one is a one-time payment and the other recurring.
- The new subscribers may be people trying the tools for a few months before buying the bundle, or people who heard about the tools through the promotion but only need one.
- Takeaway: if the price distance is big enough, you probably don't need to worry that your whole subscriber base will jump to the lifetime deal.

chunks.heading: Rule 3: Build trust by being the public face of the company
chunks.text:
- Deal sites like AppSumo, PitchGround and DealMirror made it tempting for bad actors to run an "LTD pump and dump": list the tool, hype the roadmap with insane promises, take the cash, then shut down about 3 months later citing bankruptcy. Well-meaning founders who overreach also hurt trust.
- As a result many LTD buyers are skeptical.
- His fix: build a strong reputation, with the founder as the public face of the company:
  - Be on social media and YouTube.
  - Show up in people's emails.
  - Demonstrate responsibility and that you will give users what you promised.
- If you hide behind the company, are invisible or unreachable, selling this way is hard if not impossible.
- Closing advice: whether lifetime deals or subscriptions suit your business is your call, but don't reject the idea blindly. Make sure the three things are covered: high price, tight costs, strong reputation.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon shares four A/B tests from his SaaS products (FeedHive, LinkDrip). Forcing users through onboarding with card and plan selection raised revenue 52% despite losing most signups. Hero social proof and G2 badges helped, monthly pricing as the default beat yearly, and most tests are inconclusive, so keep testing.

chunks.heading: Onboarding flow lifted revenue 52% despite a big drop-off
chunks.text:
Simon A/B tested forcing new users through an onboarding flow vs. giving direct access, on FeedHive (social media management, 7-day free trial). The same test ran multiple times over two years, with consistent results. It was also replicated on LinkDrip.

- **Group A (direct access):** 100% of users get into the tool. 11% upgrade after the trial, so 11 paying users per 100 signups. ARPU is $22/month, adding $242 MRR per 100 new users.
- **Group B (forced onboarding):** onboarding asks questions, requires adding social accounts, and requires entering a credit card and picking a plan before the user sees the tool. Only 22% finish it, so 78% of new users are lost. Of those who finish, 59% upgrade, so 13 paying users per 100 signups. ARPU is $36/month, adding $468 MRR per 100 new users.
- **Result:** paying user counts are roughly a tie (11 vs 13), but revenue per cohort rose 52%.
- His theory is the effort justification effect: people value a product more when they invest time and effort up front. He also sees the onboarding as a filter that removes unserious users who were never going to pay.
- Takeaway: judge onboarding tests on revenue per signup cohort, not on completion or signup counts.

chunks.heading: Social proof in the hero section: 9% to 16% click-through
chunks.text:
Simon tested whether adding comments and ratings to the website hero section was too much clutter.

- **Group A:** clean hero focused on features and value.
- **Group B:** hero plus comments and ratings.
- **Metric:** share of visitors clicking any "Get Started" button near the hero.
- **Result:** 9% in A vs 16% in B.
- FeedHive's site gets almost 200,000 visits a month, so the 7-point lift matters in absolute terms.
- He also keeps a dedicated social proof section on the site and recommends one for any SaaS. He uses a tool called Senja to collect and embed testimonials from many sources.

chunks.heading: Default pricing toggle: monthly beat yearly
chunks.text:
The team argued over whether the landing page pricing toggle should default to yearly (which shows the discounted price). Simon wanted yearly; the UX designer wanted monthly. They settled it with a test.

- **Group A:** monthly shown by default.
- **Group B:** yearly shown by default.
- **Metric:** clicks on any of the four sign-up buttons in the pricing section.
- **Result:** 13% of visitors clicked sign up in A vs 4% in B. Group B visitors also flipped the toggle back to monthly nine times more often.
- Monthly is now the default on the FeedHive and LinkDrip landing pages.
- Context: most "Get Started" clicks do not come from the pricing page, so overall impact is likely small. Simon notes everyone he asked was confident they knew the winner, and opinion split roughly 50/50, which is why he tests it.

chunks.heading: G2 badges as a scroll-stopper
chunks.text:
Simon tested G2 award badges below the hero. Because it was hard to measure signup impact directly, they measured attention instead.

- **Group A:** no badges below the hero.
- **Group B:** five of the most recent G2 awards below the hero.
- **Measurement:** JavaScript detects how many visitors stop scrolling at that spot, plus click-through on the badges.
- **Result:** visitors in B stopped scrolling 5x more often, and the badges had roughly a 6% click-through rate.
- The team upgraded to a paid G2 plan (which he calls "a bit pricey") because the badges build trust and clearly grab attention. He admits scroll-stopping says nothing conclusive about who signs up.

chunks.heading: How Simon runs A/B tests and what to expect
chunks.text:
- Definition: assign visitors or users to group A or B, show different versions, measure how many take a desired action (for example creating an account), and compare.
- His setup uses JavaScript to run the experiment and Amplitude to track results. Many no-code tools can do this too.
- His startup always has tests running on the website, in ad campaigns, and inside the app.
- Most tests, "hundreds" of them, show insignificant results. Every so often one makes a real difference, and that makes the rest worth it.
- Results are counterintuitive often enough that he advises against copying them blindly: "go ahead and verify that our results are also the case for you." Many factors can't be accounted for, so run your own test before implementing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon walks through how he would start a SaaS from zero (no audience, network or money) in four steps: pick a problem with founder fit, build one organic distribution channel, build in public with presales and no-code/AI, and turn everything into reusable building blocks. He draws on FeedHive, Linktrip and his failed Sigmetic.

chunks.heading: Finding a problem with founder fit before testing the market
chunks.text:
- Simon's starting scenario: no audience, no followers, no subscribers, empty bank account, no network. His approach to building a SaaS from scratch is four steps.
- Step one is finding a problem that fits him as the founder ("founder fit"), before asking whether the market needs the product. He runs three bootstrapped SaaS products (two built from scratch, one acquired).
- Three questions test founder fit:
  - **Can you dogfood it?** Are you the ideal customer? If so, you speak the users' language, so talking to users is easier, and you stay motivated because you need the product yourself.
  - **Are you passionate about the problem?** Check whether you get excited by "I'm here to make it easier for people to X". There will be "a lot of struggles and emotional roller coasters", and as a founder you have no boss, "only commitment you have is your commitment to solving this problem".
  - **What are your unfair advantages?** Everyone has some: expertise, experience in a field, rare insight, or knowing someone who knows someone. He compares it to "playing Monopoly but you're allowed to cheat". Dogfooding plus passion is already a big advantage.
- Exercise: list problems you have yourself, list problem domains you are passionate about, list your unfair advantages, then cross-reference them to find the ideal problem.
- After that, test the problem and solution in the market (covered in a separate video).

chunks.heading: How FeedHive passed the founder-fit test
chunks.text:
- FeedHive (social media management tool) started on Twitter in 2021. About six months before building it, Simon built a social media following.
- He wanted a robust social media tool for aspiring entrepreneurs, and existing tools were lacking, so he was the first user (dogfooding).
- He was committed to the problem because he had seen the power of having an audience and wanted to scale to other platforms.
- Unfair advantage: he had grown a Twitter audience of more than 30,000 followers in a few months and was good at marketing himself on social media.
- A handful of other founders spotted the same opportunity at the same time. According to Simon, none of those tools exist today, because those founders "weren't really that much into social media" and lacked the same unfair advantage.
- If starting again, he would make sure he could tick all these boxes again.

chunks.heading: Pick one organic distribution channel and double down
chunks.text:
- Step two is creating one organic distribution channel for reaching users. He would focus on a single channel and know it well enough to navigate it when things get unpredictable.
- Options he lists: blogging and SEO, social media content, a YouTube channel, an email newsletter, a community (Discord or Facebook group), or word of mouth.
- His own experience with social media and YouTube has been "absolutely outstanding". The goal is a win-win: create value, help and inspire upcoming entrepreneurs, while building awareness of your product and mission.
- Tactic:
  - Find small online groups and communities centered on the problem you are solving.
  - Note the questions and pains people repeatedly raise.
  - Answer them through content: short videos for TikTok and Instagram Reels, long-form videos for YouTube, blog posts, a personal newsletter, or a Facebook group or subreddit devoted to the problem.
  - Once one channel works well, drop the others and double down on it. That becomes the organic distribution channel.

chunks.heading: Build in public with your community
chunks.text:
- Step three is building the product. By now you know the problem well, have it yourself, and have talked to peers. The content you made has produced many ideas, so "what should I build" should no longer be a question.
- Build in public, alongside the community you have been engaging with. You are already seen as an authority on the problem.
- On fear of copycats: "just let them". Without your authority, commitment and unfair advantages in the area, others "don't have a chance to compete with you".
- Collect as much feedback and ideas as possible. Many community members like being part of the project, and they act as a board of advisors for a fresh perspective when you have doubts.
- Eager users may pay before the product is finished.

chunks.heading: Pre-selling LinkTrip before writing code
chunks.text:
- LinkTrip is a no-code link engagement builder. It was sold as a lifetime pre-sale offer "before we wrote a single line of code".
- Result: almost $100,000 in sales in around two months.
- Simon attributes this to a strong community and people being so eager about the solution that they were happy to join early.
- He says he "cannot recommend this approach enough" and would do it again from scratch.

chunks.heading: Ship the first version fast with no-code and AI
chunks.text:
- Use no-code and AI to get a first version into users' hands quickly:
  - Webflow for the landing page.
  - ChatGPT to create copy.
  - Bubble to build the first MVP of the app.
  - If confident coding, use as many open-source libraries as possible.
- Anything that gets a first version ready faster is the right choice. Then release it.
- From that point you should start to see early users, paying subscribers and revenue "just around the corner".

chunks.heading: Expect failure and build a SaaS factory of reusable assets
chunks.text:
- Step four: expect it all to fail. "Statistically speaking you will fail", so make sure the effort isn't wasted by creating reusable building blocks.
- Turn the process into an ideation framework for generating new ideas. Understand your unfair advantages, then improve them to be "even more unfair".
- Build distribution so it can be reused to target the same users with a new product.
- Make reusable templates of creatives so new videos, blog posts and content are easy to produce.
- Generalize code and publish it as private npm packages. With no-code, save recipes and templates.
- His own chain of reuse: his first SaaS, Sigmetic, never made it, but he reused a lot of it to create FeedHive a year later, then reused a lot of that to create LinkTrip a year after.
- He used the same assets to create at least three other SaaS products in the same period. They never passed initial validation, and because they were fast to build he had "zero second thoughts" about dumping them when they wouldn't work.
- Metaphor: building SaaS products is like playing darts. You often miss, sometimes hit the bullseye. Keep creating new arrows so you get another throw. "Instead of creating a SaaS you should create a small SaaS factory."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon explains the five AI SaaS categories his team rejects immediately: standalone AI copywriters, AI coding tools, AI therapists, AI detectors, and AI summarizers. The common thread is saturated markets, usage-based LLM costs that punish bootstrappers, liability risk, and ideas that are really features absorbed by big platforms.

chunks.heading: Why Simon avoids AI copywriter SaaS
chunks.text:
- Simon calls the AI copywriter market flooded and saturated. GPT-3 launched in 2022, and the low barrier to entry played out. Early movers like Copy AI and Peppertype made it big, but now it is "very easy to spin up a new AI copywriter."
- If a tool only wraps OpenAI's API, it does basically the same as every other tool. He expects a race to the bottom on pricing and one of the highest churn rates in any market.
- He notes several big LinkedIn influencers shipping the same AI copywriters. He says it "smells a little bit like a cash grab," while allowing he may not see what is going on behind the scenes.
- He sees little that these tools offer beyond what standard LLMs like ChatGPT or Gemini already provide.
- Where it works: an AI copywriter as one feature inside a bigger product. FeedHive, his social media management tool, has an excellent one, but it is one of many features of an AI-powered marketing tool. As a standalone product he would stay far away.

chunks.heading: Why bootstrappers should not build AI coding tools
chunks.text:
- Simon would avoid tools like Cursor and Windsurf as a bootstrap founder, even though they have product-market fit.
- Part of Cursor's appeal is how much it offers at a cheap price. Compared with Cline (open-source VS Code extension, bring your own API key), he concludes the average Cursor user is "very likely losing money for Cursor."
- Core problem with building on AI: LLM API pricing scales with consumption. More user interaction means higher expenses, so a successful active user base becomes a financial liability.
- A product that aggressively consumes AI has a business model that bleeds cash as it grows.
- Cursor is backed by top-tier investment funds that can absorb the losses to chase market dominance, a classic VC hypergrowth play.
- Competing there as a bootstrapper means competing on "who can afford bleeding the most cash," not on who builds the best product.

chunks.heading: Cost-per-usage economics of AI SaaS
chunks.text:
- Simon states the general rule: LLM API cost is directly proportional to consumption, so heavy-use products erode margin as usage grows.
- Bootstrapped companies normally celebrate an active user base. With heavy AI consumption it becomes a liability.
- Implication he draws: avoid product categories where each user action triggers expensive inference unless you can price to cover it or are funded to absorb losses.

chunks.heading: Why he would never build an AI therapist
chunks.text:
- The value prop is obvious (on-demand therapist in your pocket), and many people already use ChatGPT for emotional support. He still calls the idea "a complete ethical shitshow."
- Examples he cites:
  - March 2023: a man in Belgium ended his life after weeks of talking to an AI chatbot called Eliza on the Chai app. His wife said it encouraged him by convincing him he could save the planet by sacrificing himself.
  - 2023: the US National Eating Disorders Association took down its chatbot Tessa after it gave harmful suggestions such as restricting calories and losing weight, the opposite of its purpose.
- He does not claim the chatbots caused these events, since people may already have had trauma, depression or psychosis, and acting on advice is the person's choice.
- His point: if your product ends up in the middle of a case like that, it is "way, way too much to handle" for a small bootstrapper or indie hacker.
- He says Peter Levels started an AI therapist and quickly wrapped it up after pushback from his audience, which he believes was the right call.
- Rule: stick to non-critical products. Avoid anything touching people's physical or mental health.

chunks.heading: Why AI detector and humanizer tools are a bad bet
chunks.text:
- The pitch: run AI-written content through a detector, fix the flagged parts so Google will not know you used AI. Advanced tools rewrite it for you.
- He sees three flaws:
  - **Wrong problem.** Google is clear that the problem is low-quality, spammy content made to manipulate rankings, not AI use. Content passing a detector can still get deranked if quality is low.
  - **Cat-and-mouse with Google.** You have no access to Google's algorithms, and you should not build a business guessing how their internal systems work.
  - **Worse content.** Patching an already-written piece is a terrible idea.
- Better direction: build a tool or service that produces great, high-quality content with AI from the start. Google does not mind AI as long as the content is good and helpful.
- He says a few tools already do this, and he has a video on building a custom workflow for it in n8n.

chunks.heading: Why AI summarizers are a feature, not a product
chunks.text:
- Summarizing meetings or email threads is a real problem, but "it has been solved many times already." He puts it in the same bucket as AI copywriters, and says it is even worse.
- It is no longer a product but an "aggressively integrated and completely free feature" built into major productivity ecosystems.
- Example: Google Workspace summarizes emails in one click, natively and free, and every Google Meet call generates a recap with key action items.
- Trust barrier: you would need access to every email in a customer's inbox, including sensitive ones, plus every meeting and every employee's calendar. Companies do not hand that to a small bootstrapped company.
- He acknowledges users already trust Google or Microsoft with this data, and says he personally would not want to compete there.

chunks.heading: How Simon screens new SaaS ideas
chunks.text:
- Context: he runs a portfolio of AI SaaS products covering social media, link tracking, customer support and graphic design. His team brainstorms, prototypes and tests new ideas every year.
- Screening rule: when a new idea falls into a category too close to these five (copywriters, coding tools, therapists, detectors, summarizers), they reject it immediately.
- Warning sign: ideas that feel seductive after playing with the latest models or a first automation workflow, where the build and go-to-market seem crystal clear. He says some of these are deceptively obvious and will "with overwhelming certainty" set you up for failure.
- Common thread across the five:
  - Saturated markets with a low barrier to entry.
  - A feature that platforms or LLMs give away for free.
  - Usage-based AI costs against VC-funded competitors.
  - Ethical or liability exposure that a small founder cannot absorb.
  - Solving the wrong problem or playing a game against a platform.
- He points to a simple approach for unlocking thousands of worthwhile micro SaaS ideas, covered in a separate video.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: AI coding tools will flood the market with cheap, mediocre SaaS, so positioning matters more than ever. Simon walks through eight positions (low-cost alternative, light version, enterprise, unique player, first mover, niche, privacy first, integrations) with pros, cons and real examples, and says niche is the best fit for a small indie SaaS.

chunks.heading: The "Fast Fashion" problem in SaaS
chunks.text:
- Simon calls it the "Temu effect": tools like Lovable, Cursor and Claude Code mean there will be SaaS products for almost everything.
- He expects AI to write about 95% of the code for many products, design the interfaces and UX, and debug and QA its own output.
- His view: these products probably won't be amazing, but many buyers will settle, "just like cheap products on Temu."
- To avoid the race to the bottom, he says it is more important than ever to position a product uniquely in a crowded market.
- He frames eight common SaaS positions, each with pros, cons and examples. The test: which position is your product in, and should you change it?

chunks.heading: Position 1: Low-cost alternative
chunks.text:
- Be openly a cheaper alternative to a well-known tool in an established market that solves a known problem.
- Example: Papermill-style "low-cost Zapier alternative" (Simon names "Papley" as a low-cost Zapier alternative that markets itself this way openly).
- Pros:
  - No need to educate the market or convince anyone the problem exists.
  - Dropping the incumbent's name plus "cheaper" instantly aligns the right customers with the value prop.
  - Makes paid advertising an ideal channel.
- Con: the "cheap knockoff" or "AI slop" vibe can attach to you.
- Advice for indie hackers building with AI tools: nothing wrong with it, but it pays off to "call it what it is" in your messaging and offer.

chunks.heading: Position 2: Light version
chunks.text:
- Solve the problem in a simpler way, with a more minimalistic and often more limited interface.
- Examples:
  - Canva started as a light version of Photoshop.
  - Simon's own tool TinyKiwi is now a light version of Canva.
  - Mailer Lite-style "light" tools for email, a light version of Mailchimp and SendGrid, with "light" in the name.
- Pro: captures less tech-savvy users who find the alternatives too complex and overwhelming.
- Con: it is hard to stay light as you evolve. Canva grew into complex software that many users now struggle with.

chunks.heading: Position 3: Enterprise
chunks.text:
- Solve a huge, frequent, painful problem, with extra focus on customer service, tailored solutions, manual setup and account management.
- Simon sees this as where SaaS meets tech-enabled service businesses.
- He thinks these hybrid software-plus-service businesses are the most likely to survive the Temu effect "because they still heavily depend on humans."
- Examples: HubSpot and Salesforce.
- Pro: this is where real money flows. HubSpot charges more than $3,000 per month for its enterprise solution, which he says is on the cheaper end of enterprise software.
- Con: the business and infrastructure behind these services are often extremely complex.

chunks.heading: Position 4: Unique player
chunks.text:
- Offer a very unique approach, often thanks to access to certain resources or specific expertise few others have.
- Examples:
  - Grammarly was one of a kind in helping users improve writing, before the AI era.
  - OpenAI was essentially alone for its first three or four years until competition caught up.
- Con: you must constantly fight for uniqueness. Few business models or tech products are immune to being copied, so appearing unique gets harder over time.

chunks.heading: Position 5: First mover
chunks.text:
- Be first to discover a problem and claim a new market.
- Example: Slack, which pioneered chat-based team collaboration. Discord and Microsoft Teams have far more users, yet Slack is still seen as the industry standard.
- Con 1: you probably have to educate the market about a problem people may not know they have, which is "painfully difficult."
- Con 2: as the first mover you make all the mistakes, and competitors learn from them without taking the same hit.

chunks.heading: Position 6: Niche
chunks.text:
- Solve a problem for a very specific, small market segment and tailor the tool to that user.
- Example: Oberlo, at its core an inventory management system tailored to dropshipping businesses using Shopify. It served that narrow segment until Shopify acquired it and folded it in.
- Simon calls this one of the best, most tried-and-tested positions, and "probably the best position" for a small indie SaaS.
- His advice: find a small group of users and build for them. Don't worry that big players solve the same problem, because you customize the whole platform for that group.
- Con: it can cap growth. You may later have to expand to a bigger market, which can alienate your original core users.

chunks.heading: Positions 7 and 8: Privacy first and integrations
chunks.text:
**Privacy first**
- Solve a problem while prioritizing data privacy and security above all else.
- Examples: Bam Analytics, a simple privacy-first alternative to Google Analytics that is very popular. n8n markets self-hosting as a way to protect data by deploying on-prem.
- Cons: you can lock yourself into a market segment that is too small. As privacy concerns grow, alternatives may adopt the same practices and outcompete you.

**Integrations**
- Position as the tool with the most third-party integrations. For some users it is the final drop that wins them over.
- Example: Zapier, which boasts 6,000 integrations, more than competitors like Make and IFTTT.
- Pro: clearly beneficial where integrations are central to the service.
- Con: competitors can catch up by offering the same integrations, so it is hard to protect.

chunks.heading: Positioning takeaways
chunks.text:
- These eight are popular positions, not the only ones. New ones appear as markets evolve.
- A current example he gives, unique to the big AI players: "who can burn the most cash by offering the most AI requests for a fixed monthly fee."
- Reflection questions he poses: where does your product fit in, and how do you stand out?
- He says positioning is hard, and certain product types make it much harder. He says there are AI SaaS products he would avoid building entirely, and points to a separate video for that.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon Høiberg walks through five common SaaS founder mistakes drawn from building FeedHive: underpricing, poor execution of the build-measure-learn loop, fearing existing markets, staying in your comfort zone, and neglecting marketing. He offers a concrete "lean pricing" method and argues distribution beats product quality.

chunks.heading: Pricing: why $5/month was a mistake and how "lean pricing" works
chunks.text:
- Simon launched his social media marketing SaaS FeedHive with a price of $5 per month, reasoning that "a lower price and a better product" would make everyone come.
- He calls this wrong for two reasons:
  - Cost: FeedHive is a low-touch product (users sign up themselves) but integrates with third-party social platforms, so bugs and failures are inevitable. That demands solid customer support, which costs money. It also operates in a super competitive market, so growing fully organically without substantial marketing spend is unrealistic. $5 per user per month can't fund that.
  - Perception: when a product prices itself far below competitors, the first thought is "that is a shitty product." Most people won't believe a claim that it's also better.
- He warns against the opposite trap too. Some SaaS gurus say raising prices fixes everything; it doesn't. Products that position as "exclusive and premium" with prices twice as high as established competitors, without actually being premium (which most early products aren't), will backfire.

chunks.heading: Lean pricing: raise average revenue per user 5% a month until you meet resistance
chunks.text:
- Start at a reasonable price point, a little below your biggest competitors, but not too much.
- Then aim to increase average revenue per user (ARPU) by 5% each month until you meet resistance.
- Targeting ARPU rather than the sticker price gives more room to experiment. Levers:
  - Reduce the discount for yearly sign-ups, or nudge more users toward monthly billing (trade-off: may hurt retention).
  - Push users to a higher-priced tier by adding benefits and features, or by adjusting the price gap between plans.
  - Add a more expensive plan at the top to act as a pricing anchor.
  - Raise prices outright.
- Resistance shows up as stagnating or falling new sign-ups, or people telling you it's too pricey compared to competitors.
- He suggests a spreadsheet to calculate how much churn you can accept from a price increase while still growing overall revenue.

chunks.heading: Execution: Build-Measure-Learn and the two ways founders break it
chunks.text:
- Simon frames good execution around the loop from Eric Ries's *The Lean Startup*: build, measure, learn. A short feedback loop lets you create something, test it, measure effectiveness, adapt, and iterate.
- Failure modes:
  - **Stuck in learning:** endless research, trying to back everything with data, analysis paralysis. Founders rely on public data rather than their own, build a long-term plan, and never create anything, so they can't tell whether the idea works in their context.
  - **Stuck in building:** common among technical founders. They plan "just an MVP," a few hours turns into weeks or three months of coding, and no user has seen it. They have drifted far in one unvalidated direction, and launch day is usually disappointing.
  - **Over-execution (lottery playing):** build, launch, and if it doesn't catch on, start over with something new instead of adapting. They iterate only on the build step. He calls it "throwing pasta everywhere and hoping that something will eventually stick." Some indie-hacker influencers promote this and a few won millions, but he calls them "lottery winners" and not an approach to model.
- His recommended middle path:
  1. Do shallow initial research.
  2. Set initial goals and write a hypothesis for how you'll reach them.
  3. Build something quickly and get it in front of users.
  4. Compare results against the goals (you probably missed them, above or below).
  5. Hold results against your initial assumptions, adapt, and repeat.

chunks.heading: Don't fear existing markets and big competitors
chunks.text:
- Many founders think a successful SaaS must be groundbreaking, like Airbnb, Uber, Tinder or Bolt, which created new markets. Simon says disrupting the market is needed only if you want to build and IPO a unicorn.
- For a small SaaS doing a few million a year, finding huge competitors is "a super good sign": the market is big, users are already looking for a solution, and you've skipped much of the market research and initial validation.
- Proof from FeedHive, which entered a market with a handful of huge competitors plus hundreds of small ones:
  - More than 10,000 users on the platform.
  - Turning over more than $300,000 a year.
  - Growing around 10 to 15% every month (as stated in the talk).
  - Winning users from the biggest competitors every day, because those tools are "old and clunky," built on outdated technology.
- His angle: solve the same problem with less friction and adapt faster to new features and changes on the social platforms.

chunks.heading: Leave your comfort zone and do the hard thing
chunks.text:
- Founders tend to keep working on what they're already good at:
  - Developers and product people keep adding one more feature or making things faster, when deep down the missing piece is marketing.
  - Designers keep redesigning the landing page or polishing the product, while the core doesn't solve the user's problem well.
  - Marketers keep optimizing funnels, running tests and building multi-channel retargeting campaigns, while the product neither looks good nor solves the core problem.
- His view: staying in your comfort zone is never the solution, and with today's tools there are "absolutely no excuses." Developers can learn marketing from YouTube; marketers can learn enough to build with no-code and low-code tools; designers can learn both.
- If you truly can't move out of your zone, find a co-founder with the same stakes. He warns against outsourcing the parts you're bad at: "it's a trap I can almost guarantee."

chunks.heading: "A good product sells itself" is a myth: you need a go-to-market strategy
chunks.text:
- Most SaaS founders are technical, and many have a barrier to marketing. Some are simply too product-centric; others feel entitled, hate being marketed at, and think marketing is beneath them. Telling yourself you don't need marketing is "the one and single perfect way to set yourself up for a huge failure."
- No-code tools (Webflow, Bubble) and libraries (React, Tailwind, Chakra UI) make great products easy to build, so almost everyone can build a high-quality one. A better product is therefore not a competitive advantage.
- What he rarely sees is founders with a clear go-to-market strategy, distribution channels nailed down, and a scale plan. He means an actual long-term strategy, "not just we're gonna launch on Product Hunt."
- His claim: founders with this will win "even if they have a shittier product than you."
- He admits making all these mistakes himself; his first SaaS attempt "failed miserably," and FeedHive was his second.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon explains the three-part playbook behind FeedHive's first $1,000 MRR in about a month: build a social presence first, co-build the product with a closed group of early adopters, and build in public as a marketing strategy. He launched with a single tweet and no Product Hunt, Hacker News, or TechCrunch.

chunks.heading: Simon's three-tactic path to $1,000 MRR in 30 days
chunks.text:
- Simon cites public Indie Hackers data: bootstrapped SaaS takes on average nine months to reach $1,000 MRR, and five months already counts as an outlier. He notes the dataset was built by one individual creator and was small, so it should be taken "with a grain of salt", but he doesn't think the results are way off.
- His claim: almost all successful bootstrapped SaaS founders do three things consistently: build a social media presence, find early adopters to build with, and build in public.
- His own result with FeedHive: $300 MRR in the first 24 hours after launch, the first $1,000 MRR after about a month, then another $1,000 MRR added every month for the next year.
- He says this happened with no big Product Hunt launch, no Hacker News front page and no TechCrunch coverage. The launch was a single tweet, backed by the audience, the early adopters and the content he had already built.
- He adds that you still need a SaaS idea that actually works, otherwise the tactics are wasted.
