chunks.heading: Tactic 1: Build a social media presence before building the product
chunks.text:
- Simon's examples of bootstrapped founders who are very active on social media and share valuable content: Arvid (FeedbackPanda, bootstrapped to $50,000 MRR before selling), Mike (Upvoty, over $30,000 MRR and growing fast), and Tony (BlackMagic, $8,000 MRR within months of starting earlier that year).
- He argues it is less difficult than people think and takes patience, consistency and simply getting started.
- His own start was low-budget: videos shot on a phone, normal indoor lamps, and a laptop placed slightly behind the camera as a teleprompter. They were posted on Twitter and people still liked them. He barely got any likes at first and kept going, focusing on creating value.
- His steps:
  - Pick a platform; he suggests Twitter or LinkedIn.
  - Post daily, one to two posts.
  - Pick a topic you want to be known for. It doesn't have to relate to your startup, but you should be able to see yourself posting about it long term.
  - Make a free Canva account and use image templates to spice up content.
  - Schedule content ahead of time (he uses FeedHive, his own startup) so you don't spend all your time on social media.
- Proof point: he grew a following of more than 200,000 people across four platforms in a little under two years, and built the first version of FeedHive while building his own presence.
- Don't monetize the audience for a long time. No affiliate links, no ebook, no course. "Just keep sharing valuable content without asking for anything in return, no strings attached."
- Use the time to build authority, credibility, and connections with other creators and entrepreneurs. He says social media is "just as much about networking and building relationships as it is about creating content."

chunks.heading: Tactic 2: Find early adopters and build the product with them
chunks.text:
- Order of operations: while building an audience, connect with other creators who have their own personal brands and audiences. Then, before putting an MVP together, find early adopters.
- The key distinction: "You need users to build your product with, not for."
- How to do it:
  - Find a group of people interested in what you plan to build.
  - Invite them into a closed chat group or Discord server.
  - Include them in all decisions, big and small. You still build it, but they help shape the product from day one.
- Two benefits:
  - You are much more likely to build something users actually want.
  - You get advocates from day one. Users who feel part of the project are loyal, and if they are creators and entrepreneurs with their own audiences, they multiply your reach on launch day.
- What he did with FeedHive: the first users came in when the product was "a text field on a grey website and a few buttons", buggy and ugly. He built the MVP for almost two months with a closed group, discussing features, pricing and market positioning daily.
- He says that building alone on gut feeling would have "completely missed the mark."
- Common founder mistake: building far ahead without knowing who it is for, and treating validation as a few people saying "sure, that sounds great" after hearing the idea once. His rule: "You need to keep validating your product."
- The group later grew into a Facebook group of more than 1,000 members. The purpose is unchanged: building the product in close collaboration with the community, which still takes part in decisions on FeedHive's direction.

chunks.heading: Tactic 3: Building in public as a social media marketing strategy
chunks.text:
- Simon's definition: "creating content from your journey of building a startup." He acknowledges others feel strongly about the open startup movement and says he is only sharing his own perspective.
- He frames it as a social media marketing strategy: create content that is interesting and valuable to your audience, which drives awareness, leads and subscribers to your SaaS.
- No obligations: you don't have to share revenue numbers, employee pay, or any secrets or insights you think are business critical.
- What to share:
  - The ups and downs of running a startup and the process of creating.
  - Tips, advice, learnings and findings as they come in.
  - The unique, "juicy" parts, not boring generic startup advice.
- Be honest and open. He says people connect better with "realistic and small rather than extraordinary and mind-blowing", so don't try to impress anyone. People want something realistic that motivates them to feel they could do it too.
- His timing: he started sharing about FeedHive a month before it went live, and the early adopter group started doing the same. That combination produced the 24-hour launch result of $300 MRR.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon breaks down his first e-book launch: 16 hours writing, 24 hours on website, email and marketing, $531 spent, 480 copies sold in week one. His thesis is that e-book success comes from distribution and pre-built audience, not writing, so pick a topic you know cold and spend your energy on acquisition channels.

chunks.heading: Why most ebooks and info products sell poorly (and what top sellers do differently)
chunks.text:
- Simon says the typical model is: pick a topic, spend hours researching, writing and proofreading, upload to Coursera, Udemy or Gumroad, share the link on social media, and make almost no money.
- He argues the problem is that creators pour effort into writing and leave sales "up to random chance."
- People like West Boss, Adam Marthan and Kent C. Dodds make millions on ebooks and courses. Simon says that isn't just because they have big followings. They have followings and sell well for the same reason: they are good at marketing, distribution and selling.
- Top sellers prepare every launch for a long time:
  - They spend years building community and owning their sales channels.
  - They build email lists, attend conferences and spread awareness.
  - They run paid ads and create affiliate programs.
  - Most importantly, they gave away knowledge for free for a long time before asking for money.
- He notes some influencers with 20,000+ followers make under $500 on an ebook launch, while others make thousands in pre-sales.
- His point: you don't need millions. A smaller, realistic result (like his) is still very good, and anyone can do it with work.

chunks.heading: Simon's results: $7,500 in week one, about $2,500 per month ongoing
chunks.text:
- Product: "JavaScript in the Industry," a collection of best practices and tips for writing industry-level JavaScript, based on real-world experience. It is 71 pages with many illustrations.
- Simon is a software developer and startup CEO who previously worked in sales and as a freelance engineer.
- First week: he sold 480 copies. Launch price was $19, with a $9 offer for a group of selected people.
- Revenue and costs:
  - Gross revenue: just under $8,000 (the transcript's figure is garbled, so treat the exact gross as unclear).
  - Expenses: $531 total.
  - Profit: roughly $7,450 after expenses and a few fees. He frames it as "more than $7,500 in the first week of sales."
- The book still earns around $2,500 per month.
- It was his first ebook, and he wasn't a full-time ebook author.

chunks.heading: Budget and time breakdown
chunks.text:
Expenses ($531 total):
- $47 for an ebook cover (Fiverr).
- $52 for proofreading for grammar and typos (Fiverr). English isn't his native language.
- $182 to have the ebook promoted on a popular Instagram account with almost a million followers.
- About $250 on paid ads on Facebook and Twitter.

Time (about 40 hours total):
- About 16 hours writing the ebook.
- About 10 hours building a website with a Stripe checkout.
- About 4 hours on launch emails and drip sequences.
- About 4 hours on extra marketing (arranging and creating the Instagram promoted post, a few ad hoc tasks).

Takeaway: he spent more time on marketing and distribution than on writing the book. He says you can launch with no spend, but a modest budget gets you further.

chunks.heading: Pick a topic you could write in your sleep
chunks.text:
- Simon's first tip: don't use the ebook as a chance to learn something new. He calls it "probably the worst occasion you can pick."
- You're writing to sell. You're doing business, so don't wear yourself down mentally learning a new subject.
- Choose a topic so familiar you could "almost write an ebook about it in your sleep." The book should "write itself."
- His example: the JavaScript book took only 16 hours because he'd worked with the topic for about 10 years and didn't have to look anything up. It still got incredible feedback.
- Save your energy for marketing. Most people (especially in tech) haven't done much marketing, so that's where to challenge yourself.

chunks.heading: Pick your acquisition channels before you write
chunks.text:
Before writing, ask: what are your acquisition channels, and how will you reach people? He says one post on your own profile won't cut it, even with thousands of followers. Options he covers:

- **Influencer marketing:**
  - Set up agreements with influencers in your niche, ideally before you write.
  - Reach out to ones you know, or cold-pitch ones you don't for a sponsor deal.
  - Pay a fixed price per promoted post, or offer a cut of each sale they produce.
  - Line up 10 or more professional influencers in the niche in advance and keep them in the loop.
- **Pre-launch:**
  - Charge for the product at a discount before it's done.
  - It tests demand: if almost nobody buys at pre-launch, it may not be worth building.
  - It lets you build hype. Spend one to two months sharing process details, screenshots and small bits before launch.
  - Even with an existing audience, one "I launched an ebook" post isn't enough.
- **Retargeting existing leads (his personal favorite):**
  - See the free lead-magnet section below.
- **Paid ads:**
  - Easy to set up and reliable. Facebook (Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, WhatsApp) and Google (YouTube and many web pages) cover almost the whole internet and are good at targeting.
  - He cites surveys showing people are less negative toward ads and increasingly buy from them.
  - It's relatively cheap. You don't need a million-dollar budget, just a small initial amount for the platform to tune in on an audience.
- Settle on one or two channels you believe will convert. More channels don't necessarily raise conversion, and they make the data obscure and the whole thing unmanageable.

chunks.heading: Give a free ebook first to build trust and an email list
chunks.text:
- Three months before launching the paid book, Simon made a quick free ebook. He compiled the code snippets he'd shared on Twitter and LinkedIn over a year. It took less than two hours.
- More than 10,000 people picked it up over the next three months.
- Why it works:
  - **Authority:** many people see your writing quality without paying.
  - **Emails:** you collect leads. He imagines "a list of 10,000 qualified leads laying around the day you want to launch."
- He calls email marketing "super underrated in 2021" and says it has one of the highest click-through rates of any medium.
- Per the teaser at the end, a four-email drip sequence generated more than two-thirds of all sales (details were promised in part two, not covered here).

chunks.heading: His launch playbook in summary
chunks.text:
1. Gave a free ebook away to build trust and authority and collect emails.
2. Created the paid ebook and a website with a Stripe integration.
3. Made agreements with a handful of big influencers in the tech Twitter space to retweet the launch announcement.
4. Paid one large Instagram influencer to promote the ebook.
5. Sent a discounted offer to his email list.
6. Set up ad campaigns on Twitter, YouTube and Facebook.

Result: about $7,500 in sales in the first 7 days, and about $2,500 per month afterward. The detailed email drip, conversion campaigns and launch post were deferred to a part two.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon explains how he runs FeedHive, LinkDrip, a YouTube channel and a small team without burnout. He covers building reusable blocks, picking a pre-validated market and validating with 30 hand-picked users, using lifetime deals carefully, and replacing funnels with an ecosystem of products and content.

chunks.heading: Building reusable systems so one person can run several businesses
chunks.text:
- Simon treats every output as a building block. After each YouTube video he strips it apart and asks whether any part can become a reusable asset or a checklist that makes the next one faster. His rule: "every time I put something out there, there needs to be something more to it than just the result."
- He got the habit from software: turn something you built into a modular package (NPM, Gradle) instead of one-off code. He says few developers, even senior ones, do it, and he used it as a freelancer to deliver faster for clients, never reusing code owned by another client's project.
- Result: he works on "one thing" and it feeds the whole ecosystem. Because he did not start with everything at once but built each layer on the previous one, the output looks huge to outsiders.
- Example of the compounding in his YouTube workflow: a library of hundreds of short stock clips (him at a computer, with a mouse), thumbnail starter files in Photoshop, and a checklist-driven pipeline. The first 2-3 videos "took forever".
- He runs his channel on about 10 hours a week, including thumbnail, topic research, scripts, filming and editing, which he still does himself. He cautions that this sits on top of the building blocks and that a beginner should not expect 10 hours.

chunks.heading: Validating a SaaS in a crowded market with a small community
chunks.text:
- His first SaaS attempt, Sigmetic (GitHub-integrated performance tracking for software teams, inspired by sales leaderboards), failed. His lesson: he tried to innovate and imported thinking from his sales background that did not fit how engineers work.
- For FeedHive (social media scheduling, started a bit over two years before this 2023 interview) he did the opposite: pick a market that is already established and pre-validated. He listed email marketing, social media management and project management as candidates, noting that project management still produced new winners (Monday, ClickUp) despite old incumbents.
- His reasoning: if the market is large enough, a small slice of users will prefer your tool because of small differences. He calls it risky but workable. LinkDrip (link management with automation) followed the same logic: competitors were adding simple link shorteners to their tools, so he went deeper into Zapier/Airtable-style customizable automation.
- Validation steps for FeedHive:
  - After about 6 months of building an audience on Twitter, he asked people in closed chat groups why they were not scheduling their tweets.
  - Complaints: Buffer and HootSuite felt old and unmaintained; Hypefury had excellent UI/UX but did not match what they wanted. One concrete gap: a calendar view for the queue instead of a list queue.
  - He formed a Twitter group chat of about 30 of those users and built "in secret" for around two months, talking to them daily with questions like "how should this be?".
  - He treated the 30 as representing a small customer segment inside a bigger market, not guessing.

chunks.heading: Getting into private communities through audience, not outreach
chunks.text:
- Asked how he got into closed groups, he says there was no strategy: he had about 30,000 followers on Twitter by the time he started FeedHive, after about six months of being active.
- Other creators invited him into small Twitter groups because his content resonated. He only started a group himself for the FeedHive validation.
- His takeaway: first be active online and build an audience; community access follows. Arvid's phrasing, which Simon confirms: build "opportunity surface" by showing up.

chunks.heading: Lifetime deals: when they work and how to run them
chunks.text:
- He sold an early-access lifetime deal for LinkDrip, framed explicitly as part of validating interest before the product was fully built (a quick proof of concept only). He notes "nothing beats having people pick up their credit card and extra pay" as validation, and that it brings cash up front.
- Do it on a limited basis; he does not see lifetime deals as a way to build a long-term sustainable business, especially with ongoing server and support costs.
- Before launching, "make that Excel sheet" and check the finances. Hosting can be engineered to be very cheap and support can be made self-serve. Lifetime users also churn. Avoid a lifetime deal if each user carries high variable cost, e.g. AI/OpenAI usage, which can get expensive fast.
- Biggest problem in his view is reputation: a lifetime deal signals financial trouble. So communicate clearly why it is limited and why you are doing it, otherwise "people start talking".
- His definition of "lifetime": access for as long as the product exists.

chunks.heading: Letting customers leave: export and portability as a trust signal
chunks.text:
- LinkDrip lets users change a link's destination instantly, so printed links and QR codes stay alive. It can also A/B test (a dice roll between destinations) or change the destination after a set number of clicks or a certain time.
- He plans (not fully in place at the time) JSON and CSV export of links so customers can move to another redirect service. He argues knowing your data is yours can be a deciding factor for signing up.
- Caveat: the link's domain is tied to the service, so for print he recommends QR codes, which can be moved.
- Arvid adds the framing, which Simon agrees with: giving customers a way out builds trust compared with locking them in.

chunks.heading: Building in public as an ecosystem, not a funnel
chunks.text:
- Simon rejects classic funnel thinking where every post pushes people down one path to one product. He sees an "ecosystem" or "playground": hours of free content (YouTube, Twitter), plus products they may stumble on: FeedHive, LinkDrip, a newly acquired small SaaS called Tiny QE, info products, and the YouTube channel itself.
- Because of this he is relaxed about sharing numbers that might look unflattering. People who drop off one product may find another, so no audience member is "wasted". He treats the audience as reusable building blocks too.
- He is more cautious for founders who are all-in on one brand-owned product, because sharing there can hurt the single business.
- Safe-to-fail framing: he sits between "all-in" and "tiny small bets". He asks of every new bet "does this fit into the web?" If LinkDrip failed, it would still yield YouTube content and cross-pollinate other products. Failures are content too.
- He also plans for the worst case: if his products went down, he wants an audience he can invite into a new branch of the ecosystem.

chunks.heading: Running a YouTube channel that teaches rather than converts
chunks.text:
- He admits the channel works as a marketing channel and generates a significant number of leads for FeedHive, LinkDrip and Tiny QE. But the purpose when making content is to empower people intimidated by SaaS: no VC money, no investors needed, you can build a micro SaaS from home alongside a job.
- He believes channels where every video has an ulterior sign-up motive have slower growth; he avoids heavy funneling.
- Content rule: include things people cannot find elsewhere, grounded in his own experience, rather than repackaging information from the internet. Topics are "100% lesson-driven" from what he is doing, so he never runs out of ideas.
- Production: he writes scripts for five videos at a time, shoots in one weekend (about 10-12 videos' worth of footage), and schedules almost three months ahead. He has killed already-produced videos when he learned something that made the advice outdated.

chunks.heading: Avoiding burnout: joy-driven work, async teams, an empty calendar
chunks.text:
- His philosophy is "joy driven": he gamifies life around intrinsic motivation, not discipline, saying motivation can be a strong fuel for handling hard situations. He thinks people burn out from being forced to do work whose benefit is unclear, not from working a lot.
- His calendar is nearly empty: he works in his own flow and picks tasks he is excited about that day, keeping tasks as independent as possible.
- Team of five, with a culture of asynchronous written work and no meetings. He avoids interrupting team members, since "rarely" is anything too important to write in Slack.
- When something goes wrong he can drop everything for firefighting because nothing is scheduled. FeedHive depends on third-party social APIs that fail often, producing support tickets from frustrated users. He steps in himself to protect the support team, since they did not sign up for crisis management and he did.
- Each time he is forced to push through something he dislikes, he reflects and designs a process to prevent it recurring, for himself and for his team.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Simon introduces "Flights," a ceremoniless agile framework for startups and SaaS teams working under extreme uncertainty. Instead of fixed-length sprints and meetings, work ships in continuous, overlapping flights with a pilot, an ETA, and an "Emergency Landing" escape hatch so nobody stays blocked.

chunks.heading: Flights: a continuous, ceremoniless agile framework
chunks.text:
Simon created Flights while working on FeedHive. He describes it as a "new, lightweight, ceremoniless agile framework to deliver features in a lean and continuous way."

- **Lightweight:** very few predefined ground rules, implementable in many ways. Teams don't need to follow the rules fully; they can adopt the core principles on top of existing practices and still benefit.
- **Ceremoniless:** no daily stand-ups, no retrospectives, no sprint planning. He acknowledges teams still need to align, plan and reflect, but says that should be done however best suits the team, outside the framework.
- **Continuous vs. iterative:** Flights favors continuous delivery over the iterations used by Scrum and Kanban. Iterations can help bigger software organizations with large teams. For startups, SaaS development and teams working under "extreme uncertainty," he argues a continuous approach is far more beneficial.

chunks.heading: What a flight is: sprint meets epic
chunks.text:
- A flight is a merge of a sprint and an epic: a group of related tasks with its own task board.
- When you book a flight, you add tasks to it. Tasks can be anything that needs doing and aren't restricted to Scrum-style "User Stories."
- Rule of thumb: book a flight with tasks that belong together, depend on each other, or are expected to land at the same time. Unrelated tasks can be added if there's "room for it."
- The board has at least: To Do, In Progress, Done, Canceled.

chunks.heading: ETA instead of fixed length
chunks.text:
- A flight has no fixed length (like 2 weeks). It has an ETA, set when the flight is created.
- The aim is to land on time.
- "Tailwind" means the flight arrives early; "turbulence" means it is delayed.

chunks.heading: Roles: pilot, co-pilot, staff
chunks.text:
- **Pilot:** any team member. Responsible for landing the flight smoothly in production, on time. Keeps the overview and delegates tasks to staff.
- **Co-pilot:** supports the pilot.
- **Staff:** anyone on the team working on the flight's tasks.

chunks.heading: Ground rules and concurrency
chunks.text:
- A flight must have a pilot.
- A developer can be pilot on only one flight at a time, but can be co-pilot or staff on another meanwhile.
- Developers can be staff on multiple flights at once.
- Concurrent flights are naturally capped by the number of developers who can act as pilots. Optionally, a team can set a limit on flights "in the air" at once.
- Multiple flights can fly in parallel and overlap, so teams aren't forced to "finish" one sprint before starting the next.
- Tip: always have a flight booked and prepared for takeoff, so when one lands early and frees up a pilot and staff, work can start immediately.

chunks.heading: Emergency landing
chunks.text:
- If a flight becomes extremely delayed or won't reach its destination, keeping it in the air "blocks" a pilot, which he wants to avoid.
- For transparency, close the flight even with unfinished tasks so the pilot and staff become available for other work.
- An "Emergency Landing" is formally closing the flight, moving its tasks back to the backlog, and flagging it "Emergency Landed" somewhere visible to the team.

I solved OpenClaw's memory issue.
(At least, this is the best solution I tried so far).

And yes. Big surprise.
I solved it using RAG.

All major models can now take millions of tokens as context. But the issue remains...

The undisputed number #1 reason your agent is stupid and forgets simple things is because you're bloating context.

So here's how I solved it with OpenClaw.

1️⃣ I installed PostgreSQL + pgvetor
I run my OpenClaw on a Hetzner server, so I installed the database + pgvector extension directly on here.

2️⃣ Create a search tool
Ask your agent to create a search tool for itself.

Every time you ask it to remember something, it should:
- Label the memory
- Create a vector from the label
- Store the label, vector, and raw text in the database

Every time it's asked something it doesn't know, the FIRST thing it should always do is to use the search tool.

3️⃣ Memory CRON/heartbeat
The agent can write to its memory file on-the-go.
Consider this short-term memory.

On a scheduled CRON (or heartbeat), it should "flush" its own short-term memory and store it in the database.

Now, on every new session, the agent has very little context. The most important one is the description of using the search tool to enhance itself based on the task it's given.

✨ Major upsides

- MUCH better memory
- MUCH smarter
- MUCH less token-greedy

👎 Major downsides

- More moving parts
- Complex for non-devs
- Ongoing maintenance

Still. Benefits outweigh the cons here.

- OpenClaw itself
- PostgreSQL + pgvector
- n8n (for API proxies/security)

A quick example from my SaaS:

On average, it cost $85-$95 to convert a user, and the most common user we get is a $29/m subscription.

So for $100/day we can buy 1 new $29/m subscriber/day (to keep the numbers nice and even).

This means we can add $870 of new MRR every month by paying $3000 in ads.

After roughly 3.5 months, that ad spend breaks even and becomes profitable.

This is actually really good. Many ads-led SaaS has a buy-back period that's much longer, typically +12 months.

The issue is that you need to frontload the expense. If your finances are so tight that $3000 in ads need to immediately break even and return a profit, you cannot use ads to grow this way.

I know a lot of founders want to get started with ads but struggle to make them work.

One "brutal" reality I just want to share:
$100/day is bare minimum.

This is the budget I use for small tests. For winning campaigns, you want a budget that's significantly higher than this.

So if your business currently can't support at least $100/day, ads are probably not gonna work.

Your data pool is gonna be too small to conclude anything on ad experiments and even if you get some sales it'll be more like lottery than properly targeted exposure.

$20/day is a waste of time and energy. Spend your efforts elsewhere in the early stage, then use ads to amplify once you have better cashflow.

Users from ads generally pay more and churn less. They are an overall better, more healthy type of users.

The catch is: They are significantly harder to convert.

But it's actually a good thing. It humbles you in the best way possible.

When you turn away from this tiny creator bubble on Twitter/LinkedIn/YouTube and start pointing at total strangers out there - real users, with real businesses, and a real problem to solve, who don't care how many followers you have or how much ass you're shaking on social - you'll learn a lot about how strong your positioning is, how well your landing page actually converts, how good your product truly is.

I know many creators here claim that "ads don't work" - but it's mostly a symptom that their business is weak. Either poorly positioned or just not a very competitive/appealing product.

One solution is to keep shaking ass, of course. And that's fine - but if you want a more mature business, I suggest start running ads, cold calling, or cold emailing people. 

Get the experience of selling to total strangers, not fans.
